The BASS DR2 catalog provides a wealth of optical spectroscopy data, comprising 1425 newly acquired or updated spectra of 858 hard X-ray selected Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN). Among the spectra released in DR2, 1181 are made publicly available for the first time. An extensive range of optical data, encompassing high-resolution capabilities and broad wavelength coverage, is now available. Furthermore, AGN counterparts have been reassigned throughout the entire dataset and key concerns in AGN population studies have been reassessed, with novel discoveries made possible through 44 initial redshift determinations, 780 black hole mass, and accretion rate estimates. With the current data, spectroscopic information is now completely available for each AGN (100%), nearly 100% contain precise redshift data, and roughly 96% exhibit precise measurements of unbeamed AGN masses, making this hard X-ray selected AGN sample the most exhaustive and diverse in its class, spanning several orders of magnitude in key variables, such as Eddington ratio, black hole mass, and bolometric luminosity.

The distortion of galaxy power spectrum and bispectrum signals by unusual velocities and relativistic effects from a warped spacetime is a significant issue. Furthermore, studies on correlation functions of tracers in Fourier space typically make the simplifying assumption that line-of-sight vectors are parallel. In this research, it is demonstrated that a straightforward method can be used to quickly estimate beyond parallel-plane corrections to the power spectrum and bispectrum, taking into account relativistic context and wide-angle considerations. It has also been shown that the evolution of linear matter density fluctuations in a relativistic framework can be derived through a simple approach. By comparing wide-angle contributions to multipoles of the galaxy power spectrum with non-integrated and integrated relativistic corrections, it is found that they could possibly contaminate local fNL measurements by a few orders of magnitude. Furthermore, calculations have been performed for the effects of nonlinear terms on one-loop order. It has also been observed that wide-angle effects can result in imaginary, odd-parity multipoles of the galaxy bispectrum, such as dipole, octupole, etc. These contributions were calculated, and a new method for estimating the leading order bispectrum dipole from data using a symmetric line-of-sight definition has been developed. The leading order corrections to multipoles of real parallel-plane bispectrum multipoles have also been computed, revealing an apparent local fNL effect of around unity order.

This study derives lower and upper bounds for the times of solution blow-up in systems driven by two-dimensional fractional Brownian motion, governed by semilinear stochastic partial differential equations. By employing associated random partial differential equations and a formula introduced by Yor, lower and upper bounds are obtained under certain assumptions for the blow-up time of the solution. Furthermore, an estimate for solutions exhibiting finite-time blow-up is obtained by adjusting specific parameters, and a lower bound for the likelihood of blow-up solutions is calculated using Malliavin calculus.

For practical use cases in high-risk situations, there is a growing need for Deep Learning predictions that include reliable confidence measures. The Conformal Prediction framework can provide a certain level of prediction error, but its effectiveness is limited by computational inefficiencies that make it impractical for use with large datasets. In response, we introduce a new conformal loss function that streamlines the Conformal Prediction approach into a single step, allowing Deep Learning models to directly link input data to their respective conformal p-values by penalizing deviations from the expected CP distribution. By comparing the performance of this novel function against a widely accepted variant, our evaluation demonstrates substantial time savings of up to 86% on the MNIST dataset and comparable efficiency and validity for binary and multi-class classification tasks.

Our universe contains a significant amount of dark matter, with axions being a leading candidate. By employing the magnetization effect induced by axions within a magnetic rod in combination with the Faraday effect, the existing technology enables the potential discovery of axions within the $500$ to $5000~\mu$eV mass range. This includes the $3500~\mu$eV and higher portion that is presently beyond experimental reach, accessible with this technique in just one year. By placing a magnetic rod inside a precision optical cavity, the light interaction is prolonged, thereby amplifying the impact of the Faraday effect on the light. This process generates a notable and clear signal, as the light polarization is altered significantly. By employing a dc magnetic field, the technique selects specific axion masses. Photons in the optical range are then counted with high accuracy using a sensitive and efficient photon detector, ideally situated in an ideal low-noise setting. Furthermore, the setup also allows for optical interferometric methods to gather spectral information on the targeted axions.

The nonlocal BMS charges for a massless scalar field in 2+1 dimensions are represented in terms of polyharmonic operator Green functions. By leveraging Green function properties, we explore the asymptotic field behavior, ensuring the existence of charges, and confirm the realization of a 2+1 BMS algebra within the canonical phase space. Moreover, we investigate configuration space transformations, finding the algebra only closes after including skew-symmetric equations of motion combinations. This formulation using Green functions enables a more versatile approach applicable to higher dimensions and systems.

In 2D gated Rashba materials, electron pairs with specific properties known as bound electron pairs (BEPs) develop. This development stems from two primary factors: the interactions of the Coulomb fields between paired electrons and the unique structure of the energy bands that lead to an unusual relationship between paired electrons, characterized by a negative combined mass. This concept was modeled and considered in the context of the four-band Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang framework that accounts for the effects of the charges on a gate on the system. Notably, BEPs show a range of energy values that are influenced by the voltage of the gate and extend over the entirety of the two-particle energy gap. Additionally, despite being disrupted by the interactions with their environment, BEPs still possess magnetic properties due to the orbiting movement of the paired electrons and this attribute is controlled by adjusting the voltage of the gate.

The relationship between a gauge theory's confinement scale $\Lambda_c$ and the Hubble scale $H$ in a background de Sitter space has been studied for a holographic model using the Karch-Randall framework, based on the swampland principles that necessitate $\Lambda_c \gtrsim H$ for Festina Lente compliance. The research finds that purely gravitational explanations can yield unstable de Sitter solutions but only allow a limited hierarchy between other parameters. However, with a scalar sector incorporated into the model, it's possible to achieve metastable de Sitter minima while adhering to the requirements for Festina Lente, imposing further restrictions on the parameters. Nonetheless, if Festina Lente imposes a constraint within a specific parameter range, this minimum de Sitter solution may be on the cusp of collapse, invalidating its applicability. The study also investigates the lasting effects of this decay and the potential contradictions with related swampland conjectures, concluding no conflicts are found. Ultimately, this research validates the consistency and practicality of the Karch-Randall model and sheds new light on the Festina Lente requirements for holographic theories, as well as its implications in conjunction with other swampland conjectures.

Over the last few years, various domain generalization (DG) methods have been developed, achieving promising results; nearly all these methods, however, rely on convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Meanwhile, vision transformers (ViTs), which are gaining ground on traditional benchmarks based on independent and identically distributed data assumptions, still lack a thorough analysis regarding their DG capabilities, casting doubt on their deployment in real-world applications. Our work addresses this issue by exploring ViTs for domain generalization tasks. Like CNNs, ViTs face challenges in handling out-of-distribution data due to their tendency to overfit to specific source domains. We develop a simple, parameter-free DG approach inspired by ViTs' modular structure, referred to as self-distillation for ViTs. It helps mitigate overfitting by leveraging non-zero entropy guidance signals for intermediate transformer blocks. Our proposed method is adaptable to multiple ViT variants and integrates seamlessly with existing models. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method in achieving significant performance gains compared to multiple DG baselines across various challenging datasets and demonstrate its superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art DG approaches. For reproducibility purposes, we have released our code along with pre-trained models at: https://github.com/maryam089/SDViT.

This research establishes convergence and acceleration theory for applying Anderson acceleration to Newton's method in solving nonlinear systems, where the Jacobian matrix becomes singular at the solution. It has been noted that standard Newton's algorithm exhibits linear convergence near the solution. Moreover, the combination of Newton's and Anderson's methods can accelerate the convergence without additional a priori information and with minimal computational overhead. Our analysis focuses on the performance of the Newton-Anderson algorithm for singular Jacobians and proposes a novel safeguarding approach. The efficacy of these convergence results is verified through the application to the Chandrasekhar H-equation and standard benchmark test cases.

This paper examines a holistic approach to cybersecurity protection by combining a unique simulation tool with models that use optimization for informed decision-making. A notable technique, dynamic causal Bayesian optimisation (DCBO), is evaluated for its potential to serve as a cybersecurity agent within a simulated network framework, making data-driven decisions to thwart a simulated adversary's attempts. Our research tests DCBO's capacity to optimise actions on specific network nodes, thus minimising the adverse impact of security breaches. In this study, we develop and showcase an integrated cybersecurity simulation system that provides valuable data for DCBO testing, and we present numerical findings that will inform future investigations in this area.

To evaluate lepton flavour universality, we've created a semi-inclusive ratio, 
$R_\Sigma$, for $\mu/e$ universality testing in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ processes 
at $e^+e^-$ facilities that produce $B$-mesons. Combining several decay channels,
this ratio provides optimal sensitivity to potential LFU violations caused by 
short-distance effects, and retains a straightforward theoretical explanation 
in case the measurement differs from the Standard Model prediction of unity, 
$R_\Sigma^{\rm SM}=1$.

This study aims to examine whether the topological invariant known as non-barotropic generalized cross helicity remains constant in non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics. Previous research focused on ideal scenarios involving barotropic and non-barotropic conditions. However, non-ideal cases were overlooked due to their complex mathematical nature, until now, where dissipative processes such as thermal conduction, finite electrical conductivity, and viscosity are considered. Utilizing an analytical approach, we derive expressions for the time derivative of cross helicity, and the results reveal that cross helicity is not conserved in non-ideal MHD and identify the specific processes impacting this invariant, along with the configurations where cross helicity remains preserved despite these dissipative processes.

We study the fractional Burgers equation, specifically $ \Delta^{\alpha/2} u + b\cdot
\nabla (u|u|^{(\alpha-1)/\beta})$, on the space of real numbers in d dimensions where d is greater than or equal to 2. Our focus is on finding a solution given a broad class of initial conditions which include functions that fall outside any given L^p space from 1 to infinity. In applying these general results to a specific initial condition, $u_0(x)=M|x|^{-\beta}$, we find that a self-similar solution exists under the conditions $1<\beta<d$ and explore its properties, including its level of smoothness, as well as asymptotic and gradient characteristics.

We conducted a pioneering cosmological study using a dataset of eROSITA clusters, sourced from the eROSITA Final Equatorial Depth Survey. This research focused on 455 clusters across the redshift range of 0.1 to 1.2, 177 of which were analyzed via the uniform weak-lensing mass constraints facilitated by the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey. We used an empirical approach to establish correlations between the cluster mass and various X-ray and optical characteristics, then applied these relationships to infer the selection biases in the eROSITA data. This method enabled us to directly determine the completeness of the eROSITA data by examining the richness distribution of the clusters, subsequently utilizing this knowledge to inform the cosmological analysis. We evaluated the reliability of our framework by simulating mock datasets, then applied it to the actual data in a blinded analysis, confirming the results with several consistency checks. Following the removal of this blindness, we obtained robust cosmological constraints for key parameters, finding them to be in alignment with prior studies at the $\lesssim$1σ confidence level. The implications of our findings span from the cosmological constants, $\Omega_m$ and $\sigma_8$, to the cosmology of dark energy, characterized by the $w$CDM model, yielding $w \approx -1.25$ in a $w$CDM model, respectively.

Using high-resolution numerical simulations, we investigated the statistical characteristics of the energy flux transfer rate to smaller scales for three distinct turbulent magnetohydrodynamic flows, differing in magnetic field strength and complexity. Our analysis of the energy cascade in both kinetic and magnetic domains revealed the contributions of different flux components to the energy dynamics. We found that the probability distribution of the energy flux displays a high propensity for extreme events, mirroring a pattern observed in hydrodynamic flows. Each term of the energy flux exhibited unique properties and showed a high degree of sensitivity to the type of flow being studied. Further analysis of the joint probability distribution of the energy flux and field gradients highlighted a significant correlation with magnetic field gradients, but also displayed significantly greater dispersion compared to hydrodynamic flows. Our results also indicate that the energy flux is influenced by the local amplitude of the magnetic field. These findings hold significant implications for subgrid scale models and their formulation, which we discuss further.

Autonomous vehicles and mobile robots often use multi-beam LiDAR sensors to collect series of three-dimensional depth maps or 3D range scans which provide scenes with a reduced level of coverage due to limitations of scanning resolution and obstructions within a scene. However, as the sensors move, each frame offers new views that fill gaps when accumulated together within a common reference frame leading to increased detail and density within a scene. Unfortunately, fast moving objects in a scanned scene can create misaligned points within frames and only reversing the scanner's own movements doesn't correct this inaccuracy. In this study, we are proposing the accumulation of multiple 3D depth maps in a single frame as an in-between representation of these LiDAR scan sequences, we are developing a technique which uses prior assumptions of outdoor street layouts including their geometry and fixed structures. Compared to present best methods of tracking these LiDAR scan sequences, we are proposing our approach aims at accurately combining 3D points into a single frame across objects. The results from this proposed technique show significant decrease in misaligned points within frames and these aligned frames provide great value to tasks involving mapping and 3D object reconstruction.

The BAT AGN Spectroscopic Survey's (BASS) purpose is to gather comprehensive data on supermassive black holes powering local active galaxies, encompassing various characteristics such as luminosity, mass, and surrounding environment.  We outline key aspects of BASS Data Release 2 (DR2), which constitutes a groundbreaking spectroscopic survey, encompassing over 1,400 unique spectra for 858 AGNs selected based on ultra-hard X-ray radiation across the sky, including obscured galaxies.  DR2 offers an extensive dataset, including precise redshift measurements and estimated black hole masses for nearly all targets, enabling researchers to address pivotal questions about supermassive black hole growth, their effects on nearby galaxies, and fundamental SMBH physics through the extensive DR2-based data and analyses provided here.

The James Webb Space Telescope's primary objective is to investigate the early stages of galaxy formation. A photometric analysis of extremely distant galaxies in the vicinity of the SMACS0723 galaxy cluster revealed a collection of exceptionally ancient galaxy candidates, which date back approximately 250 million years after the universe's inception, around z∼16. The research further identified a galaxy candidate at z∼ 12 and six at z∼ 9-11 through a combination of data from seven filters. By utilising Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) models to evaluate the candidates' robustness, we confirmed their photometric redshift estimates. The newly discovered galaxies exhibit typical luminosities, small sizes and are consistent with disk-like morphologies, which is consistent with expectations of L*. These high-redshift candidates displayed extremely blue UV continuum slopes, young ages ranging from 10-100 million years, and stellar masses equivalent to approximately 8.8 log10(M∗/M). The rapid accumulation of these stars signifies the early stages of galaxy formation, which JWST has effectively demonstrated, thereby allowing us to gain deeper insights into the early universe's structure and the evolution of galaxies.

The solution for a wormhole could be found by modifying the Einstein field equations
in a way that allows the null energy condition (NEC) to be breached. Wormholes
in the context of $\kappa(R,T)$ gravity have been described in two distinct
manners. Initially, we derived the shape function based on a redshift function
coupled with a linear equation of state. This representation was found to be
valid for physically viable matter configurations. Secondly, we examined the
interplay between different pairs of redshift and shape functions and analyzed
the resulting solutions, which, under specific conditions, revealed that wormholes
can be sustained even with a minute amount of exotic matter.

Lattices governed by non-Hermitian Hamiltonians have an unconventional type of energy gap, which is highly sensitive to the boundary conditions of the lattice. The non-Hermitian skin effect leads to the loss of the correspondence between bulk states and boundary states. However, we establish the bulk-boundary correspondence for a fundamental class of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. These Hamiltonians are developed from driven-dissipative systems, specifically cavity arrays with engineered and non-engineered reservoirs that explicitly model non-reciprocal hopping and loss processes. By taking this approach, we avoid ambiguity in defining the topological invariant since energy shifts that differ by a complex value are distinguished, with the origin of the complex plane serving as a reference. Consequently, topologically non-trivial systems are a strict subset of those that exhibit point gaps. The non-Hermitian skin effect does not originate from topological properties, but rather from other underlying factors. By examining the obtained non-Hermitian Hamiltonians through singular value decomposition, we find that an integer topological invariant is equivalent to an integer number of singular vectors, each localized at a system edge under open boundary conditions. The sign of the invariant determines the specific edge at which these singular vectors are localized. Additionally, we demonstrate that directional amplification can occur due to coherent inputs and loss processes that exhibit exponential gain with respect to the system size.

Near magnetic impurities in the FeSe$_{1-x}$Te$_x$ superconductor, we show
the presence of stable energy-neutral states. It is found that the Zeeman field
generated by the impurity contributes to spin-triplet inter-atomic bonding over
the more prevalent spin-singlet bonding seen within the bulk. This type of
spin-triplet bonding preserves the symmetry of time reversal and has topological
character, resulting in the emergence of robust, topologically safeguarded zero
states along boundaries where distinct pairing patterns exist. Moreover, these
zero modes consist of doublets, which remain unchanged regardless of spin
orientation or the distance between impurities. We suggest that our theoretical
findings match with experimental observations made in recent FeSe$_{1-x}$Te$_x$ studies.

We are pleased to introduce the second near-infrared data release (DR2) of the BAT AGN Spectroscopic Survey (BASS), a study examining 168 local active galactic nuclei from the all-sky Swift survey. Utilizing the VLT/X-shooter in the near-infrared range, we discovered a notable connection between the emission of high-ionization coronal lines and X-ray emissions. A particularly strong relationship was found when comparing [Si vi] CL emission and X-ray emissions. Conversely, we observed a weak connection between the emission of coronal lines and the photon index of X-ray emissions. A clear pattern was detected where line blueshifts increase with rising ionization potential in multiple CLs. Notably, we discovered an underestimation bias in measuring black hole masses in some Seyfert galaxies. Conversely, Paα and Paβ emission lines were found to agree with the relationship between mass and galaxy dispersion. Building on the success of DR1, our survey now boasts 266 AGN with near-infrared spectroscopic observations, representing the largest dataset of its kind to date.

We examine the faint radio source population found in early data from the COSMOS field using the MeerKAT International GHz Tiered Extragalactic Exploration (MIGHTEE) study, with a focus on active galactic nuclei (AGN) emitting at radio wavelengths. From this research, we're able to classify a high percentage of radio sources - 88 per cent - as either AGN (with a mix of radio-loud and other varieties) or galaxies in a stage of active star formation. Focusing on radio-loud AGN, we have defined our study sample, which contains galaxies stretching back in time to the equivalent of when the universe was roughly 6 percent of its present age and have a wide range of radio emission power levels, from extremely faint to very luminous. This classification has been published in a catalog included with the present work. In contrast to earlier studies, we have found no appreciable differences in the host galaxy properties for the various radio AGN categories and discovered that the rate of accretion onto the supermassive black holes powering these galaxies does not significantly vary. In addition, we have found evidence for the existence of a previously unknown population of radio AGN that grow very slowly and were classified under an existing label at lower emission power levels, making this classification somewhat obsolete. This finding also raises new questions regarding whether these two previously separate categories of radio AGN should, in fact, be considered as distinct populations at lower emission power levels. Finally, we have investigated the interplay between the black holes powering these galaxies and their jets of energetic particles, discovering that a black hole mass exceeding approximately 6.6 x 10 to the 7th power times the mass of the Sun must be in place in order for the jet to dominate the emission power output of the galaxy, with the spin rate of the black hole also being likely a contributing factor to the formation of a strong, persistent jet.

The total entropy from identified objects within the universe falls drastically
short of the maximum possible value as defined by the holographic principle. This disparity leads to the hypothesis that, aside from dark matter observed in galaxies and galaxy clusters, a new form of dark matter might exist in the form of incredibly massive ancient black holes.

Cardiovascular diseases pose a significant threat to global health and their prevalence continues to rise, emphasizing the importance of early and precise diagnosis. Standardized 12-lead electrocardiograms have traditionally been used in both medical practices and studies for identifying a wide range of heart-related conditions, but employing a reduced number of leads can potentially enhance the accessibility and feasibility of this diagnostic tool. We have designed a cutting-edge artificial intelligence system, leveraging deep learning algorithms to effectively recognize multiple types of cardiovascular anomalies, using merely three ECG leads in a non-traditional approach.

A new method is developed to estimate magnetic fields from scattered, unstructured data. It reconstructs the overall magnetic field by combining orthogonal functions. This combination's coefficients are calculated to minimize the difference between the true field and the predicted one, based on the squared error. A constraint in the model ensures that the divergence is accurately calculated, allowing for a significant reduction in error. In tests, the method demonstrated faster evaluation and an exponential decrease in error, contrasting the less efficient polynomial decline seen with local methods. In addition, compared to local methods involving computationally expensive search algorithms, the new method is found to be much simpler and computationally efficient in its evaluation. Its application includes using magnetohydrodynamic equations' numerical solutions to generate Poincaré sections. When compared to current methods, the new method is found to be efficient and precise, even when dealing with magnetic islands and stochastic conditions.

We introduce a noise cancellation approach for deriving unbiased readings from measured data that have been impacted by n-qubits quantum channels, regardless of noise type or the number of qubits. The protocol is flexible enough to handle correlated noise and efficiently tackles any observable influenced by Pauli noise with improved performance, specifically achieving a speed boost in a quadratic manner. Notably, our technique does not necessitate precise knowledge of noise characteristics and allows for experimental estimation of noise parameters. The protocol is further validated through various illustrative examples and simulations.

Semantic and behavioral links hold significant importance for intelligent
autonomous vehicles and Advanced Driver Assistance Systems. Unlike studies
focused on trajectory, positioning, and bounding boxes, relationship data
contributes to comprehensible descriptions of object behavior, allowing for brief
analyses of an object's past and predicted futures. As a result, it's a key
method for tasks such as threat detection, environmental understanding, and
decision-making processes. In this research, we present RSG-Net (Road Scene Graph
Network), a graph convolutional network designed to forecast potential semantic
interconnections from proposed objects, and generate a graph-structured output,
termed the "Road Scene Graph". Experimental outcomes show that this network,
trained on the Road Scene Graph dataset, effectively predicts the semantic links
between surrounding objects and the ego-vehicle.

This paper introduces an extension of Proth's theorem for integers represented as $Kp^n+1$. Specifically, we establish a primality test requiring only one modular exponentiation similar to Fermat's test but without computing GCD's. Furthermore, we present two complementary tests to improve the probability of confirming the primality of $Kp^n+1$ numbers. The consequences of these tests yield three families of integers, whose primality can be determined solely by verifying $a^{N-1} \equiv 1 \pmod N$ using Fermat's test. Additionally, we generalize Safe Primes and define $a$-Safe Primes. The analysis of the distribution of these numbers prompts a conjecture about the associated $a$-SophieGermainPrimes.
We establish that every non-diagonal entry in the Moore-Penrose inverse of a tree's distance Laplacian matrix has a non-positive value.

We theoretically investigate a method to create entangled photon pairs with a low power threshold using a specific cavity setup consisting of a single three-level atom, two incoherent light sources, and two coherent driving fields. We found that the entanglement of these photons can only be produced when the incoherent light sources have minimal impact and are dominated by the coherent driving forces. Furthermore, our research reveals that the cavity's field strength can be amplified while exhibiting strong anti-bunching when only incoherent light sources are used without any coherent driving forces. On the other hand, entangled photon pairs cannot be enhanced beyond a particular level if the cavity relies solely on coherent driving forces. Nevertheless, introducing minimal amounts of incoherent light in conjunction with the coherent driving forces leads to substantial amplification of these entangled photon pairs. We interpret our findings within the context of an intricate interplay between coherent and incoherent processes, incorporating the concept of dressed cavity states. Additionally, our research shows that the correlations of these entangled fields display temporal oscillations when the cavity operates in a regime characterized by strong coupling in quantum electrodynamics. The underlying scheme to create entangled and non-classical photons can find practical applications in quantum metrology and quantum information science.

A mathematical model describes a complex system's behavior as it enters a superconducting state from an insulating state via a specific phase transition, caused by an interaction between its particles. This interaction is responsible for both the insulating and superconducting properties, resulting in unusual conductivity in the insulating phase, where resistance declines in accordance with the model, disappearing entirely at the point of the transition, resulting in an unusual quantum-critical region. As the model transitions into the superconducting phase at lower temperatures, it enters an intermediate metal phase characterized by bosonic behavior before transitioning to a superconductor.

The Scintillating Bubble Chamber Collaboration is working on a highly sensitive detection technique using liquid-noble bubble chambers, capable of distinguishing dark matter and neutrino interactions from background noise, particularly suited for low-energy particle masses. Their initial prototype, a 10 kg liquid argon bubble chamber called SBC-LAr10, has started operation at Fermilab and will help fine-tune the detector's sensitivity to nuclear recoils as low as 100 eV. To further enhance this technology, a similar but more radio-pure detector is under construction for a dark matter search at SNOLAB, with projected sensitivity levels of $10^{-43}$ cm$^2$ at a 1 GeV particle mass. This liquid-noble bubble chamber technology holds promise for future research, particularly for searches of dark matter and neutrino interactions, where it may outperform other methods.

This research paper explores constructing a confidence sequence for bounded random processes. Leveraging existing concepts from Hendriks (2018) and Jun and Orabona (2019), along with the recent work of Waudby-Smith and Ramdas (2020) and Orabona and Jun (2021), the study reinvents the idea of Cover's (1991) universal portfolio in forming confidence sequences and establishes novel properties using a two-horse racing approach to gambling strategies. A new time-efficient algorithm is proposed, utilizing a mixture of lower bounds, that nearly replicates Cover's portfolio with significantly lower computational cost per round. Additionally, the study contributes a generalized lower bound from (Fan et al, 2015) which can be independently valuable.

Multi-agent coordination challenges involving mixed observability occur frequently
in everyday situations. Our study focuses on a distinct subset of coordination
problems in which humans can detect and act on anomalies. Anomalies in actions
occurring under typical circumstances, taken with the purpose of making other
agents realize that there must be some anomaly using an agent's capacity to
think in others' terms, are termed 'anomaly-indicating actions'. This concept is
initially illustrated with a real-life example and then given a formal definition.
Next, we present a new method called IMPROVISED, designed to generate such actions
aimed at resolving confusion in coordination challenges. Lastly, we analyze its
performance in both an educational model scenario and Hanabi, the latter
representing a benchmark where it's the first approach to produce fine and highly
strategic anomaly-detecting actions that human observers regard as highly iconic.

In describing complex physical behavior of solid materials, quasiparticles based on electrons offer a simplified yet effective approach with surprising outcomes.  Although theories, specifically Landau's Fermi-liquid theory, aimed at high-temperature cuprate superconductors, have faced challenges, a groundbreaking alternative called electron fractionalization has been established.  Its relevance in systems displaying fractional quantum Hall and Mott insulating properties is evident, yet it still remains to be seen whether it captures the essence of the cuprate pseudogap and superconducting states.  We found in this study that excitonic excitations in the superconducting cuprate, Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+\delta}$, show significantly enhanced energy at a high scale far beyond the superconducting-gap energy at about 1 eV or above, proving high-energy excitons play a significant role in superconductivity.  Therefore, this observed excitonic spectral weight imposes a significant constraint on cuprate pseudogap and superconducting mechanisms.  We discovered that the change in electron behavior, specifically a model based on electron fractionalization in the pseudogap state, is the most suitable to describe these cuprate findings, presenting a new route to studying cuprate electronic structures.

This study yields a significant discovery as it systematically derives a multitude of complex self-similar solutions to the generalized surface quasi-geostrophic equation, marking a significant breakthrough given that rigorous constructions for such solutions have yet to exist previously. Our findings comprise spiral pattern solutions that are integrable within specific local areas and can display varying intensity values, showing a degree of correspondence with simulated results that suggested a singularity in the SQG model.

The Little Glaisher theorem for positive integers k, l, and n expresses that the quantity of partitions of n consisting of non-k-divisible parts appearing fewer than l times equals the quantity of partitions of n consisting of non-l-divisible parts appearing fewer than k times. A straightforward generating function computation confirms this statement, yet it lacks an explicit, direct relationship. Our paper solves this open problem by adopting a purely numerical approach and provides further insight into the l = 2 case where a related Schur-type companion to the Little Glaisher theorem may potentially be constructed using weighted words.

We've discovered four new fast radio bursts in an in-depth search of Parkes 70-cm pulsar survey data archives using HEIMDALL and FETCH algorithms, and the data were dispersed between 0 and 5000 pc cm$^{-3}$. These FRBs, distinguished by pulse widths of more than 50 milliseconds, did not show the characteristic widening effects attributed to interstellar scattering or signal dispersion within channels. Interestingly, the most prominent FRB found had a dispersion measure of 3338 pc cm$^{-3}$, a value far higher than ever recorded previously. Moreover, the detection of these radio bursts occurred much earlier than the first discovered Lorimer Burst, and the findings demonstrate that previous radio telescopes data archives can remain potential sources of previously unknown FRBs. Our data imply that extending our time scale for detecting FRBs, to durations greater than 100 milliseconds, may unveil the existence of more wide-pulse FRBs.

This paper presents a groundbreaking algorithm rooted in model predictive control that efficiently guides the upper stage of a launch vehicle. The proposed strategy not only boosts vehicle performance and resistance to external disruptions, but also reliably enforces a controlled splash-down procedure. Given the uncertainty of engine performance and particularly burn time, the method reduces the range of potential impact areas. The proposed algorithm incorporates a novel axis shift technique, reducing sensitivity to variable engine performance and minimizing the uncertainty of impact points. Contrary to conventional approaches, the algorithm automatically determines the neutral axis orientation through repeated optimization with two distinct return phases. The optimization problem quickly yields a solution, enabling high algorithm update frequencies and efficient problem-solving. The robustness and efficiency of the method were thoroughly tested through comprehensive simulations.

We are examining the outcomes of a surgical procedure known as anterior temporal lobe resection (ATLR), used to treat severe epilepsy that has proven resistant to medication. This surgery often involves the removal of a large amount of brain tissue. This study focuses on the effects of the procedure on the shape and size of the brain's surface, near the site of surgery and elsewhere. 

For this analysis, 101 people with a history of temporal lobe epilepsy (55 of whom experienced left-sided seizures, 46 of whom experienced right-sided seizures) who had undergone ATLR surgery participated. Each participant had undergone MRI scans both before the surgery and several months afterwards, when changes in their brain's structure could be assessed. To compare these scans with those from healthy individuals, 924 MRI scans from individuals without epilepsy were used. These data allowed researchers to identify how ATLR affected different regions of the brain. 

Comparing the pre-surgery MRI scans with those taken afterwards, it was found that the brain's structure had been altered in many areas following the surgery, including several brain regions in both the left and right sides of the brain that were connected to the site of surgery. These changes may result from damage during surgery, degeneration, or reorganization of the brain's structure. An additional benefit of the research methodology used here is the inclusion of a measure that reveals other, previously undetected effects of the procedure compared to traditional measurement methods.

Cosmic strings exhibiting superconducting properties can be susceptible to pinching instabilities under certain conditions, particularly within a specified range of parameters. We use the thin string approximation to forecast the onset of this instability and propose a revised analysis that can be applied to short-wavelength perturbations where the former method becomes ineffective. Simulations of perturbed strings enable us to assess the thin string approximation's accuracy and evaluate our new approach. The findings show that these instabilities occur over a broader range in magnetic strings than initially predicted, while pinching instabilities also arise in electric strings under certain conditions. Notably, however, strings close to the chiral limit are found to be free from such instabilities and our results reaffirm our previous conclusion that sufficiently large vortons can be classically stable against perturbations.

A standard imaging procedure involves three key components: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest, a device that captures the scattered light, and a detector that identifies its spatial location. These fundamental elements can hinder imaging of fragile or sensitive biological specimens because their conventional operation is limited by insufficient light detection capabilities and damage resulting from interaction with the light source. To overcome these restrictions, we've devised and experimentally implemented a novel quantum imaging approach. This method involves incorporating a Michelson interferometer with single photons into a device using induced coherence, combined with single-pixel imaging, thereby eliminating the need for object-photon interaction and greatly reducing detection requirements. This pioneering achievement enables the imaging of intricate structures using undetected photons and expands the possibilities of quantum imaging, potentially paving the way for delicate sample analysis at visible wavelengths detectable by silicon sensors.
This paper explores the subdifferential set of an operator and its connection to the subdifferential of its functional value at the point where the operator reaches its peak.

This commemorative piece commences with heartfelt and nostalgic tributes to the cherished Prof. A.P. Balachandran. Subsequently, the article delves into a recently devised model of quantum mechanics on one-dimensional non-commutative space-time via Hilbert-Schmidt operators, incorporating the Moyal framework. Additionally, the authors present a tangible example, showing how a system comprising a time-varying forced harmonic oscillator situated within the Moyal space-time exhibits an emergent geometrical phase.

To meet Metaverse's needs for large-scale data communication, high bandwidth efficiency, and low latency data processing, Semantic communication and Edge computing offer innovative solutions. However, Edge computing resource provision is typically dependent on computing service providers, making the creation of effective incentive mechanisms essential to secure access to these limited resources. A recent proposal to this challenge is the use of Deep learning-based auctions, which ensure revenue maximization and important economic properties like individual rationality and incentive compatibility. In this study, we design a Deep learning-based auction to optimize Edge resource allocation within Metaverse frameworks utilizing Semantic communication. Initially, the fundamentals and obstacles associated with Metaverse are addressed. Next, the fundamentals and obstacles associated with Semantic communication and Edge computing are explored. Following this, various existing methods of providing Edge computing resource trading are discussed. Afterwards, the mechanism of the Deep learning-based auction in the context of Edge resource allocation within Metaverse frameworks with Semantic communication is described. Experimental outcomes reveal that the Deep learning-based auction generates improved revenue, while keeping vital economic properties nearly intact.

The way we assess similarity has a significant impact on the findings of scientific experiments and studies, with significant implications for the learning process. Consequently, machine learning and scientific modeling rely on similarity metrics that serve as objective functions. One common example is the mean squared error, considered optimal when errors are distributed normally and randomly, but in various cases, this condition does not apply. Consequently, researchers must determine the appropriate measure of similarity, where information theory offers guidance on selecting an appropriate metric. We illustrate this process using a straightforward hydrologic model as a case study.

The bulk photovoltaic effect, a relatively weak process that can generate higher photovoltages than its band gap, is found to have an unusually high potential for planar BaTiO$_3$ films when tuned with strain and epitaxial growth on different substrates. We discovered that varying the polarization in these films through strain can yield very high responsiveness and photovoltaic effect, exceeding previously reported values. Surprisingly, this effect cannot be fully explained by first principles-based models of bulk materials. Instead, a new explanation for the link between ferroelectric polarization and responsiveness has been discovered. Consequently, this discovery may enable successful practical uses of ferroelectric photovoltaics in basic, planar film geometries by fine-tuning bulk, optical, and interfacial properties simultaneously.

Fake news detection is increasingly becoming a vital research area that extends beyond mere intellectual curiosity, as its outcomes have profound societal consequences.
Previous advancements have been primarily based on text-centric methods; however, to achieve meaningful results, integrating contextual data like news article diffusion patterns and user behavior on social media platforms is essential.
We propose generating composite social context graphs around news articles and reformulating the task as a graph classification challenge. Through investigating the integration of various information types to gauge the impact of social context and utilizing distinct graph neural network architectures, our research shows this approach yields significant and reliable results when tested against a standard benchmark dataset.

Modeling stance detection as textual entailment recognition could potentially provide benefits such as access to a wider range of training data and more flexible learning strategies. This idea is initially explored in our study, where we focus on a particularly challenging and relevant test scenario for which a suitable labeled dataset is currently lacking. By adopting this approach, we hope to capitalize on the insights gained from the social sciences to enhance the performance of our model. Ultimately, this investigation seeks to shed light on the feasibility of this method and to identify avenues for future research.

The widespread adoption of home-based solar panels has led to frequent instances of overvoltage due to power surges. To prevent damage to electronic systems, solar inverters temporarily stop generating power in response to overvoltage events. This results in unequal distribution of the benefits from energy production, especially for households farthest from the power source. To ensure fair distribution of these benefits, a unified strategy is necessary that requires detailed knowledge of the power network's specifications, which is often lacking. This paper examines the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in developing a fair method for regulating solar panel output by learning through trial and error with the power system. The performance of six fairness criteria is evaluated against an ideal solution and it is found that all these metrics can be learned efficiently, which implies that reinforcement learning is a promising method for balancing both the safety and fairness of solar panel management.

The study of relativistic hydrodynamics has effectively described the behavior of matter produced in heavy-ion collision experiments.  Researchers have recently made considerable progress in understanding the spin polarization of hadrons produced in these collisions.  While existing models have successfully explained some experimental data, there is still a lack of a clear comprehension of the data obtained from differential measurements.  This indicates that spin dynamics must be considered as an independent entity, not completely influenced by the system's circulation of flow.  In this context, spin should be a macroscopic property with its own equilibrium dynamics governed by hydrodynamic laws.  In this thesis, a new framework of relativistic hydrodynamics has been developed, incorporating spin dynamics from kinetic theory and applied to heavy-ion collision simulations.  It is assumed that polarization effects are minor and, based on the de Groot-van Leeuwen-van Weert pseudogauge, equations of conservation for the baryon current, energy-momentum tensor, and spin tensor have been established.  In this work, properties of the spin polarization tensor have been extensively examined and its components analyzed in detail, as well as the propagation of spin polarization components, and spin-wave velocity have been calculated for arbitrary statistics.  It was observed that only the transverse spin components propagate in the same manner as electromagnetic waves.  Finally, the spacetime evolution of spin polarization was investigated, and the mean spin polarization per particle was calculated and compared to experimental data.  Qualitative agreement was observed for some observables with experimental findings and other model calculations.

Future wireless communication systems, driven by cell-free massive MIMO technology, promise to deliver enhanced coverage uniformity and spectral efficiency. Research focuses on how cell-free massive MIMO systems can enable federated edge learning through over-the-air computation, leveraging the additive nature of wireless channels. By utilizing this approach, over-the-air federated learning (OTA-FL) helps reduce the communication burden associated with edge learning over wireless networks. Accounting for channel correlation and imperfect channel state knowledge at the central server, a practical OTA-FL implementation is proposed over cell-free massive MIMO systems. Analytical and experimental analyses validate the proposed implementation's performance and reinforce the advantages of integrating cell-free massive MIMO with OTA-FL.

The isolation of attosecond pulses through gating techniques is commonly achieved by controlling the production of high harmonics to a single laser cycle, thereby restricting energy growth through longer driving pulses. We introduce the pumping ionizing gating (PIG) technique, a method which utilizes the prolonged dynamics of plasma grating reflections in tandem with frequency conversion to repeatedly channel high energy from the pumping pulse into the generating pulse. By leveraging PIC simulations over an expansive range of parameters (0.02-0.5 n.c. plasma density, 10-60% grating depth) and 3D modeling, a PIG-generated IAP of 330 as at an input power of 1.6 ps and 1-μm wavelength exhibits an amplified intensity approximately 33 times its driving force and 0.1% conversion efficiency.

This study reveals the advantages of the LSMR algorithm for iterative least-squares MR reconstruction, surpassing the Conjugate Gradient method, which is hampered by numerical problems, in cases where the Conjugate Gradient can't be sped up through Toeplitz embedding.

Recent years have seen an abundance of research activity where the fusion of
non-Hermitian principles and topological concepts has borne a plethora of
innovative findings. In this comprehensive review, the underlying mechanisms
of non-Hermitian phases, which dictate their topological properties, will be
delivered. To exemplify key features of these systems, the topological
properties of well-studied non-Hermitian models – the Hatano-Helson model,
non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model and non-Hermitian Chern insulator –
will be employed to demonstrate characteristics such as exceptional points,
energy gaps and non-Hermitian symmetry. Additionally, the discussion will
cover non-Hermitian skin effects and a broader generalized Brillouin zone,
which aid in maintaining bulk-boundary correlations. Concrete examples of how
disorder impacts the behavior of these systems and the linear response
framework will be provided, along with an analysis of Hall transport
properties in these systems. Lastly, the significant growth of experiments
in this area and the promising paths forward for future investigations will be
evaluated.

In a subspace with a restricted range space, certain compact operator conditions ensure that subspace-valued compact operators form a proximinal subset of compact operators mapping to the range space.

This paper offers distinct, independent proofs from its three authors to prove a key finding: for an Anosov flow acting on an oriented three-dimensional manifold, a Birkhoff section with positive values exists if, and only if the flow exhibits real-axis coverage combined with positive twist properties.

SAP's Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system supports multiple business processes, such as Order-to-Cash and Procure-to-Pay. Nevertheless, managing the vast amount of processes and associated data within SAP ERP can be highly demanding. This includes identifying specific processes contained in a particular SAP instance and creating a list of relevant database tables. In order to use this data for process mining, it's essential to extract the event logs from SAP ERP. This presentation outlines a new tool called the Interactive SAP Explorer, which tackles the challenge of process identification by modeling the complex relational structure of SAP ERP in a graphical format, enabling advanced querying and visualization.

The spread of toxic memes on social media sites not only poses a challenge to these platforms but also has real-world consequences.  Identifying hateful memes can be difficult because their meaning and content evolve continuously as they adapt and incorporate various elements from popular culture.  In order to address this issue, a novel method has been developed, which incorporates multimodal contrastive learning models, like CLIP developed by OpenAI, to recognize targets of harmful online content and investigate the progression of toxic memes over time.  Researchers have discovered consistent patterns within the descriptions generated by these models, which can capture semantic relationships within the same or different types of content, like images and text.  These findings have enabled researchers to examine how harmful memes emerge through the combination of multiple images or the integration of written text with an offensive visual.  Using this framework on data collected from the platform 4chan, researchers identified over 3,300 variants of a particular anti-semitic meme, with some versions linked to specific geographic locations, individuals, or organizations.  Ultimately, this research envisions its tool aiding moderators in manually evaluating flagged memes to effectively combat online hate speech.

We studied the effect of adding small amounts of solute to a solvent, modeled with characteristics similar to water, by examining the change in the temperature at which the solvent reaches its maximum density. Our model used a potential that varies on two different scales to represent the solvent, which is known to behave like water in some cases. We investigated how varying the strength of the attractive interaction between the solvent and solute affected the solvent's maximum density temperature. Our results indicate that when the solute has a strong attraction to the solvent, it enhances the solvent's structure, leading to an increase in the maximum density temperature with added solute. Conversely, when the solute exhibits a weak attraction, it disrupts the solvent's structure, resulting in a decrease in the maximum density temperature with added solute.

Recent breakthroughs in visual recognition tasks have led to the rise of patch-based models such as Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Mixers, which have been able to outperform classic convolutional networks. However, while these models have initially ignored the unique properties of different patches, incorporating inductive bias has proven beneficial for representations. Nevertheless, previous works have predominantly focused on patch locations without considering the structure of images, which limits their performance. Our proposed approach, the OAMixer, aims to overcome this limitation by leveraging object information to improve patch interaction. Utilizing object labels obtained through unsupervised or weakly-supervised learning methods, the OAMixer recalibrates the patch mixing layers by applying a learnable scale parameter to a reweighting mask. This enhanced representation learning not only boosts the classification accuracy and background robustness of patch-based models but also generalizes to downstream tasks such as large-scale classification, self-supervised learning, and multi-object recognition.
This talk examines the challenge of creating a developable surface that intersects two curves defined by either rational or non-uniform rational B-spline equations.

To quantify the minimal surfaces that have the same boundary from a boundary geometry perspective, a fast and accurate numerical strategy is devised, grounded in the method of fundamental solutions. The numerical strategy is accompanied by convergence and error analyses for Dirichlet energy and mean curvature in the L∞ norm, where each approximate solution generated by this method is a smooth, undivided surface, distinct from previous methods reliant on meshing techniques.

The Maker-Breaker game on a graph G involves choosing a dominant set as a goal for Dominator and claiming a closed neighborhood of a vertex for Staller. We explore the scenarios where Staller emerges victorious in this game. Minimum move requirements for Staller to win, denoted by γ SMB'(G), are studied, and the number of moves is analyzed for specific types of graphs, including trees. Characterizations for trees with γ SMB'(T)=k for any positive integer k are identified. Furthermore, the application of hypergraphs results in an upper bound for γ SMB'. The problem is also investigated on the subdivided star S obtained from a star graph by subdividing some of its edges, and the exact formula for γ SMB'(S) is found, except in certain complex cases. For subdivided star graphs with at least two odd subdivisions, the number of moves is expressed as a simple formula, and the exact formulas for the number of moves for Dominator and Staller are found on caterpillars.

The evolution of social dilemmas is significantly influenced by environmental variations in complex systems. Environmental changes typically involve two key components: fluctuating global conditions and locally dependent feedback mechanisms. Despite research focusing separately on these aspects, the interplay between them is not fully understood. We have developed a theoretical model that considers group strategies and their dynamic surroundings. The global fluctuations affect a non-linear public goods element, while local feedback is described using the concept of 'eco-evolutionary game'. Our study demonstrates that the interdependent dynamics between game evolution and local environments differ based on static or changing global conditions. Notably, our results indicate that cyclic cooperation patterns between groups and local environments emerge, creating complex phase-plane trajectories. The relative speeds of global and local environment changes compared to strategic shifts influence these patterns. The findings suggest that diverse evolutionary outcomes arise from complex interactions between strategies and shifting environments.

Researchers discovered that sound-dampened fractal screens can still scatter acoustic waves even when they appear to have zero surface area. By adapting the boundary element method to use fractal sets, they created a novel technique called "Hausdorff BEM". The integration required for this technique uses a non-integer order measure instead of the traditional surface measure. Leveraging recent advances in fractal function spaces, they established that the Galerkin formulation of Hausdorff BEM converges in acoustic scattering problems in higher dimensions, given specific fractal properties. Furthermore, they analyzed the convergence rates of a class of fractals and superconvergence for specific functional forms. Additionally, they proposed and implemented numerical routines and fully discrete convergence analyses for Hausdorff BEM. Their numerical experiments demonstrated the efficacy of Hausdorff BEM and supported their solution regularity assumptions in scattering problems.

Deep learning models often falter when they encounter data drawn from distributions unlike those they were trained on. This is particularly pertinent in crucial fields such as medical imaging, where recognizing out-of-distribution data points is crucial to enhancing model reliability. Recent studies have developed DL-based techniques for identifying OOD samples in 2D medical images with some success. Nevertheless, most existing methods face insurmountable computational barriers when scaled up for 3D images and often fall short in accurately detecting even artificially crafted OOD samples, possibly indicating that DL tends to inadequately process voluminous image data. This is why we suggest that leveraging the original intensity histogram from CT or MRI scans provides a simple and sufficient basis for identifying OOD samples without necessitating deep learning techniques. The histogram-based approach our team has proposed has yielded impressive outcomes in 3D medical imaging and demonstrated robust performance across various datasets. Furthermore, it attained an impressive second place ranking in a recent Medical Out-of-Distribution challenge, narrowly surpassing other participants despite our team refraining from fine-tuning our model or leveraging task-specific expertise. After considering the approach's potential limitations, we are confident that the proposed histogram-based technique effectively tackles the issue of OOD detection at the sample level in 3D medical imaging within our defined scope.

We created and experimentally studied an acoustic metasurface that includes a series of sound-hard cavities, arrayed in one dimension and featuring a unique configuration with additional connected cavities below the surface. This intricate arrangement can be produced quickly and efficiently through three-dimensional printing. By including beyond-nearest-neighbor connections between cavities, the surface's properties can be modified, causing variations in how the acoustic waves behave as the frequency increases. This leads to variations in dispersion patterns and results in localized acoustic surface waves with 'backwards' propagation properties. This research enables new methods for enhancing acoustic sensing technology with acoustic metasurfaces.

A new determination of the $C\!P$-even fraction, denoted as $F_+$, in $D^0$ decays to $K^+K^-\pi^+\pi^-$ is provided using $2.93$ fb$^{-1}$ of $e^+e^-\to\psi(3770)$ data from the BESIII detector. By tagging one charm meson and reconstructing the other as either a $C\!P$ eigenstate or through $D\to K_{S, L}^0\pi^+\pi^-$, relative rates of double-tagged events lead to the result $F_+ = 0.730 \pm 0.037 \pm 0.021$. This is the first model-independent measurement of $F_+$ for $D^0$ decays to $K^+K^-\pi^+\pi^-$.

The PT-symmetric quantum Rabi model (PTQRM) is a system of a qubit and light field. Using the adiabatic approximation (AA) to solve this model within its relevant parameter regime allows us to explore multiple physical properties through analytical solutions and numerical diagonalization methods. By investigating the model with the adiabatic approximation and numerical diagonalization, exceptional points (EPs) were discovered in the eigenspectrum, where their behavior closely mimics the characteristics of solvable points found in the model's Hermitian equivalent. Notably, the EPs are sensitive to variations in the coupling strength of light and matter, causing them to appear and then vanish, only to reappear once more. We also analyze how physical quantities behave under the model's Hamiltonian, yielding findings that can be directly applied to various other light-matter interaction systems, offering valuable insights into non-Hermitian quantum systems as well.

The era of gravitational wave astronomy is expected to provide insights into unresolved black hole mergers, primordial wave backgrounds, and their astrophysical counterparts. In particular, a specific range of low-frequency gravitational waves from primordial events offers an optimal opportunity to accurately measure fundamental cosmological parameters, including the universe's equation of state. We investigate whether uncertainty over the astrophysical gravitational wave foregrounds, coexisting with a primordial background, jeopardises this programme of research. We outline a framework under which the astrophysical foregrounds' normalisation uncertainty is considered the main source of uncertainty, rather than their overall shape. In such a scenario, primordial signals can be separated from foregrounds by applying an optimal subtraction technique that selectively removes similar-spectrum foregrounds. We demonstrate that even with the presence of foregrounds, sensitivity to the signal is maintained with a small multiplicative factor, particularly near the frequency range where the signal's characteristics most closely resemble the foregrounds' patterns. Ultimately, accurately accounting for contributions from black hole binaries, particularly eccentric and intermediate-mass systems, is crucial to achieve precise cosmological results from primordial wave backgrounds.

Using computer models, researchers have examined the evolution and dynamics of self-propelled particles in continuous motion, drawing comparisons to a passive Ising system.  We have studied the short-term and long-term behaviors following a rapid transformation of uniformly arranged particles to a state located in the mixing regions and at the critical points, focusing on properties like spatial arrangements and characteristic size metrics.  We have also analyzed aging behavior after particles were suddenly changed into a state located in the mixing regions and have quantified the characteristics of the temporal order metric correlation.  Our overall results, as well as those from similar studies on active lattice models, are consistent with the predictions from the Ising model for rapid transitions to critical states.

This paper presents the 5th iteration of the Predicting Video Memorability Task within MediaEval2022, characterised by a more streamlined and in-depth evaluation process. Similar to previous years, participants have two datasets to test generalisation. A new VideoMem dataset replaces the previous one due to data quality issues and focuses on short-term memorability, with the Memento10k dataset becoming the primary test. A new sub-task based on EEG predictions is introduced. The task's main components are outlined, covering the datasets, evaluation methods, and participant requirements for submissions.

This research focuses on resolving two main issues: creating quantifiable measures of artificial intelligence (AI) model utilization and explaining how the underlying data influences AI models according to these metrics. The motivation behind this study is the existing lack of transparency in AI models, specifically those applied in life-or-death situations, such as self-driving cars that utilize AI for sign recognition. The investigation involves the theoretical foundation of AI model utilization analysis and understanding the patterns that arise from the data-driven sign classification in self-driving cars based on AI models, sub-models, and nodes. Utilization at each computation point in an AI model is theoretically determined based on the distribution and diversity of outcomes in a possible output space. In this study, measurements are extracted from both legitimate and poisoned AI models, where the latter are created by training them with altered traffic signs intended to deceive AI. Contrasting the behavior of poisoned AI models with legitimate ones enables analysis and highlights implications for detecting potential manipulation attempts.

To better understand how defects in spherical shells under external pressure behave, we examined how variations in defect shape impact buckling thresholds. This investigation contrasts two previously studied shell defect configurations, namely inward-curled and outward-ridged, Gaussian defects, the latter of which has seen relatively little exploration. Employing finite-element modeling, validated against prior experiments, we analyzed and compared the knockdown factors of these shells, systematically evaluating their defect geometries. Notably, our findings showed that the knockdown factor was significantly greater in the shells containing the less commonly researched outward-ridged defects, as opposed to those containing the traditionally considered inward-curled defects, across the examined parameter ranges. Additionally, the knockdown factor behavior differed between the two configurations, as did the post-buckling behavior. Based on our results, we made a tentative connection between the variations in defect behavior and the differing curvature characteristics of these configurations.

In a field where a validation set is frequently unavailable, especially in the context of few-shot learning scenarios, classifiers' generalization errors are often underestimated. This limitation has garnered little attention, yet poses a significant challenge. To circumvent this, it's common to utilize features derived from pre-trained neural networks in conjunction with classifiers based on distances, such as nearest class mean. This study develops a Gaussian model of the feature distribution and, through parameter estimation, is capable of predicting generalization errors in classification tasks with limited data. We discover that precise estimates of the distance between class-conditional densities are instrumental in obtaining accurate predictions of the generalization performance. To address this requirement, an unbiased estimator is devised and subsequently incorporated into the numerical analysis. The proposed approach surpasses established alternatives like the leave-one-out cross-validation method, yielding improved performance in few-shot learning scenarios.

Recent experiments using high-energy laser-driven gases have achieved a collective system in the thermodynamic limit that results in a boundary time-crystal state of matter, where coherent stimulation and dissipation interact in balance to sustain stability. This experimental approach provides the possibility of acquiring real-time insights into the system's out-of-equilibrium behavior by analyzing the state of the emitted light. We found that the photon count and homodyne current measurements can be utilized to recognize and analyze critical behavior at the time-crystal phase transition, where slow variations in emission dynamics alternate with brief intense fluctuations, exhibiting characteristics consistent with a nonlinear phase model. Moreover, we discovered that the cumulative homodyne current over time serves as an efficient dynamic order parameter. As a result, the time-crystal can be regarded as a matter state characterized by multiple coexisting oscillation patterns.

The Antarctic ice sheet's decadal mass loss leads to considerable elastic uplift, up to 20 mm/yr, across the ANET GNSS network. For the first time, researchers are investigating whether GNSS-observed elastic deformation can be used to determine changes in Antarctic ice mass. To do this, they employ an observer-centric model, known as the Load Sensitivity Kernel, to determine which regions of ice mass loss are driving elastic deformation at each GNSS site. The results indicate that most ANET sites are heavily influenced by mass changes occurring more than 200 km away. However, by comparing LSKs from neighboring GNSS receivers, it is possible to pinpoint near-field mass changes contributing to differential displacement. The researchers further develop a method utilizing a weighted combination of multiple GNSS sites, minimizing elastic deformation from mass changes outside a designated area of interest. The ANET configuration's dense clustering of GNSS receivers in regions such as the Amundsen Sea allows for isolating elastic deformation due to specific ice losses, like the Pine Island Glacier or the PSK glaciers. The results indicate that ANET's current GNSS receiver layout is capable of utilizing elastic deformation to constrain Antarctic ice mass changes, especially in regions with high GNSS densities.

This study focuses on the domain of formulas with satisfying solutions within the context of satisfiability modulo theories, with an emphasis on automatically generating numerous solutions to such formulas. Although satisfiability modulo theories has had a significant impact on model checking and formal verification for many years, the automatic generation of multiple solutions to satisfiable formulas is a relatively under-explored area. Research in this field is mainly centered on generating satisfying assignments for Boolean formulas and for first-order formulas without quantifiers, particularly those involving bit-vectors, arrays, and uninterpreted functions (QF_AUFBV). To expand the possibilities for first-order formulas incorporating integer arithmetic and integer arithmetic combined with arrays and uninterpreted functions, a new sampling approach has been developed. This novel approach involves simplifying the general sampling process by transforming it into an equivalent but more manageable instance of sampling from multiple intervals.

This initial measurement investigates the alignment of the spin of D*+ vector mesons and their charge conjugates, in relation to their helicity axis, in two scenarios resulting from charm-quark hadronization (prompt) and beauty-meson decay (non-prompt) following hadron collisions. Data was collected by the ALICE experiment at 13 TeV, focusing on collisions at midrapidity with a transverse momentum range. The diagonal spin density element of the D*+ mesons was measured through the angular distribution of its decay products within the meson's rest frame, in relation to its direction in the center-of-mass frame. The results indicate that the diagonal spin density element of prompt D*+ mesons matches the expected value with no alignment observed, however, the findings suggest non-prompt D*+ mesons have an evidence of larger than expected spin alignment, measured at 0.455 with a significant statistical and systematic error margin, in a transverse momentum interval of 5 to 20 GeV/c, in alignment with a Monte Carlo simulation which implements the conservation of helicity in beauty meson decays. The results imply that the alignment observed could be a mimic of the alignment effect experienced in heavy-ion collisions, where D*+ mesons are influenced by the direction of the angular momentum and magnetic field present in such collisions.

In an extended version of the Standard Model, formulas for correction parameters S, T, U, V, W, and X are provided for an arbitrary number of singlet, doublet, and triplet quarks, including quarks with specific electric charges that interact with the standard quarks having matching charge values.

The NA61/SHINE experiment at CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron seeks to identify key transitions in matter and investigate its disintegration phase through particle collisions.
Aiming to meet this goal, researchers study hadron production in collisions involving various elements and energy levels.
This presentation showcases new findings from experiments conducted with intermediate-size atomic systems at 13 to 150 GeV/c, covering kaon production in particular.
Moreover, recent data collected from p+p interactions, encompassing strange mesons, short-lived particles, and specific types of baryons are now available.

The global transition towards a decarbonized energy system is driving a rapid shift towards integrating renewable energy into conventional grids, posing both opportunities and challenges for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESSs) participating in the energy market. One major source of revenue for BESSs stems from energy arbitrage in response to rising spot market price volatility caused by discrepancies between renewable generation and electricity demand. Additionally, participation in Frequency Control Ancillary Services (FCAS) markets offers BESSs substantial returns due to their ultra-fast response times. Consequently, it is essential for BESSs to strategically allocate their capacity across multiple markets to optimize their overall earnings under conditions of uncertainty. To address this need, this study presents a novel Markov Decision Process framework for BESS bidding strategy, allowing the BESS to concurrently engage in both the spot and FCAS markets to achieve maximum profit. By leveraging the capabilities of Proximal Policy Optimization, a state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning model, our method is able to effectively adapt to the complexities of real-world energy markets with continuous bidding scales. Evaluating the proposed approach using real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, our research showcases a significantly improved profit outcome when adopting a joint market participation strategy versus focusing solely on individual markets.

To address the limitations of Distantly-Supervised Named Entity Recognition (DS-NER), particularly the risk of noisy labels generated through distant supervision, current self-training frameworks for DS-NER require improvement. Recent studies utilizing self-training teacher-student frameworks have been hindered by inadequate student learning and infrequent updates to the teacher model, resulting in underestimation of the performance. Our research endeavors to overcome these drawbacks through novel methodologies: Firstly, an adaptive learning strategy is implemented, integrating the joint training of two teacher-student networks while taking into account consistent and inconsistent predictions from the teachers, promoting robust student learning. Secondly, an advanced student ensemble is developed, allowing for a fine-grained update of each model fragment using a temporal moving average, resulting in consistent predictions despite the presence of noise. Our approach has been evaluated through extensive experiments on DS-NER datasets, resulting in notable improvements compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

A groundbreaking technology, spatial transcriptomics, is poised to revolutionize the field of tissue-based RNA expression studies.
