Traditional array-based methods generate multi-cell data that must be processed to obtain single cell insights, a labor-intensive process. Rapid progress in precise measurement of RNA at a molecular level requires a novel approach. A new method called TopACT addresses this challenge by automatically identifying cell types, allowing for precise location of isolated cells even in the absence of prior cell boundary knowledge. By combining TopACT with an advanced analytical technique, researchers were able to visually confirm a key discovery - immune cells form a ring-shaped structure within kidney glomeruli in a model of lupus nephritis, validating an important biological concept. This novel data analysis framework seamlessly integrates insights from various biological scales, encompassing both individual cell expression and tissue organization patterns.

We have established the maximum achievable Lipschitz continuity for the very weak solutions of the given elliptic partial differential equation, $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \;
\mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ within a smooth bounded region $\Omega$ of the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $\Gamma$ is a smooth hypersurface, $Q$ is a smooth density function defined on $\Gamma$, $A$ is a uniformly elliptic matrix which varies smoothly with $x$ and $Q > n$. We have examined whether the imposed restrictions on the data variables are truly essential. This partial differential equation serves as an intersection point for two harmonic functions which combine at a smooth surface, thereby making it fundamental to the solution of several free boundary problems as we will be detailing.

One of quantum theory's key axioms, the Born rule, assigns a probability value to the possible outcomes of a given quantum state, as specified by the equation P(a) = |<a|ψ>|². Despite its ability to accurately predict results, this principle still has no direct method of validation. Our research indicates that by utilizing a weak value-based measurement technique, it's now feasible to directly observe superposition wavefunctions, potentially leading to the verification of the Born rule. An experiment to support this concept is proposed.

Matrix factorization leverages the idea that complex high-dimensional data contains lower-dimensional structures where meaningful patterns reside.  In these lower-dimensional structures, sparse models are particularly useful due to their interpretability and capacity to reduce over-fitting by promoting regularization.  A Bayesian approach incorporating shrinkage priors offers an efficient strategy for factorizing high-dimensional matrices by modeling relationships between entities in row and column data and allowing sparse patterns to emerge organically.  This approach allows structures to emerge naturally, without pre-conceived assumptions, while also incorporating external information in the process.  A numerical strategy built around sequential addition and estimation of low-rank contributions, informed by the data, is combined with this approach, using data-driven stopping rules to ensure practical effectiveness.  This approach's benefits are illustrated through a simulation study and an analysis of soccer heatmap data obtained from new generation tracking systems.

This paper details the evaluation of a High Angle Time Projection Chambers prototype that will serve in the upgrade of the T2K experiment's Near Detector. The device is composed of 32 ERAM modules, situated on both endplates, which use a groundbreaking detection method that measures charge distribution on various pads. The prototype TPC has been enhanced with an initial ERAM module produced for T2K and has undergone extensive testing via DESY Test Beam to quantify spatial resolution and dE/dx precision. The ERAM and detector response are analyzed, along with novel simulation software, to achieve unparalleled performance specifications of below 800 micrometers spatial resolution and 10% dE/dx precision at all incident angles and drift distances. The data from testing matches expectations and fulfills the technical requirements of the T2K upgrade.

In the preceding article arXiv:2210.16738, we established a set of flavor mass correlations that the beta-deformed A(n-1) quiver matrix model utilizes to restore maximum symmetry within a massive scaling limit. Building upon this finding, the current letter determines specific conditions on moduli parameters that allow for the complete degeneration of the Seiberg-Witten curve, ensuring consistency with these established correlations and thereby defining the Argyres-Douglas critical hypersurface.

Our study focused on bounce solutions within holographic models of QCD and electroweak first-order phase transitions. The gravitational wave power spectra derived from the holographic bounce solution provided the strength parameter $\alpha$, inverse duration time $\beta/H$, and bubble wall velocity $v_w$. Unlike field theory predictions, the holographic models indicated that $\alpha$ is approximately 1 and $\beta/H$ is roughly $10^4$, signifying a fast and strong phase transition. In holographic models, the nucleation, percolation, and critical temperatures of the phase transition are closely aligned. The velocity $v_w$ is also observed to be less than the sound speed $c_s = 1/\sqrt{3}$, consistent with the deflagration scenario. For the QCD phase transition, gravitational wave power spectra can reach $10^{-13}-10^{-14}$ around 0.01 Hz and are potentially detectable by BBO and Ultimate-DECIGO. In contrast, for the electroweak phase transition, gravitational wave power spectra can range from $10^{-12}-10^{-16}$ around the peak frequency $1-10$ Hz. The study's findings suggest that primordial black hole formation is unlikely due to the large $\beta/H$ and small $v_w$.

This research focuses on left-invariant Finsler metrics that preserve cones on the two-dimensional non-commutative Lie group 'G', possessing spray vector fields that never fade to zero, and categorizes these metrics under certain curvature conditions. We establish that those meeting Landsberg's requirements are automatically Berwald, and based on this insight, we introduce the homogeneous conic Landsberg hypothesis and demonstrate its validity for two-dimensional instances.

A crucial obstacle in developing neural control system technology lies in verifying the safety and reliability of neural network (NN) controllers when faced with diverse sources of uncertainty such as unforeseen dynamics, non-linear interactions, and time lags. One potential solution to address these concerns is to ensure that the NN controller maintains the closed-loop system's output within a specific boundary range as its input varies, mirroring the performance of a stable reference model. This research proposes a novel approach to evaluating the performance and robustness of uncertain feedback systems governed by NN controllers, which involves transforming the complex problem into an examination of the dynamical discrepancies between a real system with a neural controller and an ideal reference model. The controller error approximation is achieved by employing the differential mean value theorem (DMV) and the Integral Quadratic Constraints (IQCs) technique, while the Relative Integral Square Error (RISE) and the Supreme Square Error (SSE) bounds are derived for the output of the error dynamical system. The proposed method combines Lyapunov theory with IQCs to conduct a worst-case analysis, offering the user predictive knowledge about the maximum RISE and SSE discrepancies between the reference model and the uncertain system controlled by the NN controller. The effectiveness of the technique is illustrated through simulations conducted on a nonlinear single-link robot system, which involves training an NN to control the robot's movement while mimicking an ideal reference model.

Ties between  amoebae from tropical geometry, the Mahler measure in number theory, and quiver gauge theories, along with dimer models, have been explored. Similar connections in their coefficients and dependence on the Newton polynomial were discovered. Utilizing genetic symbolic regression methods, a relationship was found between numerical values associated with 2d and 3d amoeba components, and the Mahler measure. This connection is defined as a polynomial of the same degree as the amoeba's dimension, which holds true for d = 2 and 3. Extensions to non-reflexive Mahler measure have also been analyzed, along with employing machine learning to identify the topology of 3d amoebae. Analytical descriptions of the boundaries for certain amoebae have also been derived.

Due to its diverse uses, the graph partitioning problem draws significant interest from researchers and experts who work with it. This problem's wide range of applications has led to various strategies such as multilevel graph partitioning and generalized solvers, which include Gurobi and CPLEX, in an attempt to effectively resolve it. However, studying the weaknesses of existing methods is crucial to overcoming this issue's computational challenges. The constraints of traditional computing power, which follow Moore's law, have necessitated the investigation of new and innovative methods like utilizing special-purpose hardware, like quantum computers or their analogs, for tackling problems like the one mentioned. This work involves testing and comparing how well the graph partitioning problem can be resolved using the Fujitsu Digital Annealer - a hardware specifically designed to tackle optimization problems - and existing top-notch solutions. This experiment showcases both limitations in current optimization solvers on denser graphs as well as those of the Fujitsu Digital Annealer when used to process sparser ones. This leads to new opportunities of merging these different approaches in a hybrid solution.

This paper focuses on finite effect algebras with a state defined, which involves constructing matrices $A$ and $B$ related to a finite effect algebra $E$, then establishing that when $E$ has a state, the ranks of $A$ and $B$ are equal.

Our analysis of magnetar spectral lines is conducted within the scope of upcoming cutting-edge X-ray telescopes that possess superior resolution, effective area, and data processing efficiency. Specifically, we explore the implications of these advanced instruments on our understanding of persistent magnetar activity and transient bursts. Furthermore, our preliminary investigations on phase-resolved magnetar emission demonstrate the need for simultaneous measurements of spectral line intensity, breadth, and energy. Subsequent simulations using current and prospective X-ray telescopes highlight the capacity of these future instruments to elucidate the geometry and dynamics of quiescent and bursting regions within magnetars.

This paper will examine the behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations in the half-plane, under initial conditions that reflect fluid movement along the boundary. Assuming the data to be analytically determined, we'll demonstrate the existence of a solution that is unaffected by viscosity, valid over a small, time-independent interval. The solution will be constructed through an innovative method combining asymptotic expansions from the Euler and Prandtl equations, along with an error component that diminishes in accordance with the square root of the viscosity. As the solution of the Prandtl equation contains singular elements, they will significantly impact the regularity of the error. Furthermore, this error will comprise separate Euler, Prandtl corrections and a residual component. An analytically-oriented setting will primarily be used due to complexities inherent in the Prandtl equation.

The AFM CrI$_3$ bilayer exhibits unique characteristics of van der Waals 2D semiconductors that have drawn significant interest due to their magnetism and potential in spintronics. Through ab initio density-functional theory, we have examined the spin texture in momentum space of the doubly degenerate highest valence band of the AFM CrI$_3$ bilayer with perpendicular Cr-spin moments. We found evidence of a Rashba in-plane spin texture, distinctively present within the main central part of the Brillouin zone. Furthermore, intrinsic local electric fields on each layer have resulted in spin textures with opposite signs on the two layers. To understand wavefunction segregation, we have introduced a small electric field, which led to a substantial splitting of degenerate states, corresponding to their occupancy within a specific layer. We found that the highest valence band wavefunctions show significant segregation within nearly the whole Brillouin zone. Moreover, this segregation of wavefunctions has resulted in a unique layer locking phenomenon for in-plane-canted spin. We highlight the crucial role of the band separation in valence bands and the band interactions in disrupting the layer locking phenomenon at the $K$, $K'$, and $\Gamma$ points. Lastly, we have contrasted the observed layer locking phenomenon with hidden spin polarization mechanisms observed in other nonmagnetic centrosymmetric materials. We emphasize the distinct nature of these mechanisms and the resulting implications for layer locking phenomena. We suggest that a similar spin phenomenon may occur in other van der Waals AFM bilayers exhibiting strong spin-orbit coupling and an isolated energy band.

Closed-shell pair geminal wavefunctions' scalar products and density matrix elements can be directly calculated using the pair amplitudes, yielding a version of Wick's theorem applicable to fermions and bosons. The computational complexity of this approach is typically insurmountable, however, a method to simplify this is identified for Richardson-Gaudin states, the antisymmetrized geminal power, and the antisymmetrized product of strongly-orthogonal geminals. Additionally, the technique is successfully applied to compute dissociation curves for hydrogen chains using off-shell Richardson-Gaudin states and the antisymmetrized product of interacting geminals, both yielding near-exact results and suggesting a possible correction for previously obtained incorrect results from ground-state Richardson-Gaudin states.

A novel technique is introduced, combining genetic algorithms and resource allocation (GA-RA) to enhance energy efficiency in multi-user massive multiple-input multiple-output systems that utilize OFDM-based transmission. A hybrid precoding framework consisting of three stages is developed: radio frequency beamforming, baseband precoding, and resource allocation. First, an integrated RF beamformer for all subcarriers is designed, employing angle-of-departure information. To boost energy efficiency, the RF beamformer reduces hardware complexity and power consumption through a limited number of RF chains. Next, the optimized reduced-size CSI is utilized for unique BB precoder and RA designs per subcarrier. A zero-forcing approach is used for BB precoder development, followed by a RA block built via the GA-RA method for optimizing throughput through resource and power allocation. Results indicate that GA-RA yields significantly improved throughput performance in MU-mMIMO-OFDM systems compared to EQ-RA and PSO-RA methods, particularly with increased subcarrier count at low transmission powers.

In this work, we address a challenging problem of reaching a decentralized consensus while ensuring the confidentiality of the involved parties' data. The setting involves multiple networked nodes, each having their own value that they seek to combine to find a group average without disclosing their individual data to the others. The distributed consensus issue is an established area of research, yet the leading consensus methods are based on nodes exchanging data with neighbors which compromises the secrecy of the users' values. To address this issue, we developed an algorithmic framework capable of reaching the same level of convergence and rate as traditional consensus methods while protecting the users' values. The key aspect of our proposed method involves constructing noisy messages exchanged between nodes, allowing the algorithm to converge to the average of the values while minimizing data exposure. By mathematically analyzing the interdependence between a node's private data and the adversary's collection of messages over time, we demonstrated the efficacy of our method in maintaining users' privacy for any network configuration without a so-called "generalized leaf." Our approach permits achieving the desired precision without compromising privacy requirements. The level of required convergence speed is inversely correlated to the level of required privacy.

Recent advancements in multi-agent reinforcement learning rely heavily on 
training in a centralized manner and exchanging policies. This centralised approach
gets rid of a significant problem known as non-stationarity in multi-agent settings 
but causes large communication overhead. Moreover, policy exchange appears to be
very effective for fast learning in some tasks even though its effectiveness
has not been mathematically justified yet. This paper provides a formal analysis of a
subset of cooperative games where the agents' behaviour follows a certain pattern
such that exchanging policies doesn't lead to inferior performance. This result 
allows us to develop a new, agreement-based decentralized actor-critic algorithm 
that applies updates to both the decision-making components (actors) and their value 
estimates (critics), guaranteeing the algorithm will converge to an optimal solution. 
Furthermore, we propose several practical variants of this method to reduce 
communication during the training phase without sacrificing policy quality, 
resulting in policies comparable to those obtained from the more complex centralized
approach.

Our research involves studying the motion of a solid sphere in a stratified liquid, consisting of two distinct layers, when acted upon by gravity, within the regime of potential flow.  Experimentally, we've observed that when the sphere has a precise critical density, higher than that of the bottom layer, it can exhibit unusual behaviors, such as bouncing or being halted after crossing the fluid's boundary.  We found that by increasing the transition layer's thickness in the fluid density, the sphere's critical density is lowered. Conversely, we also discovered that when the bottom layer's density is increased, while keeping the top layer's density constant, the sphere's critical density is increased linearly.  We suggest an estimate for the sphere's critical density, calculated based on the sphere's potential energy, and we demonstrate that this proposed estimate represents an upper limit of the sphere's critical density, differing by less than 5 percent from the sphere's critical density measured within our experiments which ranges approximately between 0.997 and 1.09 grams per cubic centimeter.

Our team collected and analyzed ultraviolet and optical observations of SN 2020jfo, a rare Type IIP supernova. SN 2020jfo occurred in the spiral galaxy M61, where eight supernovae have been observed over the past 100 years. SN 2020jfo displayed an exceptionally short-lived plateau, lasting less than 65 days. We determined the supernova reached a maximum brightness in the V-band about 8 days post-explosion, and its unique characteristics include reduced H-alpha absorption and the presence of $^{58}$Ni at a distinct wavelength during the nebular phase. We utilized the MESA + STELLA framework to model the supernova, suggesting the ejecta mass was approximately 5 solar masses and the possible red supergiant progenitor had a ZAMS mass around 12 solar masses. We identified a secondary radiation source within the first 20 days of SN 2020jfo, attributed to the interaction with a surrounding mass of material. We estimate the interacting mass was about 0.2 solar masses and likely originated from a period of increased mass loss 20 years prior to the supernova.

The electric power system is undergoing significant changes due to the increasing prevalence of renewable energy sources and the resulting shutdown of traditional power plants using synchronous generators. As main ancillary service providers are being phased out, the need for new flexibility and reserve providers is emerging. The widespread adoption of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) in modern distribution networks offers distribution system operators fresh opportunities, allowing them to fill the market gap by leveraging DER flexibility. This research introduces a novel centralized MPC-based controller, which enables a group of diverse DERs in active distribution grids to simultaneously provide voltage support and primary and secondary frequency control. An input-multirate control framework is utilized to manage the different timescales and service demands for each ancillary service, and allocate resources effectively. Moreover, an efficient approach is presented to incorporate network constraints into the formulation, using linear power flow and network reduction techniques, and applying network decomposition to incorporate different DER dynamics and capability curves. The proposed controller's performance is evaluated using dynamic simulations on various case studies, specifically on the IEEE 33-bus system.

The concept of percolation revolves around complex systems featuring disorder, typically defined as random objects positioned within an underlying network or continuous space. Although this setup appears straightforward, many percolative systems undergo a transformation from isolated groups to a single, extensive cluster when a certain threshold is reached. Similar to thermodynamic phase transitions, critical percolation often results in power-law dependencies near this threshold. Scaling and renormalization serve as valuable tools to grasp the origin of these relationships and obtain precise measurements. In this research, we delve into percolation on a hierarchical framework, leveraging decimation procedures to determine accurate values for critical exponents. Analytical calculations are provided for the complete set of geometric critical exponents, and these findings are validated through simulation results. Moreover, we introduce an intriguing renormalization framework for calculating the system's conductivity and extract the corresponding exponent through computational methods.

We formulate Beilinson-Tate conjectures for specific representations of PGSp6 tied to Spin L-function behavior at s=1, then apply the G2/PGSp6 theta correspondence and a particular archimedean integral non-vanishing assumption to validate the Gross-Savin conjecture on type G2, rank 7 motives.

An axi-symmetric galaxy model of NGC 628 has been created using a sophisticated code that simulates how starlight interacts with interstellar dust, also accounting for the presence of certain hydrocarbons, scattered radiation and dust grain heating. The successful model of this nearly face-on spiral galaxy replicates its large-scale geometry and various spectral profiles. Notably, it predicts the growth rate of dust emissivity across the submillimeter spectrum and demonstrates the insignificant influence of disk growth mechanisms predicted by some galaxy formation theories. Our results also indicate an important contribution of dust grains found at greater radii, suggesting the presence of effective transport processes. Young stellar populations are the primary drivers of dust emission in NGC 628, while the central dust is primarily heated by old bulge populations, yielding a calculated star formation rate of $\rm SFR=2.00\pm0.15\,{\rm M}_{\odot}{\rm yr}^{-1}$ for the galaxy.

Large-scale language models often encounter duplicated data, both by design to prioritize high-quality information and due to imperfect deduplication methods. Researchers have found that such repetition negatively affects model performance, prompting a more systematic exploration in this paper. We trained multiple models, exposing a small percentage of the data to repetition to examine its impact on performance. Our findings reveal a previously unnoticed 'double descent' phenomenon, in which the inclusion of duplicated data leads to an unexpected increase in test loss during training. Moreover, we discovered that a narrow frequency range of repetition severely hinders model performance, with up to 100 repetitions of just 0.1% duplicated data causing an 800 million parameter model to perform similarly to one with only 400 million parameters, despite 90% of the data being unique. Our research suggests that a crucial turning point might exist when the model begins to prioritize memorization over learning generalizable patterns. Our findings, also informed by mechanistic interpretability methods, demonstrate how repeated data disproportionately compromises critical copying and structural elements required for successful generalization, potentially leading to an overreliance on memorization, thus shedding light on why even a small percentage of duplicated data in large models can cause substantial harm.

This work investigates the Maximin Share (MMS) concept in allocating indivisible tasks fairly. Researchers have achieved 11/9-approximate allocations under additive valuation models. However, for valuations beyond additivity, the scenario significantly diverges when it comes to indivisible tasks. We find that constant approximation in submodular valuation models, in contrast to goods allocation, has a best-case scenario of n-fold. We proceed by studying specific task-allocation settings involving bin-packing and machine scheduling, in both of which we find efficient constant approximation algorithms for fair allocation under the original conditions, but the proportionality up to an item notion yields a best-case scenario of n-fold.

Films thinner than a micron drifting through space can escape the galactic plane 
due to pressure exerted by radiation from nearby stars. This can be due to 
either natural dust formations within newly forming planetary systems or from 
artificial creations made by technological societies.  The accumulated material, 
whether natural or synthetic, will gradually rise above the galactic disk due 
to its relation to the mass halo containing dark matter. However, observations of 
starlight indicate this interstellar film contains a very small proportion of the 
interstellar medium's total mass, at less than two thousandths.

We've developed an algorithm for systematically and accurately proving that specific energy ranges create gaps in the spectral properties of materials with quasicrystalline structure through numerical calculations on a contained area. This algorithm is used to verify the presence of energy gaps in the Hofstadter model when arranged in the Ammann-Beenker pattern, confirming a spectral gap that prior numerical tests could not determine with certainty. The proposed algorithm's effectiveness can be applied to a broader class of materials with finite complexity and can identify all relevant energy gaps, thus surpassing earlier theoretical limitations regarding the computational determination of energy gaps in more general Hamiltonian systems.

Our focus lies in addressing the issue of optimal charging timing for electric vehicles, by translating this challenge into a complex mathematical model that aims to minimize charging losses. To mitigate the difficulty associated with solving this model, we introduce the PXA algorithm, a relaxation approach that yields accurate global solutions under specified conditions. Building upon the PXA, we also developed a PXA-MPC strategy that enables the PXA to be effectively utilized in real-time. Notably, our proposed algorithm showcases considerable improvement over traditional balancing methods in several key areas, including energy delivery optimization, reduced charging costs, and more comprehensive energy management planning. These claims are substantiated by experimental results derived from a live adaptive electric vehicle charging network.

Our research explores the link between productivity, R&D, and innovation for Estonian companies at different stages. Uniquely, a significant number of firms in Estonia innovate despite only a small proportion investing in formal R&D. The study reveals that the effectiveness of innovation is notably higher for new companies than established ones. Specifically, companies that innovate are 21-30% more productive than non-innovators within the same category. The picture is less stark for established firms where productivity gains are 10-13% for innovators versus non-innovators. Another interesting finding shows that established Estonian companies can match the performance of their peers in developed countries when translating scientific and technological advancements into productivity gains. The study also finds that upgrading capital can drive productivity gains but is even more effective when combined with R&D efforts. The study ultimately concludes that the effectiveness of some policies promoting productivity growth may be less relevant for developing countries due to different structural factors.

The eigenfrequency of gravitational waves emitted by cold neutron stars can be a complex number, with the real part indicating oscillation frequency and the imaginary part indicating damping rate, resulting in a two-dimensional eigenvalue problem. However, to simplify calculations, one can adopt an approximation that reduces the eigenvalue problem to one dimension. We investigate the validity of one such approximation, the zero-damping approximation, for its accuracy in determining fundamental and first-pressure modes of oscillation. Despite limitations in applying this approximation to the spacetime mode due to similar oscillation and damping frequencies, we identify an empirical relationship between the damping rate and oscillation frequency, primarily influenced by a star's compactness. By leveraging this empirical relationship, the eigenfrequency problem can be recast in a one-dimensional eigenvalue framework. Consequently, we demonstrate that this approach yields reasonable frequency estimates, including for the first spacetime mode.

This work diverges from standard knowledge distillation methods by focusing on a more robust teacher. We find that utilizing an exceptionally strong teacher results in students often making more disparate predictions, disrupting training if an exact prediction match is required. To resolve this, we develop a novel approach, DIST, that emphasizes maintaining the connections between the teacher's and student's predictions, employing a correlation-based loss function to capture inter-class relationships directly. Additionally, we adapt this concept to better account for varying semantic similarities between instances and classes within the same class. The simplicity and effectiveness of our method are validated by its ability to deliver outstanding results across a range of models, training strategies, and tasks including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, as demonstrated in our extensive experiments. The code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD.

Building Information Modeling has demonstrated considerable potential in improving energy efficiency within buildings. By employing deconstruction and retrofitting strategies in existing buildings, energy usage can be significantly optimized. Many older cities, constructed without energy-saving principles in mind, are now seeking smarter approaches to energy management. Unfortunately, current BIM generation methods, centered on individual buildings, are time-consuming and costly when applied to larger communities, such as entire cities. In this research, a novel method is proposed to efficiently create prototype buildings, facilitating the compilation and analysis of essential statistics. Our method suggests enhanced energy-efficient models for existing buildings, identifies and geolocates them in 3D point cloud data, and showcases its efficacy through experiments on a synthetic dataset.

When a single input image is insufficient for accurate object classification, considering multiple images depicting the same object from various perspectives can significantly enhance scene understanding and boost performance. Nonetheless, addressing the challenge of incomplete or missing data inherent in this'multi-view image classification' process has been a hurdle. To resolve this, we present an innovative method for multi-view image classification that incorporates deep learning techniques and metric learning to effectively mitigate data deficiencies. By employing state-of-the-art methodologies, our method offers flexibility for seamless adaptation across diverse applications and domains. Comprehensive testing of our proposed approach on two distinctly different multi-view aerial-ground datasets yields promising results, indicating notable improvements in classification accuracy relative to existing methods. The associated code has been made available for public access.

This article re-examines smoothing bounds across two key cryptographic areas: lattice structures and error-correcting codes, initially linked by the pioneering work of Micciancio and Regev, and have since underpinned many lattice-based encryption systems. By stepping back from direct practical considerations, we delve into the fundamental methods for deriving these bounds for both lattice structures and error-correcting codes, and transfer these methods across these two domains, considering multiple types of noise distributions that conform to a spherical symmetry.

This research evaluates the potential of well-established quantum computing algorithms for error-resistant computations in simulating the behavior of laser-energized electrons within molecules like lithium hydride on a quantum computer simulator. Comparisons were made with the time-dependent full configuration interaction method to validate the outcomes. Utilizing the Jordan-Wigner transformation and Trotter product formula allowed the reproduction of actual electron dynamics. Moreover, the time-dependent dipole moment was calculated through the Hadamard test as an example of a time-dependent expectation value. By employing the quantum imaginary time evolution algorithm to incorporate non-Hermitian operators into the dynamics, the model accurately simulated the ionization of a hydrogen molecule influenced by a complex absorbing potential. Due to their polynomial scaling as opposed to exponential, the quantum computing algorithms used here hold great potential for significant advancements in understanding the behavior of electron dynamics within larger molecular systems in the future.

We investigate how a generalization of the Heisenberg uncertainty relations and the theory of general relativity interact. We find that, in cases where these modified uncertainty relations apply, the standard interpretation of the equivalence principle no longer holds, since the mass of particles can change based on position. This finding is obtained by analyzing the implications of these relations for particles described by both scalar and spinor fields. We discover that, in non-relativistic systems, the mass ratio remains constant regardless of these modifications.

$^{180m}$Ta, an exceptionally stable nuclear isomer and naturally occurring isotope, has drawn attention from various fields due to its applications in dark matter detection, gamma laser technology, and astrophysics. Its excitation energy had previously been estimated from existing nuclear reaction data but had yet to be measured directly. We have utilized a state-of-the-art mass spectrometer to accurately measure this isomer's mass, finding that the mass difference between its ground and excited states is 76.79 keV, with the associated error. This is the first precise direct measurement of the excitation energy for $^{180m}$Ta, exceeding the accuracy of the previous estimate of 75.3 keV.

Using 3 prominent models that correlate radiative efficiency with parameters of active galactic nuclei, we calculated the efficiency and spin of nearby galactic nuclei (z < 0.34). The resulting data analysis revealed a decrease in spin over cosmic time, aligning with the findings of theoretical studies by other researchers. Notably, spin increased with the mass of the supermassive black hole and the bolometric luminosity, a prediction that aligns with theoretical expectations. Examination of the spin distribution showed a prominent peak within the 0.75-1.0 range. Approximately 40% of the objects possessed a spin greater than 0.75, while around 50% exhibited a spin greater than 0.5, findings consistent with our previous work and that of other researchers.

Our evaluation of the 'optimal fingerprinting' methodology as presented by Allen and Tett (1999) is examined from the standpoint of statistical analysis in the light of McKitrick's (2021) recent critique.  It's determined that the 'optimal fingerprinting' approach can largely withstand criticism by McKitrick (2021) if two requirements are met: (a) the null simulation generated by the climate model is independent of real-world observations, and (b) the null simulation produces consistent estimates of the covariance of real-world observations' residuals, which is contingent on climate model performance.  If these requirements are not met, while still providing an unbiased and consistent estimator under typical circumstances, the 'optimal fingerprinting' approach loses its primary advantage.  A test for residual consistency suggested by Allen and Tett (1999) is also shown to be a suitable tool for verifying the agreement between the covariance of the null simulation and the covariance of real-world observations' residuals.  Finally, we elaborate on the connection between the 'optimal fingerprinting' approach and the Feasible Generalized Least Square technique.

Historically, sign language resources were mainly collected within controlled
environments for the purposes of guided sign categorization and linguistic analysis
requiring specific annotation types. So far, limited research exists that utilizes
signed content available on social media platforms along with the implementation
of unsupervised methods applied to such datasets. The call for increased data diversity
is driven by the fact that obtaining a satisfactory model performance with the new data,
which varies from training data, necessitates the utilization of external resources.
Given that collecting and annotating sign language data is often a resource-intensive task,
it's desirable to expedite the annotation process, which has been a significant concern
of late. Taking into account these developments, this study endeavours to tap into online data,
pursuing an automated creation and annotation of sign language databases through phoneme
aggregation methods for efficiency.

Robots designed for tracking people have a wide range of uses, including security systems, assisting the elderly, and social companions. Notably, this task is complicated when a person is part of a crowded group. Existing trackers have achieved notable improvements but typically fail to handle scenarios with large uniform crowds. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes an object tracker designed to enhance a robot's perception in real-time, focusing on developing a more accurate person following system. We introduce a new RGB-D tracker called Deep Tracking with RGB-D (DTRD) which can successfully operate in environments characterized by large uniform crowds. Our tracker combines a transformer architecture with RGB and depth information to help distinguish the target person from similar distracting individuals. In a series of comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our tracker in achieving superior results in key performance metrics, outperforming other current state-of-the-art trackers.

Our study on thermoelectric properties in 2D materials involves materials with two Dirac bands and a nonlinear band, based on three- and two-band models analyzed through the linearized Boltzmann transport theory with the relaxation time approximation. We discovered that, in the three-band model, combining Dirac bands with a heavy nonlinear band (be it parabolic or pudding-mold shaped) has limited impact on their thermoelectric performance. The apparent difference in their thermoelectric performance arises when varying the position of the nonlinear band relative to the maximum figure of merit (ZT), and the three-band model reaches its optimal ZT when its nonlinear band intersects with the Dirac bands near the Fermi level. We achieved better thermoelectric performance when we eliminated the linear conduction band and transitioned from the three-band model to the two-band model, resulting in significantly higher ZT values.

In modern life, powerful mobile and wearable devices working in conjunction with stationary anchors in indoor settings, offer a widespread solution to meet the growing need for indoor location-based services. Among various localization technologies, BLE- and RSS-based systems have gained significant attention for their affordability and widespread device accessibility, although they can be error-prone due to changing signals, insufficient or poorly placed anchors, and differing device capabilities. This research develops an alternative method to tackle these challenges by harnessing data from neighboring devices to supplement a broader positioning network, where a sophisticated neural network interprets the devices' positional and signal data to calculate relative distances, applying lateration to derive collaborative location estimates, which ultimately combines stand-alone and collective estimates for a final device position. Experiment results confirm that this collaborative method outperforms standalone lateration in positioning accuracy.

Our study examines polarized gravitational waves originating from chiral fermions during the early universe's formation, with a particular focus on the contribution of left-handed neutrinos in thermal equilibrium, taking into account temperature and chemical potential. The analysis involves calculating the correlation functions of gravitational waves that correspond to the Stokes parameter V, which is key to characterizing gravitational wave polarization in both Minkowski and expanding spacetime settings. In an expanding universe scenario, we observe that thermalized neutrinos produce a non-zero V value directly proportional to the neutrino degeneracy parameter and the wavenumber of gravitational waves in the long-wavelength region. While current and future third-generation gravitational wave detectors cannot measure the tiny amplitude of gravitational waves generated by thermal neutrinos, advanced detectors for high-frequency signals might help uncover information about the early universe's neutrino degeneracy parameter.

Numerous studies have examined the empirical distribution functions (EDFs) based on ranked set sampling (RSS) and its modifications in infinite population contexts. Investigating EDF estimators for finite populations is more beneficial in areas like environmental science, ecology, and agriculture, among others. This research proposes new EDF estimators based on level-0, level-1, and level-2 sampling designs within RSS and establishes their asymptotic properties. It also compares the estimators' performance when ranking is imperfect under different distributions, finding level-2 sampling to outperform level-0, level-1, and simple random sampling in efficiency. Furthermore, the study demonstrates the application of level-2 sampling design to a real-world problem, estimating a distribution function and the median weight of seven-month-old sheep using RSS.

Our research focuses on how the presence of a binary companion influences black hole superradiance, especially at frequencies outside of the gravitational-collider-physics (GCP) resonance range. When the superradiant state couples to an extremely absorptive state via the tidal disturbance from the companion, it leads to reduced superradiance. If the companion is too close, the superradiance rate turns negative, and the surrounding boson cloud is engulfed by the black hole. This proximity constraint severely limits GCP. Furthermore, for companions with a mass ratio exceeding $10^{-3}$, all GCP high-energy transitions are disallowed, except in the $|\psi_{211}\rangle$ state; while nearly all Bohr transitions cease, except in the specified state. Notably, the reaction of the companion results in an unstable binary, which could result in rising or sinking orbital paths observable through pulsar timing. It may also be instrumental in removing constraints related to ultralight boson mass that were imposed by past non-observable results.

The appearance of charged lepton flavor violation is an unmistakable indicator of the presence of New Physics.
In this paper, a concise overview of the theoretical and experimental findings on the search for charged lepton flavor violation is presented, with a focus on heavy particle decays such as those involving the Z boson, Higgs boson, and top quark.
This study also examines potential deviations from Standard Model expectations through decays involving exotic particles, including a Z' or additional scalar bosons.
Additionally, we assess the possibilities for conducting such searches at upcoming high-energy electron-positron colliders.

The phase $\phi_s$ from CP violation, $B_s$ decay widths and the differences in these widths are particularly responsive indicators of potential new physics phenomena that could impact the theory of heavy quark expansion. Investigation into measuring these aspects at future facilities that use the Z-particle (referred to as Z factories) revealed that operation in a high-capacity mode could lead to precision at the following levels: $\sigma(\phi_s) = 4.3~\mathrm{mrad}$, $\sigma(\Delta\Gamma_s) = 0.24~\mathrm{ns^{-1}}$, and $\sigma(\Gamma_s) = 0.072~\mathrm{ns^{-1}}$. The attainable accuracy in determining $\phi_s$ compares favourably with projections for how accurately it could be calculated via the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, and the required precision in determining this factor is just 30% higher than anticipated at the latter location. If instead the high-capacity Z-particle operation is increased tenfold, it is theoretically possible to calculate $\phi_s$ to a value only 41% higher than anticipated at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider. On the other hand, it is found that measurements of $\Gamma_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ will not significantly benefit from the superior time-resolution capabilities or the tagging power present at future Z-particle factories. It will be necessary for ten times increased capacity at the high-capacity Z-particle operation before $\Gamma_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ reach levels 18% higher in accuracy compared to that of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider.

A fundamental mapping of brain function onto the organization of its folded cortex has long been sought, as understanding the distinct roles of its building blocks can revolutionize the study of both biological and artificial neural systems. Yet, existing theories and computational models fall short, mainly due to the inherent complexities of this nonlinear relationship and its susceptibility to variability among individuals. Our approach centers around incorporating functional gradients from resting-state brain scans and employing a cutting-edge model combining attention with convolutional mesh analysis, which considers the interconnected dynamics of both cortical folds and functional patterns. By harnessing this synergistic relationship, our model demonstrates superior predictive capabilities over current methods. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the key contributors to cortical folding are not those that hold dominant functional gradients but rather a network of interconnected regions that subtly influence this complex process. Our results suggest that custom-built artificial intelligence models hold the key to accurately deciphering the intricate link between brain function and its folded architecture.

We are proposing a combined influence of Terahertz and Gigahertz electromagnetic waves in a cryogenic environment with electrons suspended on liquid helium. Terahertz waves have a near-optimal frequency for the surface electrons, aligning with the transition energy between their lowest energy levels. Meanwhile, the Gigahertz wave induces a Stark effect in these electrons, causing asymmetry. Our research demonstrates a significant connection between these two types of electromagnetic waves, which occurs at the threshold where the difference between the electron energy and the Terahertz wave is equivalent to the frequency of the Gigahertz wave. By interacting, the Terahertz and Gigahertz waves cooperate to excite electrons, leading to low-frequency electrical currents perpendicular to the liquid helium surface. These currents can be measured using the image-charge technique and offer an alternative way to detect Terahertz radiation.

Due to numerous false alarms in automatically generated static code warnings, 
developers currently address only a small proportion of them. To enhance 
identification of warnings deserving attention, researchers propose delving into 
algorithms to identify optimised parameter choices tailored to their specific 
problem context. Our study reveals that developing accurate warning predictors 
can be achieved through techniques adjusting the boundary between actionable and 
dismissed warnings. By locally fine-tuning this threshold, the effectiveness 
in recognising valuable static code warnings can be substantially increased. 
Results of applying this approach on eight Java projects demonstrate exceptional 
success in 50% of the test cases and, in total, an average prediction rate of 
92% for the selected datasets.

We examine the conditions for the operator $H=-\frac{1}{\rho}\nabla\cdot \rho \mathbb D\nabla +V$ to be essentially self-adjoint, given specific domain requirements, across a broad spectrum of coefficients. Our findings provide key insights into the boundary behavior of coefficients $\rho$, $\mathbb D$, and $V$, necessary for $H$ to be essentially self-adjoint, accompanied by a newly proven weak anisotropic Hardy inequality of independent significance.

This paper investigates elliptic relative equilibria in the restricted 4-body problem where three primary masses form a collinear Euler configuration within a two-dimensional space, resulting in symplectic reduction for a generalised N-body problem. Through an analysis linking this restricted problem to elliptic Lagrangian solutions, we utilize the omega-Maslov index to assess linear stability. Additionally, our numerical calculations yield stability conditions related to mass parameters in symmetrical cases.

We develop a Rademacher-type theorem involving Hamiltonians $H(x,p)$ with very mild requirements in both Euclidean and Carnot-Carathéodory settings. Notably, $H(x,p)$ is assumed to be merely measurable with respect to $x$ and quasiconvex and lower-semicontinuous in terms of $p$. Furthermore, applying the Rademacher-type theorem enables us to establish the existence of absolute minimizers for corresponding $L^\infty$-functionals, thus advancing or broadening previously known findings in the literature.

The field of generating highly realistic images has experienced significant progress in recent years, primarily driven by the advancements of deep neural networks and generative models. Specifically, face photos have garnered substantial attention, resulting in the development of numerous models for generating and manipulating faces. One crucial application in this domain is facial attribute manipulation, a technique that allows for the modification of one or more facial attributes without altering the remaining image attributes. The modifications can be inputted in the form of attribute vectors or using a reference face image. This paper presents an in-depth review of recent research advancements in semantic facial attribute manipulation. It covers key concepts, architectures, evaluation methods, datasets, loss functions, and applications of these models. Moreover, it categorizes and analyzes the state-of-the-art models based on their architectures into encoder-decoder, image-to-image, and photo-guided models. The current challenges and limitations of these methods are also thoroughly discussed.

Skin cancer's most severe type, melanoma, requires doctors to invest more time to differentiate it from its benign counterparts, due to their similar appearance. Current diagnosis primarily relies on an invasive tissue analysis. Developing a more precise tool can help reduce skin cancer's damaging impact and significantly boost patient survival chances. This study presents a novel multi-class classifier based on the CoAtNet model, a fusion of traditional convolutional neural networks and transformative models that uses self-attention mechanisms to enhance accuracy. The proposed system boasts an impressive performance, yielding a precision of 0.901, a recall of 0.895, and an AP of 0.923, significantly outperforming other cutting-edge networks.

Objective: We aim to refine the orbital characteristics and determine the orientation of five planetary systems with eccentric transits. These systems consist of a Jupiter-class exoplanet, with HAT-P-26 being an exception due to hosting a Neptune-class exoplanet. Methodology: By leveraging precise velocity measurements obtained via HARPS-N spectroscopy, along with archival Gaia data, and newly collected TESS and medium-class telescope data, we obtained a more in-depth understanding of the planets' systems. These data allowed us to recalculate parameters, such as photometric data, assess the influence of stellar atmospheric characteristics, and evaluate the planets' spin orientation. Outcome: By applying our analysis of the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect to each system, we obtained projected planetary inclination measurements of approximately 13, -26.3, -0.7, -26, and -26.3 degrees for the planets of HAT-P-15, HAT-P-17, HAT-P-21, and HAT-P-29, respectively. Unfortunately, due to suboptimal data quality, the orientation for HAT-P-26 could not be reliably ascertained; however, it is suspected to have a prograde orbit. Observations of HAT-P-21 also suggested that the star has a rotational period of about 15.88 days, allowing us to establish its degree of misalignment as approximately 25 degrees. Review of the existing parameters of the five planetary systems indicated conformity with prior literature values. It was further observed that the transit timing of HAT-P-26 system demonstrated signs of temporal variability, with possible explanations suggesting a companion object within its system.

To identify brief planetary signals, researchers analyzed the extensive datasets generated by high-cadence microlensing surveys, uncovering four new planetary systems - OGLE-2017-BLG-1691L, KMT-2021-BLG-0320L, KMT-2021-BLG-1303L, and KMT-2021-BLG-1554L. In spite of their short observation periods ranging from hours to days, all systems displayed distinct planetary signals in the combined lensing data. It's discovered that three systems possess planet-to-host mass ratios around $10^{-4}$ while the other is approximately $10^{-3}$. The mass calculations suggest that all newly found planets possess sub-Jovian masses. KMT-2021-BLG-0320Lb and KMT-2021-BLG-1554Lb correspond to roughly $0.38$ and $0.10$ of Jupiter's mass while KMT-2021-BLG-1303Lb and OGLE-2017-BLG-1691Lb correspond to roughly $0.38$ and $0.38$ of Jupiter and Uranus mass, respectively. KMT-2021-BLG-1554L's estimated mass is approximately $0.08~M_\odot$, which indicates it lies near the boundary between stars and brown dwarfs. Besides KMT-2021-BLG-1554L, other planetary host stars are characterized by low masses ranging approximately $0.3-0.6 M_\odot$. The successful discoveries of these planets demonstrate the capability of current high-cadence microlensing surveys in detecting low-mass planets.

In scientific computing, various applications necessitate the approximation of functions mapping between Banach spaces. Recently introduced FNO and DeepONet can achieve this. However, their approach, involving neural networks, leads to outputs that are  difficult to interpret and susceptible to bias from grid sampling inaccuracies. To overcome this limitation, an alternative proposed in this article utilizes Chebyshev and Fourier series for domain and codomain representations. The resulting Spectral Neural Operator provides interpretable results, resists aliasing, and can include lossless operations on functions, capitalizing on established, fast, and stable spectral method algorithms that require basic linear algebra. Benchmark results show SNO's superiority to FNO and DeepONet in several cases.

The current natural language understanding (NLU) benchmarks set by transformers can be limited due to the generation of unpredictable and highly confident output probabilities, thus hindering the ability to rely on their results for various decisions. We introduce the inductive Venn-ABERS predictors (IVAP), constructed using various pre-trained transformer models, ensuring that these predictors yield consistently well-calibrated predictions within minimal constraints. We conduct a series of tests on a set of distinct NLU tasks and demonstrate the success of IVAP in delivering uniformly calibrated and accurate predictive outcomes, ranging from 0 to 1.

A $k$-dimensional $[n,k]$ binary linear code, $\mathcal{C}$, can be viewed as a subspace of the vector space $\mathbb{F}_2^n$. When $\boldsymbol{x}$ belongs to this space, the resulting collection of sets $\boldsymbol{x} + \mathcal{C}$ defines a coset structure within $\mathcal{C}$. Our work involves exploring a partial ordering among these cosets for a code of length $n$, with an aim to represent their relationship through a graph constructed using an orphaned structure within the code.

We introduce an approach to named entity linking (NEL) leveraging entity representations from multiple embeddings. To examine the effectiveness of this method, and its reliance on specific parameters, we evaluate it using Namesakes, a dataset with particularly challenging named entity ambiguities. Our analysis indicates that the minimum number of entity mentions necessary to establish a knowledge base entity plays a significant role in NEL performance, whereas the number of embeddings is less crucial, and may be minimized with as few as ten. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the performance of knowledge base entity representations can be refined solely using KB data, yielding enhanced NEL performance. Notably, NEL performance is improved by generating embeddings via tuning a language model on a diverse range of news texts, as opposed to fine-tuning on the more uniform text found in public datasets like XSum and CNN/Daily Mail.

In the field of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), a different method for agent interaction is proposed. This method uses an intelligent mediator to process signals from agents, enhancing the collective performance of these agents. To avoid the mediator controlling the system, incentives are provided for agents to decrease their reliance on mediator information and messages influence policy selection, not instantaneous actions. This alternative architecture shows improved performance compared to existing methods in multiple cooperative MARL environments.

Three recently introduced quantum money schemes, first proposed in 2012 by Aaronson and Christiano,  in 2015 were questioned by a conjecture,  in 2017 and then in 2021 by Kane, Sharif and Silverberg,  our research investigates and challenges the underlying security assumptions of these public-key quantum money schemes. The 2012 scheme utilizes vector space $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ with hidden subspaces. In 2015, Pena et al speculated that the problem of this scheme can be resolved in quasi-polynomial time and our results confirm that it is achievable in polynomial time via an algorithm that involves the computation of the Zariski tangent space at random hidden subspace points. In 2017, a multivariate hash-based money scheme was introduced by Zhandry. Using the verification circuit, a banknote can be easily forged via an algorithm that runs in polynomial time and a serial number from a banknote given can easily generate another one. The 2021 money scheme of Kane, Sharif and Silverberg, is centered around the cloning of quantum states which serve as the eigenvectors of certain operators known as Hecke. In this scheme our results indicate that the problem of this quantum cloning can be reduced to a simple linear algebraic problem, thus reducing this hard task to a simpler form and, with our results providing an opening into a better understanding of this quantum scheme via the opening of possible future cryptanalyses and a better understanding of its potential for breaking this quantum-based money.

We establish the precise conditions under which modules over certain types of ring structures, known as Morita contexts, qualify as Gorenstein-projective. Specifically, this involves exploring semi-weak and weak compatibility between these structures, while generalizing existing research and expanding upon its scope. By removing prior restrictions, we identify both necessary and sufficient conditions, providing further insights and a broader application of the concept to noncommutative systems and structures.

Measurements of differential cross-sections in proton Compton scattering have been conducted for scattering angles of 55 degrees, 90 degrees, and 125 degrees. The experiments utilized quasimonoenergetic photon beams with a weighted average energy of either 83.4 megaelectronvolts or 81.3 megaelectronvolts. The High Intensity Gamma-Ray Source facility at the Triangle Universities Nuclear Laboratory played host to these experiments. The data gathered are compared against prior findings, analyzed through the chiral effective field theory framework to determine proton polarizabilities from Compton scattering, ultimately yielding dipole polarizabilities values of $\alpha_{E1}^p = 13.8 \pm1.2 \pm 0.1 \pm 0.3$ and $\beta_{M1}^p = 0.2 \mp 1.2 \pm 0.1 \mp 0.3$ times ten to the negative fourth power, expressed in units of cubic femtometers.

This document aims to address the challenge of minimizing adders/subtractors for implementing massive constant multiplications within a shift-add architecture. To tackle this intricate issue, an approximate algorithm known as T~OLL has been developed, which segments very large constants into smaller parts. By integrating graph-based techniques and eliminating redundant expressions, T~OLL reduces the number of operations involved while taking into account the multiplier-less design delay, measured as the maximum number of operations in series. Experimental findings suggest that the number of adder-steps in a shift-adds design can be greatly reduced with only a small increase in the number of operations. Notably, this shift-adds approach has been shown to yield significant benefits, including a 36.6% decrease in gate-level area compared to designs using a multiplier. Additionally, delay-aware optimization can lead to an impressive 48.3% reduction in minimum achievable delay when compared to area-aware optimization.

Recent advancements in large language models, such as Codex, have demonstrated their potential to produce code for a wide range of programming tasks. However, existing models often fall short, yielding inaccurate results for complex tasks due to a fundamental lack of understanding of program semantics. In this paper, researchers investigated the efficacy of automated program repair (APR) techniques in fixing code generated by large language models, specifically those submitted to LeetCode contests. The goal was to determine whether APR methods could improve the reliability of such code. The study yielded several key findings: Firstly, automated code shares common pitfalls with manually crafted solutions, implying that APR may be effective in fixing code generated by large language models. Secondly, by leveraging statistical fault localization approaches, new editing features in Codex were shown to be on par with, if not surpass, existing tools for repairing Java code, such as TBar and Recoder. The study provides several recommendations for the future of APR tools, including: enhancing patch search capabilities; shifting from pattern-based fixes to synthesis/semantics-based approaches; and exploring the integration of large language models and APR methods to create optimized patch ingredients.

In an analysis involving the Einstein gravity, we introduced a perturbation of the Neumann boundary condition as an end-of-world brane within AdSd+1 spacetime for d > 2. Specifically, for a tensionless brane, we derived an explicit mode expansion of the perturbations. Moreover, for a d-dimensional conformal field theory (BCFT), we found that the energy-momentum tensor must adhere to novel constraints in addition to boundary conformal symmetry constraints when interacting with a d-dimensional gravity under specified boundary conditions. Importantly, these constraints were shown to hold true for a free scalar BCFT. Lastly, within the context of AdS/BCFT, our findings reveal that the Neumann boundary condition permits the tensionless brane to couple with gravity, whereas a nonzero tension brane is enabled to couple with gravity under the conformally Dirichlet boundary condition by exploiting holographic relationships.

This paper enhances the masked image modeling (MIM) technique by introducing novel modifications.
By masking the input image and having the unmasked part predict the missing section, the MIM method teaches the model to identify essential image characteristics. Through our research, we identified three areas to further optimize MIM: First, instead of solely using encoders for downstream tasks, our enhanced model integrates both encoders and decoders for representation learning, even though decoders have an insignificant parameter count. Secondly, our new approach focuses on improving the encoder's performance for downstream tasks by isolating the tasks for comparative learning and token position prediction from the image prediction task, rather than treating it as an interconnected whole. Thirdly, our modification addresses the challenge of handling variable proportions of main and background objects by applying the ContrastiveCrop method, which effectively isolates the main subject in the image. Based on the mentioned enhancements, our new model, Contrastive Masked AutoEncoders (CMAE), achieved a Top-1 accuracy of 65.84% on the tinyimagenet using a ViT-B backbone, significantly surpassing the state-of-the-art methods when other conditions are equal. The corresponding code will be released for further development.

Large-scale text retrieval tasks have shown that pre-trained models such as BERT are highly effective. Current text retrieval systems use a'retrieve-then-rerank' structure, combining high computational costs of pre-trained models and the size of large datasets. In a two-stage framework, researchers have primarily optimized each stage separately to enhance overall performance, with limited exploration into linking features from both stages directly. This study develops Hybrid List Aware Transformer Reranking (HLATR), a subsequent reranking module that merges features from the retrieval and reranking stages to enhance overall performance. HLATR's compact design allows seamless integration into existing retrieval systems, facilitating efficient processing within a single step. Experiments using two large-scale datasets demonstrate HLATR's effectiveness in boosting existing retrieval methods.

Recent advancements have led to the development of mean-field equations capable of approximating the Deffuant model's dynamics. These equations effectively describe both random interactions among individuals in a mixed population and those restricted to network edges. However, interactions can only occur between people with differing opinions below a confidence threshold, strongly influencing the model's behavior. This work delves into a mathematical analysis of mean-field equations to determine the impact of confidence levels on key outcomes. It explores a small confidence interval, pinpoints the driving forces behind opinion changes, and demonstrates how linear stability analysis can predict the formation and location of opinion clusters, aligning with simulations that show accurate results in mixed and two-degree networks as well as fully-mixed populations at the start and the end of the simulation.

In this project, we present DeepFlame, an open-source C++ framework that
allows for seamless integration of machine learning techniques and pre-trained models
to efficiently handle reactive flow simulations. DeepFlame combines the
technical strengths of the widely used computational fluid dynamics library
OpenFOAM, machine learning library Torch, and chemical kinetics program Cantera. The
core of our platform, focusing on cross-library functionality and data
interface management, is carefully designed to facilitate simple and efficient
workflow maintenance, enhancements, and updates. Our platform showcases the
potential of deep learning-based simulations, illustrated by a case study from our
recent research on deep learning-based chemical kinetics prediction (Zhang et al.
Combust. Flame vol. 245, 2022). Thorough validation of our platform was performed
on various reference cases to evaluate its performance and accuracy. Our
algorithms, including those for steady-state and transient simulations, have been
tested for their reliability and precision, and promising outcomes were obtained. The
study also covers several methods aimed at increasing the efficiency of our
computational process, including dynamic load balancing and adaptive mesh
refinements. These techniques' performance has been examined, and significant
improvements in efficiency have been reported. When employed in simulations, our
integrated deep learning model results in approximately two-fold computational speed
improvement in hydrogen ignition on a medium-grade graphics processing unit (GPU).
It's expected that this level of efficiency gain will also be seen in simulations for
more complex fuels like hydrocarbons. Our research indicates a comparable speed-up
can be achieved using an AI-centric chip called a deep computing unit (DCU), thus
suggesting DeepFlame can effectively take advantage of the evolving next-gen
computing architecture.

A light source from a distance d will have a wavefront arrival time difference of approximately 120 (d/100 Mpc)^{-1} nanoseconds at two detectors 100 AU apart, resulting from the wavefront curvature. With gigahertz interferometry, arrival time differences down to better than a nanosecond can be accurately determined, allowing for precise geolocations. Given centimeter-accurate space-time positions, such as with very long baseline interferometry or GNSS geolocations, and sub-nanosecond timing, competitive cosmological constraints are achievable. A four-detector constellation spaced over 10 AU can achieve sub-percent distance measurement precision for extragalactic sources, and correspondingly, determine cosmological parameters like the Hubble constant with comparable precision. Inverse baseline length, distance from the source affects the precision measurement quadratically. Bright, point-like FRBs allow precise extragalactic source measurement but scattering from the Galaxy limits frequencies <3 GHz, and dispersion limits at higher frequencies, with Shapiro time delay also affecting longer baselines. Corrections to detector uncertainty due to variations like the Sun's irradiance and gravitational forces can be made using a weekly GNSS-like positioning method or with precise accelerometer calibration, and the detector position offsets from nearby objects and gravitational waves can be calibrated off of distant FRBs. In addition, such an interferometer can potentially resolve Galactic pulsar radiation regions, determine mass distribution in the outer Solar System and detect gravitational waves of 0.01-100 micro-Hz sensitivity.

Accurate investigations into the physical and chemical properties of line-emitting gas systems rely heavily on plasma diagnostics and require the proper correction of input spectra for extinction. The physical characteristics of the line-emitting gas directly impact the assessment of extinction levels, underscoring the importance of simultaneously and consistently performing extinction correction and plasma diagnostics. Our comparative study of nine bright planetary nebulae in M 31, undertaken with and without accurate extinction correction and plasma diagnostics, demonstrates the detrimental impact of making incorrect initial assumptions about the physical conditions of line-emitting gas on analysis outcomes. Although electron density and temperature are somewhat immune to inconsistent assumptions, compromised extinction levels cause systematic errors in line strength measurements, subsequently affecting inferred elemental abundances and conclusions. Our findings for the M 31 planetary nebula sample confirm their alignment with existing models of planetary nebulae formed from low-mass star progenitors, thereby casting doubt on previous claims of anomalously high nitrogen levels, which were likely attributed to inadequate extinction correction. As a result, it is essential to reevaluate plasma diagnostics results that were not conducted in conjunction with self-consistent extinction correction.

We establish the $q,t$-Catalan measures, a sequence of two-dimensional polynomial measures defined through certain path statistics in the plane. These measures bear resemblance to $q,t$-Catalan numbers due to several combinatorial similarities. Our primary outcome involves the $q,t$-Catalan measures being expressible as a limiting case of a sequence of $q,t$-Catalan numbers as a parameter tends to infinity. Furthermore, the $q,t$-Catalan measures are interpreted in a geometric context as the Duistermaat-Heckman measures of a specific scheme describing subschemes within $\mathbb{C}^2$ centered at the origin.

The current QA models face a limitation known as "disconnected reasoning" where they rely on shortcuts rather than utilizing multi-hop reasoning over multiple supporting facts to arrive at an answer. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach is proposed, specifically a counterfactual multi-hop QA, that incorporates a causal-effect methodology. This methodology involves two aspects: explicitly modeling the causality behind shortcuts and the true multi-hop reasoning, which is subsequently represented as a causal graph. The causal graph enables the implementation of a counterfactual inference, allowing for the isolation of disconnected reasoning and the true multi-hop reasoning, thus offering a more effective method to learn a QA model that relies on genuine multi-hop reasoning. The proposed approach is validated through comprehensive experiments on the HotpotQA dataset, yielding notable improvements in the model's ability to perform true multi-hop reasoning, specifically a 5.8% increase in the Supp$_s$ score. The code implementing the method is provided in the supplementary material.

CORL is a free and publicly available library containing self-contained
single-file implementations of several complex Deep Offline Reinforcement Learning algorithms. It provides a clean coding experience by utilizing a structured codebase with a modern tracking tool. In CORL, individual methods are kept separate and simple, making it easier to notice and improve performance-critical details. Furthermore, users can leverage the experiment tracking functionality to upload various metrics and dependencies to the cloud for easy reference. Additionally, CORL ensures that its algorithms are reliable and efficient by utilizing a standardised benchmarking process on a commonly used dataset called D4RL.

Recent breakthroughs in semantic segmentation have seen impressive outcomes with
transformer-based models, but their time-consuming processing has hindered their use
in real-time applications. This gap has led us to develop RTFormer, a novel, real-time
semantic segmentation network, which strikes a superior balance between performance
and efficiency than CNN-based models. To achieve optimal efficiency on GPU-like
hardware, RTFormer incorporates GPU-friendly attention with a linear time complexity,
alongside omitting multi-head mechanisms. Furthermore, we've found that attention
spanning multiple resolutions offers a more efficient approach to capturing context
information at high resolutions by spreading knowledge acquired from low-resolution
features. Exhaustive tests on benchmark datasets have demonstrated the superiority
of RTFormer, achieving the best results on Cityscapes, CamVid, and COCOStuff, and
promising outcomes on ADE20K. The source code is available on PaddleSeg: 
https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleSeg.

As self-supervised models have grown in size, compressing them has become increasingly important. Notably, shortening the input duration can be an effective alternative to simply reducing model size, which has traditionally been the primary focus. This study investigates fixed and variable length subsampling along the time axis within self-supervised learning to gauge its effect on specific tasks. Results reveal that applying subsampling while training models enhances performance on certain downstream tasks while also significantly accelerating inference. Notably, variable length subsampling performs well, especially at lower frame rates, with the model even exhibiting minimal degradation when using low frame rates, such as 10 Hz, especially if the model is provided with access to phonetic boundaries.

This note establishes that the multiplicative Grothendieck-Springer space inherently features a quasi-Poisson structure. The corresponding group-valued moment map arises as the resolution morphism, with the quasi-Hamiltonian leaves defined as the connected components of the preimages of Steinberg fibers. This finding is a multiplicative counterpart to the conventional Poisson structure on the additive Grothendieck-Springer resolution, serving as an explicit example of a broader reduction method along Dirac realizations, which has been explored in recent research by the author and Mayrand.

We present a quantum field theory model that accurately describes spin-half particles in curved spacetime. By incorporating Einstein's equivalence principle and general covariance into the quantum-particle state definitions, our model paves the way for calculating key observables in gravitational environments. We discover that in curved spacetime, even without torsion, the spin of quantum particles may precess. Notably, this finding contrasts with the spinless case where non-universality of free fall was recently documented.
