To obtain decompositions of 3x3 matrices and to analyze bounded linear operators and endomorphisms, commutators are used, leading to representations of terms as satisfying polynomial equations, also applied to free modules with infinite rank. Furthermore, it is shown that any bounded operator on an infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space can be represented as the sum of four order-3 automorphisms, and every simple quotient ring of the endomorphism ring of an infinite-dimensional vector space, following a maximal ideal quotient, can be decomposed into three nilpotent subrings.

In the context of massless particle states, the Wigner little group's stabilizer, also known as the Borel subgroup of dimension four, is derived from the maximal solvable subgroup of the proper orthochronous Lorentz group. In massless particle scenarios, the state vectors decouple into two separate chiral components - left-handed and right-handed - each represented by distinct solvable subgroups, ${\rm sol}_2^{\pm}$, of order two. Upon inducing Lorentz transformations on generalized particle representations, they can be systematically applied, revealing a fundamental connection between the appearance of nonphysical spin operators and the resulting spin-flip effects.

To construct a call graph without false edges, researchers must make compromises between thoroughness and accuracy. Most static analysis methods create call graphs that contain unnecessary edges due to imprecision. Machine learning models have been proposed to rectify this by fine-tuning call graphs post-processing by identifying unnecessary edges through structural features for classification using a machine learning model. Despite improvements, they still fail to analyze source code effectively due to limited insight. To address this shortcoming, we've created AutoPruner, an advanced edge removal method combining statistical, structural, and semantic code analysis to remove call graph false positives. AutoPruner refines a pre-trained code model to analyze semantic relationships in call graph functions and then uses it to classify each edge in the graph, combining structural features for optimal performance. Our evaluation shows AutoPruner far surpasses previous techniques in call graph accuracy by identifying up to 13% more false-positive edges correctly in call graph edge analysis.

The purpose of this research is to examine specific structural characteristics of sandpile groups within a unique set of self-referential graphs.  In particular, our focus is on Abelian sandpiles on Sierpinski gasket graphs, where under normal boundary conditions we derive the identity element's description and develop a recursive explanation of the sandpile group.  Additionally, we explore the performance of Abelian sandpile Markov chains on these same graphs, resulting in the improvement of existing limits on the rate at which these systems achieve equilibrium.

This study employs local projections to compute impulse responses in high-dimensional data. Using the desparsified lasso, we estimate the high-dimensional local projections while excluding the target impulse response from the penalization. Under broad conditions, we show the proposed estimator's uniform asymptotic normality. Additionally, our work includes a small-sample evaluation through simulations and presents empirical findings in monetary policy and government spending research within macroeconomic analysis.

Real-time object detection in drones is difficult because edge GPU devices are restricted by their processing capabilities. This study addresses this issue by developing FasterX, a novel lightweight AI architecture that improves upon YOLOX's capabilities for edge GPU object detection. We created PixSF, a smaller version of the original head in YOLOX, and integrated it into a depthwise convolution. This is combined with a slim FPN neck, and attention mechanism in the head layer to boost feature extraction. We've also revised label assignment strategies and loss functions to mitigate category imbalance issues and UAV-specific challenges. Our FasterX model has auxiliary heads that enhance feature extraction in PixSF and support real-time distillation on drone data. Testing our FasterX model on NVIDIA's Jetson NX and Nano GPUs shows improved trade-offs between speed and accuracy on the VisDrone2021 dataset compared to the state-of-the-art.

High-performance ground-based telescopes, such as 30-meter class telescopes, can produce near-diffraction-limited observations, yet understanding their point spread function (PSF) is essential to unlock the full scientific potential of these observations. This requirement for detailed knowledge of the PSF has fueled interest in the development of precise tools for accurately reconstructing the PSF in adaptive optics systems, a capability that is critical for the scientific goals of next-generation instruments. Our research group is developing a PSF reconstruction service as part of the MICADO@ELT project. This service uses a "blind" PSF reconstruction method to make the tool widely applicable across various science applications, without requiring access to the actual science data, and instead relying on telemetry and calibration data. Our PSF reconstruction algorithm is now mature enough to test its performance using real observational data from the SOUL+LUCI instrument at the LBT, and this work presents our analysis of its results for a set of bright, on-axis observations. Our reconstructed PSFs and scientific data were analyzed and found to have small errors - less than 2% for the Strehl ratio and 4.5% for the full-width at half maximum. As part of our analysis, we also performed a simulation-based scientific evaluation of our algorithm using idealized observational data from a science application.

Multiple small, independent linear systems in fields such as plasma physics and astrophysics often need to be solved, and also occur in areas such as chemistry and computational simulation methods. Typically, one can combine these systems into a single larger system to be solved, utilizing established sparse solver algorithms. But, this ensemble approach neglects the individuality of these systems and the maximum efficiency possible with specialized Krylov solver algorithms. In current high-performance computer architecture featuring numerous parallel processing elements, each of these systems can be solved individually in an efficient way. Utilizing this "batch" method preserves the optimized efficiency achieved by specialized Krylov solver algorithms, decreases the amount of required kernel launches, and also minimizes redundant communication between processors. This current research aims to develop highly adaptable solver tools, using established libraries like PETSc, that can run an entire linear system solve independently on one processor with a single execution.

The extent to which the redshift space anisotropy of the bispectrum can be quantified using multipole moments depends largely on the statistical fluctuations present in a given survey. A novel approach has been devised to compute these statistical fluctuations, specifically for galaxy surveys like that of the {\it Euclid} mission. By analyzing specifications for such surveys, researchers have developed two key metrics to assess the viability of multipole measurement: the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and rank correlation. These metrics reveal the potential for {\it Euclid} to accurately measure the bispectrum multipoles up to a certain level ($\ell=4$), depending on the shape of the triangles formed by vectors in Fourier space. Analysis of the data indicates that linear triangles produce the most favorable SNR values. However, this metric also demonstrates dependence on the observational scale and redshift. For certain lower-order multipoles ($\ell \leq 2$), high-quality measurements are possible even on relatively large scales. Nonetheless, more detailed analysis of the data on smaller scales is needed to accurately quantify the higher-order multipoles ($\ell > 2$). Moreover, analysis of error correlation across multipole measurements reveals relatively weak correlation across most triangle shapes. Consequently, this finding facilitates the potential for data combination to enhance effective SNR values.

This paper delves into the realm of online Reinforcement Learning for partially observable dynamic systems using the Predictive State Representations model. A key feature of this model is its ability to represent states through the anticipation of future observations, a characteristic shared with models like Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. A new algorithmic approach is presented that allows the model to learn near-optimal policies efficiently. Notably, this approach leverages function approximation, facilitating its applicability to systems with large state and observation spaces. A pivotal finding in this work is the establishment of polynomially scaled sample complexity, a breakthrough which demonstrates a level of performance comparable to the globally optimal policy in the model. Lastly, this paper also demonstrates how its theoretical underpinnings can be employed to derive specific bounds for several special cases, including m-step POMDP variants, low-rank POMDP models, and linear emission/latent transition POMDP models.

Significant reductions in the costs associated with neural network inference may be achieved by developing faster matrix multiplication approximations. Building upon previous research that employed table lookups by fitting hash functions to training data to substitute costly multiplications, this work offers improvements tailored to the deep learning inference context where training data and fixed model weight matrices are accessible. Additionally, this work presents a fine-tuning procedure aimed at accelerating entire neural networks while minimizing a loss in accuracy. We also examine the effectiveness of our proposed approach on a straightforward image classification task and demonstrate its improvements over previous research; however, the resulting classification accuracy falls behind the precision offered by exact matrix multiplication, albeit highlighting potential avenues for the development of novel techniques using fast nonlinear hashing methods.

We perform direct computations of Vafa-Witten invariants in the case of 3-dimensional manifolds, building on Floer groups within Donaldson theory. We specifically calculate the Vafa-Witten invariants of 3-dimensional manifolds in several well-defined, relevant examples that relate to various surgical modifications such as the Gluck twist, knot surgeries, and log transformations. We outline anticipated properties applicable to general 3-dimensional manifolds, encompassing the behavior of modular groups, connection to Floer homology, the infinite-dimensional nature of these manifolds, and the absence of instanton effects.

Heavy Higgs bosons with doublet-like properties in certain model extensions of the Standard Model make for attractive targets in high-energy particle searches, such as those being explored at the Large Hadron Collider. However, a heavy doublet state is heavily restricted by the SU(2)_{L} symmetry in its decay channels, favoring decay into fermions, except possibly into bosons that might lead to cleaner signals in the experiment results. Yet the inclusion of singlet Higgs particles complicates these decay channels, giving Higgs-to-Higgs decays a possibility to take over as dominant channel, depending on the mass accessibility. To make sense of this data through a particular theoretical model, one needs accurate control of one-loop level radiative corrections and also must pay attention to infrared types and how these can create sizable, non-resonant contributions to certain final states.

Even in suspensions made up of inert frictionless particles with very low or relatively moderate densities, shear thickening that isn't continuous is shown to occur. This effect can be viewed as a switch between a burning state and one of sudden extinguishment, within such suspensions' inertial characteristics. A less exact model based on kinetics has demonstrated good alignment with findings produced from numerical simulation, taking into account various volume concentrations without incorporating any parameters meant to correct discrepancies.

Sustainable development and climate objectives rely significantly on the effective functioning of dam reservoirs. Unfortunately, there is a substantial data deficiency in pinpointing the locations of these small-scale dam reservoirs worldwide. An efficient method to address this issue would be the use of remote sensing data. This data could facilitate fine-grained dam reservoir identification as a subcategory of water body extraction from aerial imagery. This process requires extracting areas containing water from the images, followed by distinguishing dam reservoirs from natural water sources. To achieve this, our innovative approach proposes a multi-step DNN pipeline. Initially, it uses a segmentation model to separate water areas from land in an image, with a secondary classification model to classify each identified water body as either a natural body or a dam reservoir. This process benefits from employing advanced learning techniques, including point-level metric learning, to minimize inaccuracies and prior-guided metric learning, to optimize the reservoir identification. In an effort to advance future research in the field, a comprehensive dataset has been created using earth imagery data combined with manually identified reservoirs in West African and Indian river basins. Extensive tests were carried out using our approach on this dataset for separate water body segmentation and dam reservoir identification tasks, demonstrating superior results in comparison with prevailing methods.

Localized stresses and elastic strains in microelectronic devices, especially at microscopic scales, significantly impact electronic functionality, resistance to heat-related damage, and resistance to radiation exposure. The main challenge is characterizing these stresses and strains using conventional methods since they operate on extremely small scales. This study utilizes X-ray microscopy with differential apertures at synchrotron facilities to detect stress and strain concentrations within microelectronic devices without causing any damage, especially at multiple depth levels. The microscopic properties and behavior of gallium nitride in transistors under normal and radiation exposure conditions were evaluated using DAXM to visualize the 2D strain distribution within HEMT specimens, achieving sub-$\mu$m spatial resolution. The analysis showed that the lattice plane of gallium nitride shrinks when the sample is subjected to gamma radiation, resulting from radiation-induced damage on components bonded to it during the irradiation process.

Evaluating the performance of software-based medical devices under real-world data variations is vital for assessing their reliability and efficacy before being introduced in clinical settings. Due to regulatory constraints and limited access to large datasets for medical purposes, predicting the accuracy of any given AI model without modifying its initial training process or making assumptions about its original data is considered essential. We present a novel method that leverages conformal prediction to estimate the performance of "black-box" models without modifying the existing training process. We test this approach using medical images from various domains and types of data shifts to establish a standard for assessing AI tools in clinical settings, thereby increasing their reliability and credibility.

We have developed a novel forward modeling framework that accurately predicts galaxy redshift distributions using photometric surveys. The framework consists of multiple components: a comprehensive model detailing the physical characteristics of galaxies and galaxy evolution physics; a synthesis model linking galaxy properties to photometric observations; a characterization model capturing the observation and calibration processes for specific surveys; and explicit consideration of selection criteria for the main analysis and subsequent tomographic redshift categorization. The benefits of this approach include reliance solely on photometric data and explicit control over modeling assumptions, enabling a direct link between photometric redshift inference and galaxy evolution physics. In addition to predicting redshift distributions, our framework allows for robust inferences about the galaxy population's statistical properties. To validate our framework, we applied it to the Galaxy And Mass Assembly and Vimos VLT Deep surveys and found it to accurately predict tomographic redshift distributions, yielding mean biases of 0.003 and 0.01 respectively, sufficient for Stage III cosmological surveys. We anticipate further enhancements, such as hyper-parameter fitting, will enable our framework to provide accurate predictions for even more demanding Stage IV surveys.

We propose an analytically tractable model for biped walking, comprising an inverted pendulum supported by two articulated, massless legs capable of stable locomotion on sloping surfaces and uneven terrain. The forward motion of the robot stems from the interplay between the standing leg's pendular motion and the articulated trailing leg's movements, facilitated by the sequential switching of the legs' roles. Gait adaptation is achievable through alternating leg function, maintaining energy conservation during pendular motion, and dynamically adjusting the timing and stride length. By implementing a uniform maximum angle between the legs at stride transitions and allowing adaptable stride durations, our model accommodates motion on varied inclines and surface types. Moreover, our model has been shown to have a closed-form solution and be reversible, accurately modeling various biped walking scenarios. Additionally, optimization analyses have been conducted to determine the impact of robot parameters on optimal walking speeds.

Our investigation centers around the impact of insoluble surfactants on the dynamic evolution of turbulent jets in both space and time. Leveraging three-dimensional computational simulations, an interface-tracking/level-set method that takes into account the effects of surfactant-driven Marangoni stresses has been utilized. This research extends the scope of a previously conducted study, Constante et al., which delved into the intricate interaction between vortices and surfaces in the absence of surfactants. Through the use of computational modeling, solutions have been obtained across a broad range of Weber and elasticity numbers in which surface deformations and Marangoni stresses generated vorticity production. Notably, this study reveals for the first time the significant influence that Marangoni stresses have, which are generated by gradients in surfactant concentrations, on the formation of consistent, hairpin-like vortex structures. The emergence of these structures plays a significant role in shaping three-dimensional interfacial dynamics. Theoretical equations that describe the factors affecting circulation rate production in the presence of surfactants are also presented for general, three-dimensional two-phase flows, and Marangoni stresses are identified as having a leading role in this context.

To understand how radiation impacts the formation of globular clusters, a series of simulated head-on collisions between turbulent molecular clouds were carried out. In these radiation-hydrodynamic simulations, the effect of radiation from stars or supernovae on the process was examined. A gravitationally bound star cluster forms within three million years as a result of gas cloud collisions, and is composed of gas clumps and newly formed stars that merge over time. Without radiation, the resulting star cluster would have a mass twice as large. In these simulations, radiation plays a key role in suppressing gas collapse, and is enhanced once enough stars have formed, and in models with stronger Lyman alpha feedback the effect becomes even more pronounced. After star-forming clouds disperse due to radiation, the metal-enriched supernova ejecta are then not recycled into forming new stars.

Étant donné une variété projective lisse définie sur un corps de nombres, Colliot-Thélène et Raskind ont montré que la condition $H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0$ entraîne la finitude du sous-groupe de torsion $CH^2(X)_{tors}$. Cette note examine la famille des variétés $X$ afin de déterminer les bornes uniformes du groupe fini $CH^2(X)_{tors}$.

In superconducting quantum devices such as qubits and sensors, excess quasiparticles are key components to understand. We investigate the behavior of these quasiparticles in finite-length weak links, which exhibit multiple Andreev subgap states, when paired with a microwave resonator for measuring the even/odd parity. According to our model, precise control over parity state in one sector can be achieved by applying a tailored microwave pulse triggering a parity change in the opposing sector. This theoretical work aligns with recent research findings in Josephson junctions composed of semiconducting nanowires, providing practical advice on how to manage the parity state in Andreev qubits effectively.

This research builds upon prior knowledge for a specific type of soliton, referred to as the q-soliton, by examining its full version involving non-compact solutions. By implementing specific conditions on the vector field X and curvature conditions on the surface M, it's demonstrated that such non-compact q-soliton solutions are both stationary and have the q-flat property. We conclude with case studies involving obstruction solitons, Cotton solitons, and Bach solitons, which showcases the application and efficacy of the developed theorems across different types of flows.

The initial stages of binary star systems with exoplanets frequently occur within star-forming clusters which can lead to the dynamic evolution of these binary-planet systems. Numerical simulations were performed for S-type planets that share similar characteristics and layouts with the solar system's 4 gas giants in the gravitational influence of a binary companion of half a solar mass. The integrated model considers the interaction between the planetary system and an encompassing stellar cluster environment, revealing that roughly 10% of these systems lose stability when external disturbances from the cluster environment propel the binary orbit towards the planets. This destabilization emerges even when systems initially have stable configurations, allowing planets in the absence of the cluster environment, resulting in the displacement or loss of less massive planets along with an enhancement of eccentric orbits of surviving larger planets. Many systems, which experience instability in the cluster environment, may also shed their binary companions before the cluster dissipates, thereby masquerading as hosts of eccentric exoplanets formed in solitude. The influence of binary orbital evolution triggered in the simulations by cluster-driven processes also leads to the generation of planetary systems with mismatched spin-orbit axes, typically resulting from planetary system precession under the gravitational effect of an inclined binary system. This particular outcome often occurs when systems with more extreme spin-orbit alignments frequently retain their binary companions along with multiple planetary survivors.

Neural networks are able to approximate non-linear functions that are often complex, which can be expressed through various mathematical operations or be seen as a black box with numerous interactions. Initially, the Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) was introduced in 2019 with the use of precise approximation theories. Since its development, more simplified neural operators based on graph neural networks and Fourier transformations have been published. While neural operators rely heavily on data for training when it comes to black box systems, incorporating known governing equations into the training process can lead to more precise, physics-informed models. Furthermore, trained DeepONets can serve as a substitute for real-time calculations and component systems with moderate adjustments in complex, multi-physics applications. This work is a comprehensive overview of existing neural operators, which are examined alongside their utility and extensions for use in a variety of applications such as porous media, fluid and solid mechanics, which fall under the umbrella of computational mechanics.

Predicting emotions is a vital aspect of mental health and affective computing, yet its intricacy stemming from the interplay between an individual's physical well-being, mental status, and environmental surroundings makes it an extremely difficult task. Our research utilizes mobile sensor data to forecast happiness and stress, taking into account both the physiological aspects of a person and the influence of the surroundings, which include weather and social interactions. Leveraging phone data to build social graphs, we develop a machine learning framework that combines data from various users within a network while considering temporal changes in data to accurately predict emotions for all users. The construction of these social graphs does not result in additional expenses or data collection requirements from users and avoids any concerns related to privacy. Our proposed system automates the integration of a user's social network in affect prediction, effectively dealing with the dynamic distribution of real-life social networks and thus making it scalable for large networks. The extensive evaluation we conducted shows the improvement achieved through incorporating social networks, and we also explored the effect of the network topology on the model's performance.

We're examining how the irregular movement of a gas and liquid interface, often observed during splashing or fragmentation, produces intricate liquid patterns within a surrounding fluid. In our investigation, we apply the technique of skeletonization to minimize the information needed to describe these geometric patterns. To this end, we've developed an approach to model the dynamic process of a recurring liquid jet by adapting a previously introduced method to model the coarse behavior of multi-phase fluids while maintaining the clarity of the interface. Our process entails dispersing an indexing function, which simultaneously shifts the boundaries, until they combine to form skeletal structures. These skeletal forms capture the fundamental topological structure of the jet. Notably, we've developed methods to quantify and distinguish these skeletal forms, incorporating parameters such as branch length distribution, following the segmentation of branches, as well as a more sophisticated representation known as the Topology Morphology Descriptor (TMD), which condenses topological information in a concise manner.

The complexity of Recommender Systems stems largely from their multifaceted integration within various applications and user interfaces that significantly influence user experience. Traditionally, research has primarily concentrated on RS accuracy and ranked item output, overlooking the evaluation of RS performance in authentic real-world contexts. As a result, RSs are hindered by a narrow scope that jeopardizes their lasting effectiveness and renders them susceptible to detrimental behavior such as amplifying pre-existing data biases. We introduce EvalRS, an innovative challenge aiming to encourage collaboration among practitioners and promote the development of open, user-centered testing methodologies for real-world RS evaluation.

Understanding complex visual scenes hinges on accurately detecting human interactions with objects, which relies heavily on analyzing the spatial connections between humans and objects. A graph-based approach called SGCN4HOI has been developed for this purpose. SGCN4HOI uses graph convolution to model fine-grained relationships between humans and objects, integrating spatial, visual, and geometric features from these interactions. Furthermore, it introduces a new way of representing objects, focused on their structural key points, which enables better detection of human-object interactions. Evaluations on the V-COCO dataset demonstrated the model's effectiveness, yielding superior results compared to current state-of-the-art models based on pose information and competitive results against other approaches.

In Europe, delays in the expansion of the electricity transmission network have been frequent over the past few decades, hindering the integration of renewable energy. Developing a hydrogen network, utilizing existing fossil gas infrastructure, can help satisfy demand for low-emission fuels, mitigate the impact of variable renewable energy sources, and avert costly power grid expansions. Our research explores how integrating hydrogen and electricity networks affects a low-carbon European energy system heavily reliant on renewable energy. Our model accounts for multiple sectors and a high level of geographic and temporal detail, identifying transmission bottlenecks and supply variability. Our results confirm that establishing a hydrogen network across the continent provides benefits, including significant system cost reductions, by linking regions with high production capacity to demand centers, fuel production sites, and storage facilities. Utilizing repurposed gas pipelines to build a portion of this network can help alleviate construction costs. Nevertheless, a hydrogen network can only supplement power grid expansions and the greatest savings can be achieved through their joint development.

Using measurements from the first three years of the Dark Energy Survey, in conjunction with external data, we constrained various extensions to the $\Lambda$CDM model. Our analysis, supported by both simulated data and blinded real data analysis, focused on two-point correlation functions of weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering. Limited by a lack of nonlinear predictions at high precision, the results highlight the importance of robust data validation methods. Our model constraints include: dark energy with time-varying equation of state, non-zero spatial curvature, sterile neutrinos, modified gravity, and a model probing structure growth through binned $\sigma_8(z)$ functions. Our findings include: dark energy constraints yielding $(-0.99^{+0.28}_{-0.17}, -0.9\pm 1.2)$ at 68% confidence with $z_{\rm p}=0.24$, improved constraints on $\Omega_k$ and $N_{\rm eff}$ from external data, tightened 95% upper bounds of $0.28$ and $0.20$ eV for $\Delta N_{\rm eff}$ and $m_{\rm eff}$ respectively, and $\Lambda$CDM model constraints on $\Sigma(k,z)$ and $\mu(k,z)$. These results suggest no significant evidence for new physics beyond $\Lambda$CDM.

Schmidt's latest research identifies further relationships between generalized
bent functions, cocyclic Butson Hadamard matrices, and abelian splitting
relative difference sets. Our study reveals a larger interconnected framework by
exploring Butson matrices that share a shared cyclic pattern rather than strict
group invariance. This development holds significance in generating Boolean
functions that incorporate expansions derived from generalized partially
bent functions, including instances where a traditional bent function is not
possible to create.

Short pulses of high-speed electrons offer exciting opportunities to explore research topics including rapid structural transformations and extremely high radiation effects on living cells. A direct method of creating beams of MeV-class electrons in ambient air has been devised using high-energy pulses from intense infrared lasers. This results in an exceptionally high radiation dosage of up to 0.15 Gy/s within a time frame as short as one second, underscoring the necessity for implementing safety measures. Computer simulations support that the acceleration of these high-speed electrons stems from the powerful influence of electromagnetic waves and match well with the actual electron energy. Furthermore, this approach's potential for growth aligns with the advancement of higher powered lasers, and its applications may provide a useful alternative for Flash radiation therapy.

We explore the limits on quantum processes by identifying the fundamental time frames of quantum change and measuring the rates of these transformations. We extend these speed limits to a more general form, relevant for unitary operator flows, which appear in both quantum and classical physical contexts. We identify and investigate two categories of these speed limits, including examples using a qubit and a random matrix, and find the boundary where one limit transitions to the other. Furthermore, we use this research to derive restrictions on the behavior of quantum autocorrelation functions, giving calculable constraints for the study of quantum response to changes and quantum precision in measurement.

This paper presents a three-dimensional reconfigurable robot comprised of cubes, utilizing a unique actuation framework based on electromagnets that facilitate 3D reconfiguration through pivoting motion. Existing self-reconfigurable robots are often hindered by high production costs, complexity, and size requirements, motivating the development of an electromagnet-based actuation system for the cubes. The actuation framework relies on electromagnets embedded within the cubes, which enable the creation of both repulsive and attractive forces, thereby facilitating pivot maneuvers and robot reconfiguration. To achieve this, our robot system utilizes a voxelized configuration, actuating each Electrovoxel through electromagnetic pivoting to execute various self-reconfiguration maneuvers. To demonstrate its efficacy, our team designed and built a fully untethered, three-dimensional reconfigurable robot and successfully tested it on an air-table, and during microgravity conditions aboard a parabolic flight, thereby demonstrating both 2D and 3D reconfiguration capabilities. Furthermore, this paper outlines the hardware and pivoting framework design of the robots, our software approach to planning reconfiguration maneuvers, and an in-depth evaluation of the dynamic and electrical characteristics of the system to facilitate scalable and efficient design of self-reconfigurable robots.

This research focuses on noisy matrix completion, the process of reconstructing a low-rank matrix from incomplete and erroneous data points. By establishing the prerequisites of uniform sampling and incoherence, it has been demonstrated that a noise-independent, matrix-based completion algorithm achieves optimal performance in solving noisy matrix completion problems. Similar to its high-dimensional linear regression counterpart, the matrix completion algorithm's robustness does not rely on the known size of the noise variability. Although a convex program solves the matrix completion algorithm, the analytical examination of its statistical performance draws heavily from its inherent connections to a non-convex rank-restricted completion method.

This article investigates the linearized form of a previously posed mathematical problem, related to high-order polyharmonic operators, drawing inspiration from the work of Calderón. The problem seeks to establish the unique identification of coefficients, to a certain order, while allowing for a degree of gauge flexibility. The method of inverting momentum transforms plays a key role in achieving this result.

Protoplanetary disks exhibiting unusual distortions serve as an ideal environment for pressure trap development. One of the key hurdles in planetary formation's initial stages is the meter-sized threshold, significantly limiting planet growth timescales. Researchers have proposed various solutions to this barrier, including pressure traps - localized disk regions characterized by divergent pressure, causing planetesimal drift cessation. Despite this concept's promise, the formation mechanisms of pressure traps remain poorly understood, leaving their profile uncertain. Widespread in accretion disks, distortions in protoplanetary disks are posited to facilitate the creation of pressure traps, aiding in overcoming the meter-sized threshold. By investigating pressure trap profiles generated by an external torque, our research sheds light on the early planet formation stages across different environments such as circumbinary disks and gap edges.

A novel program for analyzing the global properties of generalized parton distributions, based on conformal moments, is proposed. The approach of universally parameterizing moment parameters enables the simultaneous fitting of parton distribution functions derived from phenomenological models, lattice calculations of form factors, and direct GPD calculations using the large-momentum effective theory. The research focuses specifically on analyzing t-dependent parton distribution functions, a limiting case of GPDs, as ξ approaches 0. The approach, however, is also adaptable for regions beyond this limit with the inclusion of extra parameters and can thus potentially be used to interpret future experimental findings. By illustrating fitted generalized parton distributions, we can see how this program allows us to quantify both quark transverse angular momentum within protons as well as quark spatial distributions, for unpolarized and transversely polarized protons alike.

We use d-separation criterion to examine compatibility between joint probability distributions and directed acyclic graphs. In this research, we explore categorical probability theory, introducing a novel causal models framework, a topological notion of d-separation, and a proof of the d-separation criterion's abstract version. This approach offers several advantages, primarily because it is highly intuitive due to topological connections. Moreover, the results have broader applications, covering measure-theoretic probability with Borel spaces, as well as extending beyond probability theory into deterministic and possibilistic networks, ultimately verifying equivalence of Markov properties and causal compatibility across multiple variable types.

The study of two-dimensional materials with twisted multilayers is becoming increasingly vital for understanding quantum properties and electron behavior, especially when it comes to electrons strongly interacting with one another. The formation of a moir\'e pattern by the layers twisting against each other results in longer wavelength potential wells that cause electron localization. Despite the prevalence of two-dimensional materials, not many of these twisted layer combinations have been studied up until this point. This research introduces a first-principles approach based on continuum theory to investigate the electronic bands produced by the moir\'e pattern of twisted Janus transition metal dichalcogenides (TMD), including both homo- and hetero-bilayers. The proposed model incorporates relaxation, stacking-dependent mass, and a Rashba effect which causes the rotation of electron spin as it moves through the crystal structure. By producing and analyzing a comprehensive set of continuum models based on over a hundred distinct materials and layer combinations through the high-throughput approach and Density Functional Theory (DFT), we uncover that moir\'e effects, the symmetries that arise in these structures, depend heavily on material properties, the layers' vertical orientation, and their twist angle. Consequently, the wavefunctions that represent the movement of electrons within these structures can arrange themselves in various forms like triangles, honeycombs, or lattices. Moreover, the distinct characteristics of these systems can cause Rashba effects to significantly influence the size of these structures' energy bands, especially at smaller angles. This work makes possible a comprehensive examination of these Janus twisted layer combinations and their novel electronic behavior, allowing researchers to make breakthrough discoveries and control the phenomenon with precision.

We examine the earliest curvature distortions in the universe through observations of dark matter structure. Considering the possibility of an increased distortion at wave numbers above 1 Mpc^{-1}, we track the growth of galaxy clusters and subclusters in a semi-theoretical framework. Accounting for uncertainties related to tidal stripping's impact on subcluster development, our analysis sets a new, more robust boundary on the distortion amplitude from observed galaxy counts and star stream observations in the Milky Way. This bound finds the distortion amplitude's upper limit is approximately 10^{-7} at wave number around 10^3 Mpc^{-1}. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the distortion may enhance indirect detection signals for dark matter by up to a factor of approximately 10^4.

A retinal feature that captures a specific aspect of a retinal image can be condensed into a single value for easier analysis. But translating this complex image data into a single, meaningful number is a challenging task, typically involving a complex multi-step process that only works with high-quality images. Consequently, researchers have to exclude a considerable portion of available data due to poor image quality. To resolve this, we introduce Deep Approximation of Retinal Traits (DART), a simpler method using a neural network to approximate existing multi-step pipelines on synthetically degraded images. In our demonstration using retinal images from the UK Biobank and VAMPIRE, DART shows high agreement with traditional retinal fractal dimension calculations, even with heavily degraded images. This suggests our method has the potential to significantly reduce data exclusion rates. DART can process images at an extremely fast rate of over 1,000 per second, further supporting its application as a useful tool for retinal analysis.

Fast-moving ejecta from binary neutron star mergers will impact the interstellar medium and generate radio to X-ray emissions through shock waves. Analytic formulas were created for such events where the ejecta is divided into two groups: the primary mass, following a shallow distribution at lower velocities, and the smaller, fast-moving 'tail,' following a steeper distribution. Using values from simulated merger events, a more accurate model was developed that accurately accounts for flux changes throughout the event, even when ejecta decelerate. In comparison, previous methods led to significantly overestimated results and this new model allows for more reliable determinations of ejecta characteristics. For instance, with typical values and considering GW170817, a binary neutron star merger event that occurred in 2017, a 'fast tail' should result in detectable radio and X-ray signals lasting approximately ten thousand days.

Laboratory-grown icicles contaminated with a variety of substances, including dyes, were found to develop distinctive ripples on their surface due to morphological instability. Investigating these structures using fluorescence imaging, it was discovered that a percentage of contaminants became embedded within the ice, forming characteristic patterns of chevrons aligned with the ripples' peaks. A secondary layering within these chevrons was observed to exhibit the shape of a crescent. We conducted further analysis on both the grain composition and crystal structure of contaminated icicles in order to reveal the first comprehensive account of growth patterns on the inside of icicles. We explore these observations in relation to ripple formation to uncover a more detailed understanding of this mechanism.

The importance of spontaneous conversations for personal well-being and interactive social technology is substantial. Previous research focused on conversation quality using limited definitions, such as the frequency of trivial discussions. Conversely, studies examining interaction experiences have indirectly assessed quality through separate factors like rapport and engagement. In this work, we establish a comprehensive approach to measuring conversation quality, incorporating key components of effective group interactions. Taking a layered perspective, we create and validate two assessment tools for perceived conversation quality, targeting the individual and collective levels. We support capturing raters' holistic impressions from small segments of behavior and gather annotations from real-life conversations recorded on MatchNMingle. Additionally, our analysis of behavioral traits that determine conversation quality reveals significant connections between positive quality perceptions and conversations characterized by smaller groups, fair turn-taking with minimal interruptions, and efficient physical coordination.

This research presents BRILLsson, a new type of binary neural network designed
for a wide variety of speech-related tasks that don't rely on semantics.
BRILLsson is trained using a method called knowledge distillation, but with only a small portion
of the data used to train the more extensive TRILLsson model. As a result, the compact BRILLsson
models, measuring only 2MB in size and operating in under 8 milliseconds, are perfect for use in low-power
devices such as wearable technology. BRILLsson is assessed across eight evaluation criteria (covering
tasks such as identifying spoken language, detecting emotions, identifying health issues, and detecting specific
keywords) and shows that our proposed ultra-lightweight models are capable of matching the performance of more
resource-intensive models.

Researchers in machine learning fairness have converged on key definitions for fair models, known as fairness criteria, but they come with several critical drawbacks. To overcome these limitations, we pinpoint four significant shortcomings of existing fairness criteria, and propose a novel solution by integrating distributionally robust objectives into performative prediction frameworks.

We consider the possibility that early formed primordial black holes, still present in the universe, possess an electric charge. Due to the influence of charge fluctuations and particle collisions during the universe's early stages, we conclude that PBHs would have acquired a non-zero initial charge. Although these initial charges were initially unassigned and could rapidly be discharged, our research indicates that rotating black holes generate dipolar magnetic fields, preventing this discharge for all PBH masses. Additionally, our analysis shows that rotating charged PBHs generate strong magnetic fields, neutralizing both the Hawking emission and the Schwinger effect, thereby maintaining their charge for a longer period. Moreover, our calculations indicate that PBHs, embedded within dark matter halos, eventually obtain a net negative charge. This is reflected in the resulting charge-to-mass ratios of approximately -10^-32 and -10^-22 C/kg for masses ranging from 10^20 kg to 10^30 kg. Given that this acquired charge falls beneath the Schwinger limit for discharge, we conclude that PBHs of various masses may carry an overall charge. This accumulated charge could span several orders of magnitude lower than the maximally allowed value imposed by the sub-extreme Reissner-Nordstrom model or the extremal limit for PBHs with a Planck mass. This has significant implications, suggesting the possibility that PBHs of various masses may form charged stable relics that compose the universe's dark matter entirely.

Capturing the mass distribution in strong galaxy-scale gravitational lenses has become increasingly challenging. The extensive detail and depth in imaging data now make it difficult to accurately model the diverse lens structures spanning various spatial scales, masses, and shapes with simple analytical methods. In response, we've developed a novel multiscale technique using wavelets that addresses this issue. This method has been tested using simulated high-resolution images from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST), which depict strong lenses containing distinct mass irregularities, such as small dark matter halos, randomly dispersed mass populations along the line of sight, and asymmetrical mass distributions at a galaxy-scale. The wavelet method successfully retrieves these structures accurately by leveraging optimization through automatic differentiation and efficient sampling of model parameters. This technique seamlessly integrates two primary modeling approaches – analytical and pixel-based – with machine-learning techniques to form a comprehensive modular framework. The new method also enables fast lens modeling for large datasets. The accompanying code, contained within the Herculens package, is publicly available.

This work investigates how variations in the net baryochemical potential impact hydrodynamic simulations of fluid behavior in high-energy particle collisions. Existing research often overlooks how changes in a system's baryon density and temperature might influence its behavior. This study explores the effects of these changes using the hybrid approach SMASH-vHLLE, incorporating the effects of baryon density and temperature in a generalized parameterization of the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio, with constraints taken from experimental results and hadronic transport models. We find that varying this ratio can affect intermediate-energy collision dynamics, where the net baryon number is non-negligible. We also observe that this effect is primarily evident in the initial stages of collisions and has little to no significant impact on elliptical flow observables in equilibrium conditions. Our results suggest that this parameterization can effectively model shear viscosity behavior outside equilibrium conditions.

Our investigation of the Sivers asymmetries, weighted by transverse momentum, in the reactions involving a transversely polarized proton target has been conducted for the SIDIS process where $\frac{P_{hT}}{zM_p}\sin (\phi_h-\phi_S)$ is used, as well as the $\pi^- p$ Drell-Yan process where $\frac{q_T}{M_p}\sin (\phi_S)$ is used. The resulting weighted asymmetries, derived through the integration of the transverse momentum, can be broken down into the product of TMD PDFs and FFs. Numerical calculations for the Sivers weighted asymmetries have been conducted using established parametrizations for the proton's Sivers function, the proton's unpolarized PDFs, the charged hadron's unpolarized FF, at the kinematics specified for the COMPASS setup. The resulting predictions are consistent with recent measurements in the SIDIS process. The high degree of uncertainty in the existing preliminary COMPASS data from the Drell-Yan program necessitates high-precision data to validate our understanding of the Sivers function sign change and to provide a basis for the sea quark Sivers function.

Helium-3 is now considered one of the primary candidates for research in multiple disciplines including fundamental physics, atomic structure, magnetometry, chemistry and medicine. Its potential for application in these fields is particularly highlighted by proposed $^3$He nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) probes that can serve as a new standard for absolute magnetometry. To maximize this potential, however, a precise value of the $^3$He nuclear magnetic moment is necessary, a value which has yet to be directly and accurately measured, being currently known with only a relative precision of 12 parts per billion. To directly determine this value, we investigated the $^3$He$^+$ ground-state hyperfine structure within a Penning trap and were able to accurately measure its nuclear $g$-factor and zero-field hyperfine splitting. Our results also allowed for the direct calibration of $^3$He NMR probes, significantly increasing their precision, while the zero-field hyperfine splitting we observed was found to greatly surpass the previously recorded most precise value, also allowing us to calculate the Zemach radius of the $^3$He nucleus with much improved accuracy.

The accelerated failure time (AFT) model assumes a log-linear relationship between failure times and various influencing factors. Unlike other prominent survival models that rely on hazard functions, AFT models directly affect the timing of failures, making the interpretation straightforward. The flexible, semiparametric AFT model that does not presuppose the error distribution offers significant benefits, making it an attractive alternative to the Cox model for analyzing right-censored data. However, AFT models typically assume linear predictors for the mean, with limited research focusing on non-linear scenarios. Recent advancements in deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated their capability in handling complex non-linear relationships. By harnessing the potential of DNNs, we suggest combining a DNN-based AFT model with a sub-sampling technique and Gehan-type loss to effectively tackle non-linear predictor scenarios. Our investigation into the proposed model, named DeepR-AFT, indicates that it outperforms its counterparts when predictor non-linearity is involved. When covariates have a high dimensionality, DeepR-AFT also excels, even for linear predictors. The superior performance of DeepR-AFT is exemplified using real-world datasets, demonstrating its practical benefits.

The Gaia Data Release 3 presents a comprehensive collection of data products that significantly enrich the community with novel astrophysical insights. 

Produced through the Astrophysical parameters inference system (Apsis) in the Gaia Data Processing and Analysis Consortium, these parameters were crafted using mean spectra from blue and red photometers along with astrometric and photometric data. 

Within this dataset, we derived a range of crucial parameters for an enormous number of sources, including classification information and associated probabilities for approximately 1.6 billion objects. 

Additionally, we obtained details of interstellar characteristics and estimated distances for approximately 470 million sources, as well as produced an intricate map illustrating total galactic extinction and provided millions of redshifts of quasars and galaxies.

The dataset contains numerous stellar parameters and evolutionary markers for an equivalent of nearly half a billion sources, which include a set of temperature, luminosity and metallicity measurements, size estimations, mass determinations and ages based on available spectra from both photometric and radial velocity sources.

The compiled parameters were carefully evaluated and classified using various methods. 

As the most exhaustive and homogeneous database on astrophysical parameters to date, the Gaia dataset exclusively relies on the Gaia observational dataset.

We examine the weak universality of a two-dimensional nonlinear wave equation, specifically its fractional variant. By developing a comprehensive framework for high-degree potentials that converge to $\Phi_2^4$, we derive a decisive condition for the convergence of invariant measures to $\Phi_2^4$ and show that a corresponding sequence of wave dynamics converges to the cubic wave equation, independent of the nonlinear degree's influence. Our research extends the work of Gubinelli-Koch-Oh by addressing scenarios with nonlocal properties and highly supercritical nonlinearities.

The Top Two algorithm was initially inspired by Thompson sampling and improved to achieve the best results in multi-armed bandit models (Russo, 2016), especially when the arms' parameters were known. By alternating between a leader and a challenger, the Top Two algorithm effectively chooses which arm to select from. Despite the positive results from experiments, there were certain theoretical limits for the method when the arms had a known and normally distributed outcome with specific variance. In this paper, we explored the mechanics of the Top Two algorithm and established its theoretical foundation for a broader scope, that is non-normal and unknown variance distributions of the arms, which are more flexible in practice. Our method showed that it is possible to choose a leader in alternative ways, for instance by randomly picking the empirical best performing arm.

We establish a relativistic spin density matrix theory for vector mesons using Kadanoff-Baym equations within a closed-time-path framework. Our approach lays the groundwork for computing key spin-related variables like $\rho_{00}$ with accuracy. By formulating $\rho_{00}$ for the $\phi$ meson, we isolate the variables and express it in a simplified factorized form, which distinguishes between momentum and spatial properties. Notably, we demonstrate that the dominant contributions to $\rho_{00}$ at lower energies arise from the influence of the $\phi$ fields on both the strange quark and antiquark, in a manner analogous to electromagnetic interactions. Crucially, we highlight that the existence of correlations between quark and antiquark polarization within the $\phi$ meson is reflected by the square of fields that comprise the contribution to $\rho_{00}$. Furthermore, we suggest that analyzing the fluctuations in the strong force fields as captured in the $\rho_{00}$ of quarkonium vector mesons can provide insights into the underlying principles of quantum chromodynamics.

To create powerful sequential recommenders, a set of innovative methods have been introduced that learn representations of user history through sequence modeling. Existing sequence representation learning techniques, which rely heavily on explicit item IDs, show some effectiveness but struggle to adapt to new recommendation contexts. This is because modeling item IDs explicitly hinders the portability of these methods. Our research proposes a new universal sequence representation learning method, called UniSRec. This approach utilizes the associated item description to generate transferable representations that can be applied across different recommendation settings. To achieve this, we developed a lightweight architecture based on parametric whitening and the mixture-of-experts enhanced adaptor. This architecture can learn universal item representations, which in turn are used in two contrastive pre-training tasks. By employing negative sampling from multiple domains, we enable the pre-trained model to adapt effectively to novel platforms or settings under either inductive or transductive configurations. Experiments conducted on real-world datasets validate the proposed approach's efficacy, and the associated code and pre-trained model can be found on the GitHub page: https://github.com/RUCAIBox/UniSRec. Our method's results demonstrate a performance boost when transferred across different platforms, highlighting the strength and portability of UniSRec.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are frequently applied in data analysis, integrating graph information, yet their capacity to represent data has only been thoroughly investigated in relation to tasks performed on graphs as a whole, not at the individual node level, which involves predicting missing labels based on observed ones. This study aims to assess GNN's potential in node-level tasks such as node classification by treating them as a type of function interpolation problem. In particular, we establish the minimum number of layers and weights needed for a GNN to approximate a band-limited function in d-dimensional space, revealing a more significant advantage than using a fully connected neural network, which would necessitate a vast increase in necessary weights to achieve the same approximation with accuracy to $\epsilon$, where only $O((\log \epsilon^{-1})^{d})$ weights and samples suffice to approximate a discretized band-limited signal in d-dimensional space, thereby drawing on a connection with classical sampling theorems to achieve this result, which represents a novel attempt at this approach.

In many domains where sequences are naturally variable in length, with some reaching lengthy extents, it's crucial that an effective modeling tool captures long-range relationships within them. Yet, existing neural attention models are generally restricted to short sequences and typically rely on cumbersome approaches like chunking or padding to enforce uniform input lengths. To address this limitation, we've devised a straightforward yet potent neural building block called ChordMixer, which is specifically designed to facilitate efficient modeling of attention mechanisms in long, variable-length sequences. The proposed architecture comprises a position-wise layer with inherent positional cues and a corresponding element-wise multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that intermingles input signals towards learning objectives. Experimental assessments, involving the synthetic adding problem, classification tasks with extensive text data, and a taxonomy classification based on genomic DNA sequences, reveal ChordMixer outperforms other established attention-based models.

Achieving domain generalization, where models can adapt to new unseen domains,
hinges on developing domain-invariant feature representations that capture object
semantics across different categories. Recent progress in weakly supervised vision-
language models has shown promise in capturing object characteristics through noisy
text annotations. However, the cost and effort required to gather text data for
every image can become overwhelming when dealing with multiple source domains.
To alleviate this issue, we explore the potential of pre-trained multimodal
networks in leveraging intrinsic modality for enhancing domain generalization
performance. We propose INDIGO, a straightforward method that combines intrinsic
and visual modalities to boost generalization on unseen domains at test-time. We
evaluate INDIGO on various domain generalization settings, achieving superior
performance in unseen domains. Furthermore, we conduct a comprehensive analysis
of INDIGO to foster a deeper understanding of its underlying principles.

The effectiveness of modern navigation systems heavily relies on standalone inertial sensor performance, particularly in situations with limited external data availability. In cases of data loss, inertial navigation systems can suffer from degradation over time due to instrumental noise from consumer-grade low-cost sensors. Model-based estimation methods are often used to reduce noise and enhance meaningful information for better navigation outcomes. However, guaranteeing optimal performance of these models is difficult due to variations in sensor quality, noise modeling, and calibration precision. While many inertial denoising models are traditionally model-based, some recent studies suggest using data-driven approaches for denoising gyroscope measurements. Due to complexities arising from unknown gravity projections on accelerometer axes, accelerometer denoising tasks are even more challenging. To address this, we introduce multiple learning-based methods for accelerometer denoising and evaluate their performance against prominent denoising algorithms using both signal removal and stationary alignment tasks. The results of field experiments demonstrate that learning-based models are superior to traditional filtering, that non-parametric kNN models outperform state-of-the-art deep learning models, and that denoising can significantly improve inertial signal reconstruction as well as navigation tasks by reducing errors up to one order of magnitude.

The strong gravitational lensing effect around rotating black holes in various gravitational theories is being examined through a calculation of deflection angles.  Using the calculated lensing observables like image position, separation, magnification, and time delays for different rotating black holes, we find notable discrepancies in image positions and separations between those in modified gravity and general relativity.  Interestingly, these discrepancies are more pronounced in SgrA* compared to M87*, but the time delays for these theories in SgrA* show less disparity than those in M87*. These assessments can potentially be used to differentiate between the predictions of modified gravity and general relativity. Furthermore, we analyzed shadow observables of various rotating black holes and utilized EHT data on the shadow radii of M87* and SgrA* to establish constraints for the MOG parameter.  Our upper limits for this parameter are between 0.162 and 0.485, contingent upon the rotation rate of these supermassive black holes.  Our analysis is significant because it is the first time that such a constraint has been put on the MOG parameter in relation to shadow radii of supermassive black holes.  Additionally, these limits are far stricter than those found from previous research regarding the precession of stars near SgrA*.

This examination explores the multinomial coefficients and their recurrence relations within the context of generalized quantum deformed algebras. Furthermore, we establish and derive both the $\mathcal{R}(p,q)$-deformed multinomial probability distribution and its negative counterpart, identifying their associated recurrence relations. Through a generalized formalism, we are also able to derive specific instances from these results that correspond to the quantum algebras found in existing literature.

Since the discovery of twisted bilayer graphene, which pioneered the field of twistronics, boron nitride moiré systems have continuously revealed remarkable characteristics. In a study on boron nitride twisted bilayers, we found that five distinct stackings are present, preserving monolayer hexagonal symmetry, unlike the two previously documented configurations. To address ambiguity in describing hexagonal bilayers with threefold rotation symmetry, we propose a definition and nomenclature. Furthermore, we utilize density functional theory to analyze the evolution of the band structure as a function of the twist angle across the five stacking configurations of boron nitride bilayers. Notably, we demonstrate that a direct gap persists at all twist angles, across all stackings, and identify invariant features inherent to each specific stacking arrangement.

Deep learning model interpretability typically revolves around how input variations influence predicted outcomes, utilizing gradients as key performance indicators. Several techniques use a universal approach to explain the logic behind each prediction made by a model, regardless of its complexity. This paper explores the significance of understanding how the relationship between input and model parameters shapes post-hoc explanations and demonstrates its benefits through a proposed method known as geometrically-guided integrated gradients. This innovative technique, building on integrated gradient calculations, examines multiple scaled inputs to determine the most effective attribution for each specific input and showcases its superiority over conventional methods through extensive testing. Furthermore, the proposed method also involves introducing an alternative model validation test, model perturbation, alongside the standard model randomization assessment.

Developing an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Algorithm for Fluorescence Angiography 
In an effort to expand the utility of fluorescence angiography in reducing anastomotic leaks, we sought to develop a computer vision system capable of evaluating tissue perfusion. This goal was hampered by human subjectivity, with surgeon variability in interpreting fluorescent signals hindering broad application of the technique. We designed an AI model to classify colonic tissue as either adequately perfused or not based on images from fluorescence angiography scans during surgery.

AI Tissue Classification in Fluorescence Angiography 
A convolutional neural network (CNN) was implemented, with a ResNet architecture trained using data from fluorescence angiography scans during 7 patients undergoing colorectal resection at a referral center. This model used images from segments of colon with visible fluorescence to classify images into two categories: those that were and were not perfused with blood. We assessed the model's accuracy on images from patients not included in the original training data set, both with images from the same camera equipment and images from different camera equipment. We calculated the model's accuracy metrics, created maps of what parts of each image the model used to make predictions, and set the cut-off line (or "boundary") the model used to classify images into one of the two categories. This model, in essence, enables surgeons to apply a specific threshold or standard to images from fluorescence angiography scans during surgery.

Automated Fluorescence Angiography Analysis 
A high-precision automated system for classifying fluorescence angiography images, was successfully developed by training it on images from 7 patients, with validation performed using images from 14 patients, resulting in an accuracy of 100% on the original training data set, 80% on the validation data set, a precision of 100% on the original training data set, 68.8% on the validation data set, a recall of 100% on the original training data set, 91.7% on the validation data set, with saliency analysis, a web-based tool has also been deployed to apply this system in a clinical setting.

Automated Fluorescence Angiography Analysis Enables Standardisation 
Automated fluorescence angiography analysis is now feasible, with potential benefits for standardising its application during surgery, thus enhancing accuracy of tissue classification and improving outcomes in this field. This model can potentially help reduce inter-surgeon variability in interpreting fluorescent signals and could be deployed as a web-based tool for clinical use.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) show great promise for food image recognition due to their ability to learn distinct visual patterns. However, identifying distorted images poses a challenge for existing CNNs. To overcome this limitation, a novel ensemble model was developed that can learn from clean and noisy images while specializing in particular types of distortions. This approach, dubbed G-Specialist, employs a data augmentation technique called RQMixup that mixes and alters images during training, forcing each model to adapt to multiple distortion levels. As a result, the ensemble gains a wide range of skills and can improve accuracy when combining the output from its diverse experts. This approach, built into a single training process, allows for seamless transfer learning across various supervised CNN models. Experimental testing on several real-world datasets confirmed the model's ability to achieve state-of-the-art results for both distorted and pristine food images.

We suggest a new computationally efficient technique to calculate Bayesian methods' predictive risks for various loss functions. This technique employs posterior covariance to yield estimators of the generalization errors according to the Gibbs and plugin methods. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees for this approach, exploring its relationships to the widely applicable information criterion, Bayesian sensitivity analysis, and infinitesimal jackknife approximation of Bayesian leave-one-out cross validation. In addition, we also discuss the technique's applicability in the context of differentially-private learning.

We're examining specific linear differential operators with positive-definite symbols defined on Euclidean space, characterized by the operators Lambda and their symbols P. Each operator Lambda generates a semigroup, defined by the convolution kernels H^t_P, with large-time behaviors for H^t_P(0) being more complex than predicted by standard scaling arguments. To demonstrate this, we analyze several examples of these operators, including one defined by the polynomial P((η, ζ)^2) = ((η, ζ)^2 + η^4), where (η, ζ) are two-dimensional vectors. By employing a novel method to study the asymptotic behavior of these semigroups at large times, we find the convolution kernels H^t_P(0) exhibit various large-time asymptotics. These findings have implications for analyzing convolution powers of complex functions defined on integer lattices. Moreover, we demonstrate that such large-time asymptotics can be preserved under certain types of perturbations. However, a more nuanced understanding of these semigroups is hindered by the need to establish precise bounds for H^t_P, especially when considering off-diagonal elements.

In integrable models, purely ballistic transport is a highly uncommon phenomenon.  We numerically examine the Heisenberg chain with distance-dependent exchange, where $J\propto1/r^\alpha$, to show that at specific values of spin anisotropy, the system displays a near-ballistic spin transport along with persistent fermionic excitations lasting up to long periods $\sim10^3/J$. This outcome is supported by the study of spin domain dynamics, the evolution of spin conductivity, the examination of spin-current matrix elements, and a comprehensive analysis of conserved quantities. The discovered correlation unifies two well-known models exhibiting perfect ballistic transport: the free nearest-neighbor hopping model and the Haldane-Shastry model.

This study defines LieYRep pairs by combining a Lie-Yamaguti algebra and its corresponding representation. Key contributions include establishing the cohomology of these pairs and identifying their deformations using the second cohomology group. Relative Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures on LieYRep pairs are introduced, and their properties explored. A significant finding is that these structures can result in a pair of compatible relative Rota-Baxter operators under certain conditions. Furthermore, an equivalence is demonstrated between $r$-matrix-Nijenhuis structures and Rota-Baxter-Nijenhuis structures on Lie-Yamaguti algebras.

Modal logic has been successfully used to express conditions related to first-order logic within the context of Kripke frames. The discovery by Henrik Sahlqvist of a particular subset of modal formulas provided an essential method to identify their corresponding first-order conditions in a methodical way. Building upon this breakthrough, researchers have successfully adapted this approach to handle more complex variants of modal languages. In this study, a comparable line of research has been pursued by developing a correspondence theorem, similar in nature to the classic Sahlqvist result, specifically for Linear-time Temporal Logic (LTL). A widely utilized formal language, LTL expands on the foundation of basic modal logic through the inclusion of dedicated temporal operators - 'Next' and 'Until'. As a result, this extension increases the intricacy of the subset of formulas having first-order equivalents. The present work has isolated a significant subset of LTL formulas comprising modal operators F, G, X, and U, and demonstrated a method to prove that they correspond with frame conditions expressible within the bounds of the first-order language.

To reconstruct a 3D scene and its camera angles, Structure-from-Motion relies on corresponding image details. However, this process is often hindered by visually similar but distinct scene features that lead to incorrect 3D models and camera angles. Most previous approaches addressed this problem by adding constraints or inferences based on feature points or two-view geometry. We propose to use high-level contextual scene information to aid this reconstruction. We've created a new scene structure, 'track-community,' where groups of image tracks, referred to as communities, are identified to segment local parts of the scene. By detecting ambiguous areas in track neighborhoods and correcting camera pose discrepancies, we then partially reconstruct and align each segment using a new bidirectional consistency cost function, considering both 3D scene and camera relationships. Our experiments demonstrate that our method can effectively prevent and resolve 3D scene construction failures resulting from visual duplicates, and precisely integrate partial models.

To address the issue of deep learning models making incorrect decisions due to biased datasets, we have developed a human-in-the-loop system for guiding attention in image classification tasks. This system enables users to specify relevant image regions by simply clicking on them, effectively minimizing the influence of co-occurrence bias and enhancing model transferability and interpretability. Unlike previous approaches, our method involves interactive annotations and an innovative active learning strategy to substantially decrease the number of annotations required. Through both numerical analysis and user testing, we have evaluated the effectiveness of our proposed system on various datasets, revealing it to be a more efficient and cost-effective alternative compared to existing methods reliant on labor-intensive polygon-based segmentation masks. The experiment results show that our system yields a more precise fine-tuned network that performs well even when the dataset is biased.

We suggest the introduction of Hyper-pool, a sophisticated, offline, utility-based algorithm that consolidates separate ride requests into high-capacity shared trips. This innovation is derived from our previous ExMAS ride-pooling algorithm, which grouped single rides into door-to-door trips. Hyper-pool goes a step further with two demand-side techniques that facilitate the formation of even more efficient pooling clusters. These strategies involve aggregating rides from individual pickup and drop-off points and then re-aggregating those groups, yielding 'hyper-pooled' rides comparable to traditional public transportation. Hyper-pool is structured in a stepwise manner, allowing the level of pooling to be systematically increased to ensure the continued appeal of aggregated trips at various levels. This method provides a collection of optimised shared trips per travel service variant given the specified demand data. Additionally, the associated algorithms are made publicly available, making it possible to replicate our findings, and have the potential to be applied to real-world large-scale demand datasets, thereby offering opportunities to fully capitalise on ride-pooling potential. As part of our Amsterdam case-study, we have successfully aggregated over 220 passengers into 40 efficient 'hyper-pooled' shared trips with an average occupancy of 5.8 people per vehicle.

To expedite the neural architecture search process, strategies that predict the performance of candidates are implemented to reduce the number of training required. The performance estimation strategies employed exhibit varied degrees of efficacy based on their precision, adaptation, and processing speed. This research presents EmProx Score, an innovative technique that utilizes an encoder-decoder structure to transform candidate architectures into continuous embeddings. The performance of candidates is then estimated via weighted kNN based on the known architectures' embedding vectors.
