The proposed EmProx Score achieves performance estimates similar to those of the MLP predictor, yet it is nearly nine times faster to train than NAO. Benchmarking indicates comparable to enhanced accuracy in comparison to other current strategies, with training times that are 5 to 80 times faster.

Recent research in federated learning has accelerated convergence with large batches, yet at a cost of increased computation. To bridge this gap, we developed FedAMD, a comprehensive framework that partitions clients into distinct groups, referred to as anchor and miner groups, where membership is determined by shifting probabilities over time. Clients within the anchor group compute gradients with large batches considered as a primary target. Those within the miner group execute a sequence of local updates through consecutive small batches. Each update is steered by the average global target derived from the clients' core targets. Consequently, the miner group obtains nearly optimal updates toward the global minimum, allowing the model to be continually refined. According to theoretical analysis, under non-convex objectives and using an anchor sampled at a constant probability, FedAMD attains a convergence rate of O(1/epsilon). Notably, FedAMD outperforms existing BVR-L-SGD at O(1/epsilon^3/2) while minimizing the communication overhead by at least O(1/epsilon). Furthermore, FedAMD was experimentally validated to be effective and superior through real-world datasets.

In order to assess the quality of natural language requirements, metrics such as passive voice and sentence length have traditionally been used, but as their potential impact at later development stages suggests, they do indicate defects.  Unfortunately, a comprehensive overview of quality factors is still missing within the research community.  Consequently, a thorough comprehension of existing research knowledge and efficient utilization of these factors is not feasible at this point.  To address this issue, a comprehensive ontology of quality factors is proposed for textual requirements, comprising (1) an underlying framework linking quality factors to associated elements and (2) an integrated database with an internet platform for these factors to be made accessible and applicable for the general public.  Our study creates an initial model and public portal through a systematic approach based on 105 initial primary studies and constructs the initial portal and database.  To demonstrate its utility, a model and to promote a joint community effort to maintain and develop it, we present an early model and welcome fellow researchers to join the project.  Our goal for the proposed ontology is for it to reflect a community-agreed perspective of requirements quality factors, facilitate new quality factor reporting, and provide access to existing research data.

When examining the mass effects from identical particles and leptons in the multi-body decay $H \rightarrow Z^*(\rightarrow \tau^+\tau^-) + Z^*(\rightarrow \tau^+\tau^-)$, it is clear that lepton masses are crucial due to their influence set by the off-shell gauge boson energies, specifically $p_a^2$ and $p_b^2$ falling within the bounds $4m_\tau^2 \leq p_a^2,p_b^2 \leq (m_H - 2m_\tau)^2$. This leads us to calculate and analyze rates and single-angle decay distributions of these events. Our results will be compared with the outcomes from decays with negligible lepton masses such as those in $H \rightarrow Z^*(\rightarrow e^+e^-) + Z^*(\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-)$.

The third data release of the Gaia dataset offers significant new opportunities for
research in the field of astronomy, notably through astrophysical parameters
obtained for over 500 million stars. Our research showcases the value and accuracy
of this data, as well as demonstrates practical ways in which it can be applied in
diverse astrophysical contexts. To this end, we have utilized the tables in Gaia DR3,
along with complementary data, to gather samples of particular interest. Our results
were verified through direct reference to Gaia and cross-referenced against external
datasets, thereby ensuring the reliability of our findings. Our research provides
access to six distinct samples of stars possessing precise astrophysical parameters
in a unified framework across the HR diagram for other researchers to explore. Our
first set of examples centres around three groups with significant characteristics: 
young, massive stars (~3 million) found in star systems, the middle-sized stars (~3 million) that comprise the core mass of our galaxy,
 and a group of unusually small ultra-compact stars (~20,000). To supplement this,
 we have developed and provided the data sources as detailed tables in the Gaia
archive. Moreover, we have successfully isolated approximately 15,740 real carbon stars,
 5,863 stars resembling the Sun, and provided the first fully-homogeneous set of data on Spectro-Photometric Standards.
 To further illustrate its potential, we have utilized the characteristics of one subset of our B and A class star data sample
to map out the shape and speed of our galaxy in three dimensions.
We then examined how the middle-sized stars are connected with the planetary systems they contain. Our analysis further went
together examining whether middle-sized stars have companions which themselves lack visible star systems, the middle-sized stars age that would be.
We then proceeded by predicting the apparent colors the Earth (which resembles our middle-sized star very closely)
would display in different light-waves under various different contexts (e.g. visible to near infrared) utilizing
middle-sized star data, the data sample for middle-sized star systems resembling the Earth (which are similar to
middle-sized stars like the Earth very closely), a solar-analog group we have developed.

A novel form of high-speed radiotherapy known as ultra high dose rate electron beam (FLASH) is gaining significant attention in various cancer treatment research. Yet, due to its high irradiation rate, there is currently no real-time dosing system in place. In this study, a beam current transformer is developed, encompassing aspects from the selection of the ferromagnetic material to shielding, followed by a low-noise front-end electronic system, all aiming to accurately measure the electron beam's current. Our developed transformer prototype has the capacity to detect a beam current range from 1.2 micro-amperes to 200 milliamperes, displaying an impressively fast rise time and negligible signal loss. In-situ measurements were also carried out and are included in this work. Our overarching goal is to synthesize this current-measuring system with a device that assesses the electron beam's form and location, creating an integrated system that provides accurate real-time dosing readings.

A new method for single-channel partial wave analysis, driven by energy dependency, has been developed, eliminating the need for complex theoretical models of two-body reactions. This alternative approach utilizes fundamental principles of analyticity instead of the conventional method of creating a theoretical model, solving it, fitting free parameters, and reconstructing partial waves from obtained reaction amplitudes. To replace the elaborate theoretical model, partial waves are expressed in Laurent form with the regular part expanded in a rapid converging series using Pietarinen expansion. Then, by fitting pole parameters and Pietarinen coefficients to a comprehensive collection of observables, the parameters can be determined without requiring complex model constructions. For reactions like $K\Lambda$ photoproduction, with its well-documented data set, this approach offers significant advantages. Nonetheless, due to intricate formalism and a large number of fitting parameters, simplifications of the Laurent+Pietarinen expansion's analytic structure are necessary and effectively implemented using the amplitude+partial wave analysis (AA/PWA) method to accommodate computational constraints. To address the problem posed by complex computations, simplifications of the expansion's analytic structure have been introduced.

Fermi J1544-0649 was initially discovered during GeV flares in 2017, showing characteristics common in blazars, as evidenced by multi-wavelength observations and its variable spectral energy distribution. Between flare events, Fermi J1544-0649 resembles a normal galaxy and remains relatively inactive in the GeV range. The detection of broad absorption lines further sparked an investigation into the'misaligned blazar scenario.' Analysis of VLBA and EAVN data from 2018-2020 revealed four distinct jet components from Fermi J1544-0649, with a likely viewing angle of approximately 3.7-7.4 degrees. This finding has implications for the gamma-ray emission cycle, with the lower angle indicating a low duty cycle, while the upper angle supports the'misaligned blazar scenario.' Following the discovery, further multi-wavelength observations found that Fermi J1544-0649 has maintained a low level of activity across the GeV, X-ray, and optical spectrums. Neutrino analysis of this source also showed an excess at a significance of approximately 3.1 standard deviations.

Semi-supervised learning is an indispensable technique in diminishing the reliance of machine learning on annotated data. This approach has effectively been applied to complex data structures such as images and languages, using techniques like pre-trained models and data augmentation. However, these methods are not adaptable when there is no available structure within the data. Pseudo-labeling techniques, favored for their simplicity, are also unreliable due to susceptibility to noisy data points and arbitrary assignment thresholds that are difficult to identify. This paper overcomes these challenges by introducing the Confident Sinkhorn Allocation, a method that assigns labels solely to data points with high confidence levels and determines the optimal label allocation using optimal transport principles, ultimately surpassing existing semi-supervised learning solutions. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/amzn/confident-sinkhorn-allocation.

We introduce a new expression, ζ^k(s), defined by ζ^k(s) = ∑_{n=1}^∞ τ_k(n) n^(-s), with the condition Re(s) > 1. Given the correlation sum ∑_{n≤X} τ_3(n) τ_3(n+h), we present three key results with numerical evidence for our method. The first conditional proof addresses the correlation sum's main term for the specific shift h=1, assuming an arithmetic distribution level for τ_3(n) up to two-thirds of its maximum value. The second result establishes the asymptotic leading term for the correlation sum across all composite shifts h. The third proof shows that for the shift h=1, the correlation sum's polynomial expansion fully aligns with the delta-method, providing identical results. Building upon a previously discovered result, we improve upon an unconditional proof and apply numerical tests that confirm the effectiveness of our strategy with error terms that show a squared value decrease. This procedure leverages basic concepts and congruences, and it generalizes beyond our initial scenario, providing power-saving error estimates for various arithmetic function correlations of the form ∑_{n≤X} τ_k(n) f(n+h), applicable to any composite shift h and any arithmetic function f(n).

A novel scheme for creating photons from a vacuum state has been proposed. This process occurs through a time-dependent modulation of a quantum system, indirectly coupled to the cavity field via an intermediate ancilla quantum system. For the most basic case, this system comprises an artificial 2-level atom and an ancilla stationary qubit that both interact with the cavity. When specific resonance conditions and frequency adjustments are made, the resulting tripartite entangled state can emit photons with minimal presence. Such photon emission from a vacuum state can persist in environments affected by common dissipation mechanisms.

Neural networks with quantized weights have garnered significant interest for their potential to reduce both memory requirements and computation complexity during the inference process. Interestingly, some experts suggest that quantization serves as an inherent form of regularization that enhances neural networks' ability to generalize, though prior research has failed to provide concrete evidence. To shed more light on this notion, this paper views the binary weights of a neural network as stochastic random variables subject to rounding. By modeling how these weight distributions propagate across different network layers, we develop a neural network with a smooth activation function and continuous parameters to approximate this behavior. By calculating the neural tangent kernel (NTK) of this approximating model, we demonstrate that its eigenvalue follows a rate comparable to a randomized Gaussian kernel, revealing a crucial difference between the representational capacities of binary and real-value weight neural networks. To validate the accuracy of our model, experimental results indicate its capability to closely mimic binary-weight networks. Notably, binary-weight networks tend to produce a lower generalization gap than real-value weight networks, a distinction analogous to the contrast between the representational powers of the Gaussian and Laplace kernels.

This study extensively examines the production of doubly-charmed baryons resulting from the decay of Z bosons using the framework of nonrelativistic QCD factorization, specifically taking into account the di-quark states that include a cc combination. According to this study, the Z boson's likelihood of producing these baryons is estimated to be within the range of 10^-5, making them measurable experimentally. By comparing this production to that of Λ^+_c in Z decay, it's predicted that the ratio of Z boson to Ξ^+_cc, Ξ^+_cc decaying to Λ^+_c, and K^-π^+, will be around 0.85 x 10^-4 and for Ξ^++_cc, it will be around 1.70 x 10^-4, values that differ from the results given by SELEX but align more with the findings from the LHCb and Belle collaborations.

A bipartite system-ancilla state with the capability to store complete information about an unknown quantum transformation is termed faithful. The proof linking faithfulness with the invertibility of its associated Jamiolkowski map, originally proposed by D'Ariano and Presti but initially flawed as it only accounted for non-increasing operations, has facilitated a useful ancilla-assisted process tomography method. We now fully validate this equivalence and expand on the applicability of faithfulness to various quantum transformation categories. Additionally, we explore an extended notion known as sensitivity, representing a quantum state's vulnerability to alterations via quantum channels. We investigate these two properties, particularly focusing on significant classes of quantum channels like unitary and unital operations. Contrary to our expectations, our research reveals intriguing results regarding these channels, ultimately suggesting that merely two classes of quantum states are required to classify them as faithful or sensitive across multiple quantum transformation categories. The discovery unexpectedly links quantum process tomography and quantum correlation. We discovered that for sensing the effects of unital channels, specific bipartite states devoid of local classical observables are crucial.

As technology advances and vulnerabilities become more apparent, the incidence of credit card fraud continues to escalate, underscoring the pressing need for a robust solution to detect these frauds effectively. Machine learning algorithms hold significant potential for tackling this issue, given their ability to refine accuracy and make reliable predictions. However, a limitation emerges when dealing with class imbalance, a common issue where samples are disproportionately represented. Typically, datasets contain only a few instances of the minority class – often around one percent. When this imbalance persists, it can skew the behavior of learning models, prompting them to consistently predict the majority class and reducing the scope for generalizing predictions. To address this class imbalance and improve the generalizability of the data, we employed a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to generate a substantial number of high-quality synthetic minority class examples, ultimately enhancing the training dataset's ability to support more effective learning outcomes.

For half-integral weight Kohnen plus space eigenforms $h_1$ and $h_2$, let's consider their respective Siegel cusp form lifts, $I_n(h_1)$ and $I_n(h_2)$, generated using the Duke-Imamoglu-Ikeda method.  These forms arise in conjunction with the Cohen Eisenstein series $E_{n/2+1/2}$, which has weight $n/2+1/2$. In this context, the Rankin-Selberg convolution $R(s,I_n(h_1),I_n(h_2))$ between $I_n(h_1)$ and $I_n(h_2)$ is expressed as the Dirichlet series $D(s,h_1,h_2,E_{n/2+1/2})$, resembling the product of the three functions $h_1$, $h_2$, and $E_{n/2+1/2}$. Our expression then allows us to apply our mass equidistribution for the Duke-Imamoglu-Ikeda lift, under the condition of the holomorphy of the function $D(s,h_1,h_1,E_{n/2+1/2})$.

We've developed a novel, automated technique to calibrate ultrasound probes, which utilize specialized 3D-printed test models for more precise tracking. To identify distinctive markers in each scan, our system relies on a custom-built AI tool that isolates and locates unique tip points in each cone. Following image analysis, these features are then systematically monitored throughout successive sweeps using a sophisticated RANSAC algorithm for more precise tracking, further enhanced through advanced computer vision techniques. Compared to established methods, our system's unique test design significantly reduces setup complexity while maintaining accuracy across different probe types and vendors, as our experiment results confirm. Moreover, our calibration results match those obtained from an expert's manual process.

This research evaluates the ability of cosmic microwave background polarization (E-mode) data to confirm potential inconsistencies in the CMB temperature data through the examination of large angular-scale correlations, quadrupole-octupole alignment, point-parity asymmetry, and hemispherical power asymmetry. Using simulated CMB data with the same level of noise as current experiments like the Planck satellite and future experiments like LiteBIRD, our results reveal that correlations between E-mode estimators and temperature data are minimal, with values typically less than 0.1, while point-parity asymmetry has a correlation coefficient of approximately 0.17 in noise-limited simulations. This shows that polarization measurements can independently validate anomalies without being reliant on temperature data. Furthermore, our results suggest that LiteBIRD's survey would significantly improve estimators of hemispherical power and point-parity anomalies by a factor of three, while large angular-scale correlations and Q-O alignment could be reduced by a factor of approximately 26 and more than 100, respectively. These gains in accuracy with LiteBIRD's survey are intermediate when compared to the improvements seen with CLASS's survey.

If the slow-roll parameter is less than $H^2/M_{\rm Pl}^2$, inflaton quantum fluctuations following horizon crossing will sufficiently trigger eternal inflation, although insufficient for generating a significant inflaton density fluctuation that produces a black hole. However, these fluctuations may produce substantial radiation density fluctuations due to rapid growth in degrees of freedom, according to the distance conjecture. The no eternal inflation condition is equivalent to ensuring that radiation from horizon crossing doesn't generate a black hole by the end of inflation. When horizon-emitted radiation isn't black hole-inducing, an information paradox doesn't occur, given certain thresholds of the slow-roll parameter and time scale, especially with values of $\epsilon_H$ larger than $10^{-7} (H^2/M_{\rm Pl}^2)$ and a time scale shorter than $10^4 (M_{\rm Pl}/H^2)$. Furthermore, regardless of the paradox's existence, an information retrieval issue exists even for stationary observers. This issue is consistent with complementarity.

Any morphism between the free monoids ${\cal A}^*$ and ${\cal B}^*$ which is non-erasing can be used to transfer a measure from the measure cone associated with any shift space X to the measure cone associated with its image under this morphism, which is also a shift space. We study this measure transfer in depth and find that it is continuous, linear, functorial and onto. Furthermore, a practical method is given for computing the value of the measure being transferred onto any particular type of set called a cylinder in this context. We then prove a significant theorem regarding this measure transfer. We first develop a key proposition as part of the proof of this theorem which involves the concept of recognizability, which is an established idea within symbolic dynamics. To be recognizable means to have certain specific properties that make it easier to work with and study within this field of study. We demonstrate here that this means two distinct but related properties - one regarding how words in one of the spaces map over to another, and the other involving periodic behavior within these spaces.

Building upon the pure Yang-Mills model in [9], we investigate the tree-level components of perturbative quantum field theory and establish their compliance with gauge invariance, which does not involve any anomalies. Furthermore, a more comprehensive proof of this invariance property is to be presented.

Most technological systems heavily rely on package managers, which guarantee a reliable and efficient handling of dependencies for various applications by correctly installing, setting up, and deleting packages. Owing to an array of packages with unique features across different systems, it remains unclear what problems users face when utilizing package managers, and what specific details are necessary to resolve them. Through a comprehensive study, this research investigated the issues end-users encounter with package managers by analyzing content from Stack Overflow (SO), a prominent question-and-answer forum. In this empirical investigation, the authors analyzed a substantial number of user queries (over 1,100) and their respective answers for three widely used package managers, specifically Maven, npm, and NuGet. Our study confirmed that users experience challenges with managing their packages with around 64-72% difficulty rate. Furthermore, it was observed that users generally struggle due to insufficient instructions from and unclear error messages by package manager tools. Interestingly, it was discovered that users largely rely on sharing external links for resolving package manager-related issues. More specifically, it was observed that links pointing to helpful resources such as documentation websites, tutorials and other support materials are most commonly shared, suggesting that these resources hold significant potential in providing useful support and essential information to end-users experiencing package manager-related challenges.

A multinorm one torus related to a commutative etale algebra L over a global field k has Kummer type properties when each component of L is a cyclic Kummer extension. In this research, we determine the Tate-Shafarevich group for such tori by applying results from Bayer-Fluckiger, T.-Y. Lee and Parimala's work and that of T.-Y.~Lee. Furthermore, an effective algorithm based on the recent developments has been implemented in SAGE, which calculates the Tate-Shafarevich groups when each component of L is a part of a fixed, concrete bicyclic extension of k.

Recent developments in biological technologies, including multi-way chromosome conformation capture techniques, necessitate the creation of tools to effectively analyze complex interactions.  Given their precision, hypergraphs are ideally suited for modeling and studying multi-way interactions, and we have developed the Hypergraph Analysis Toolbox (HAT), a software application designed to visualize and investigate such interactions within intricate systems.
Given any two minimal models of a generalized lc pair, there exist minimal birational transformations connecting them, through a chain of flop transformations.

To reduce the influence of outliers, the kNN ensemble algorithm finds the most relevant observations nearest to a new data point, making a prediction based on a majority vote from its neighboring training instances, by employing a distance calculation to identify the k closest training points within the surrounding region. 

Standard kNN-based procedures can fail in cases where test data points exhibit patterns beyond the range of nearest neighbors located within the specified boundary. Furthermore, these approaches often involve numerous base kNN learners with high error rates, resulting in subpar ensemble performance. 

In order to address these limitations, an enhanced ensemble is proposed based on an optimal neighborhood expansion strategy. This approach identifies nearest neighbors in a sequential manner by beginning with the closest sample to the unknown observation, and iteratively adding the closest neighboring point until a total of k observations is obtained. 

In constructing this ensemble, each base model utilizes a bootstrap sample of data, paired with a random subset of features. Once a large number of models is created, the most accurate models are chosen based on their performance on data that they did not use, also known as out-of-bag data.

In today's complex applications such as social networks, healthcare and finance, point process data is increasingly used, yet challenging due to its intricate non-stationary dependencies. Popular RNN models struggle to fully capture these dependencies because of their inherent structure. A more promising approach represents point processes as neural networks which learn influence kernels. Our research improves on this approach by proposing a novel method that uses a general low-rank decomposition for non-stationary spatio-temporal point processes. This enables efficient deep learning models with improved performance. We enforce the critical non-negativity constraint of the conditional intensity by incorporating a log-barrier penalty, thereby achieving enhanced efficiency and accuracy on real-world data sets and simulated examples, respectively.

This paper proposes an end-to-end approach called NeuMap that efficiently localizes cameras in a scene by converting the scene into a compact grid of latent codes. This innovative method utilizes a scene-agnostic Transformer-based decoder that accurately determines the 3D coordinates of individual pixels from the scene representation, achieving impressive compression ratios without compromising performance. By storing scene information in dynamic latent codes and employing a universal decoder that learns robust scene-invariant patterns, NeuMap can efficiently learn from large datasets and rapidly adapt to new scenes. Our comprehensive evaluations of five benchmark tests demonstrate NeuMap's superiority in coordinate regression, with a scene representation size that is orders of magnitude smaller than existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, NeuMap can attain 39.1% accuracy in the Aachen night benchmark using merely 6MB of data, surpassing comparable methods that struggle to operate under similar compression constraints.

We approach the core challenge of real-time control of a linear system through two primary lenses: minimizing regret and analyzing competitiveness. Our findings demonstrate that the most competitive policy can be effectively approximated by a class of parameterized, convex DAC policies, which optimize disturbance-action combinations. By establishing this fundamental insight, we show that various existing online control methods achieve the best of both worlds by achieving sublinear regret comparable to the best DAC policy in hindsight, as well as an optimal competitive ratio. This understanding extends to scenarios where the system's dynamics are unknown, including situations where a pre-existing stabilizing controller is not available.

Discovering update rules for evolution strategies that are more adaptive is key to advancing black-box optimization. To overcome the limitations of conventional heuristics in evolution strategies, a novel meta-learning approach can provide an efficient and generalizable solution. Our proposal utilizes a self-attention architecture-based search strategy that is order-invariant, thereby enabling effective optimization across various scenarios. By meta-learning on a limited set of simple optimization problems, we can develop evolution strategies capable of tackling complex unseen problems with variable population sizes and time horizons. Notably, these strategies not only excel on their own but also outperform established baselines in a wide range of tasks, including supervised and continuous control scenarios. Our further analysis involves breaking down the components of our method and deriving an explicit heuristic equivalent that retains its competitive edge. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach can successfully be employed for meta-learning, where the learned update rule fuels the optimization process, thereby leading to remarkable performance improvements.

Traditional studies on converting text to SQL queries are often restricted to a
single task with a predefined dataset. However, when confronted with a constant
stream of queries common in real-world scenarios, current methods struggle due to
inadequate supervised data and the high cost associated with continuous retraining.
This results in overfitting for new databases and forgetting previously learned SQL
structures and database schemata. To overcome these limitations, this research
introduces a framework combining semi-supervised learning and continual learning,
presenting two possible approaches in the context of text-to-SQL queries. Firstly,
the "Vanilla" solution relies on self-supervised learning through the creation of
pseudo-labeled instances for the current task and replacing extensive retraining
with memory recall to balance efficiency with prior task performance. Secondly, the
more advanced solution, SFNet, leverages the relationship between CL and SSL to aid
current learning and improve future memory recall through the incorporation of high-quality past data. Experiments on two test datasets demonstrate SFNet's superiority over existing SSL-only and CL-only benchmarks on various performance metrics.

An analysis of the Ground Wide Angle Camera (GWAC) archives yielded significant results: among 43 stars emitting white light flares, 3 displayed homologous patterns and 1 also featured quasi-periodic pulsations occurring every 13 minutes, with 19 of the 43 stars being newly discovered active ones. In addition to identifying stellar flares from TESS and K2 light curves, 34 of the flare stars were found to have rotational or orbital periods of under 5.4 days. Moreover, using spectroscopy from the LAMOST telescope and the 2.16m Xinglong telescope, data pointed to a saturated state in the star's rotation-activity diagram. The discovery of double H$\alpha$ emissions in one star (Star #3) indicated that it comprised a binary system. Thirteen flare frequency distributions from TESS and K2 light curves further confirmed the likelihood of flares, ranging in frequency from 0.5 to 9.5 per year. Research also considered the effect of flares on planets: certain GWAC flare stars were found to have enough energy to potentially destroy their ozone layers, but no flare activity was strong enough to trigger the chemical building blocks of life on these habitable planets.

Advanced recommender systems often involve numerous marketing strategies and diverse user demands. For effective multi-domain recommendations, it's essential to optimize the performance of multiple domains simultaneously. Existing graph neural network based methods generally treat domains individually, failing to exploit cross-domain behaviors, or train a single model for all domains, disregarding domain-specific preferences. To overcome these limitations, it's crucial to learn from multi-domain feedbacks and capture users' unique preferences within each domain. To address these challenges, a hierarchical hypergraph network based correlative preference transfer framework called $\mathsf{H^3Trans}$ is proposed for multi-domain recommendations. $\mathsf{H^3Trans}$ unifies multiple domains into a single graph, enabling preference transfer by utilizing users' comprehensive behaviors across domains. $\mathsf{H^3Trans}$ comprises two key modules: Hyper-I for item representation consistency and Hyper-U for user preference aggregation and high-order connection exploration. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of $\mathsf{H^3Trans}$ in multi-domain recommendations using both public datasets and large-scale production data.

The inclusion of Yukawa interactions within grand unified theories, often results in the emergence of novel scalars. These scalars interact with fermions, leading to novel observational phenomena. The incorporation of colour sextet diquark scalars within the realistic renormalizable models of SO(10) GUT is examined. The resultant spectrum comprises five distinct sextets with specified transformation properties. The couplings of these scalars to quarks are calculated, leading to predictions for their impact on processes such as neutral meson-antimeson mixing and neutron-antineutron oscillation, caused by B-L violating trilinear interactions. The mass constraints of these scalars are determined using the values of the B-L breaking scale and Yukawa couplings, leading to the conclusion that certain sextets must be heavier than the B-L breaking scale to avoid perturbativity. Consequently, these predictions indicate a lack of observable n-$\bar{n}$ oscillations in upcoming experiments. Alternatively, models where the sextet Σ and two copies of the sextet S exist, can viably account for the baryon asymmetry observed in the universe.

Mobile network operators' drive for cost-efficiency is propelling 5G and subsequent networks toward flexible, adaptable deployments that meet diverse stakeholder demands in real-time. To address this challenge, cloud-based deployments integrated with end-to-end monitoring are considered promising solutions. A live demonstration on an end-to-end cloud-native 5G testbed, incorporating real-time over-the-air transmissions, illustrates how automated orchestration can relocate applications in response to dynamic user needs. Consequently, our experimental evaluation demonstrates the feasibility of our cloud-native platform in enabling agile, intent-driven 5G network deployments.

Investigation of laser-generated bubbles in confined environments has led to the exploration of their potential use in driving liquid micro-jets within microfluidic devices, specifically in needle-free jet injectors. This study examines the process of bubble formation using continuous-wave and pulsed lasers inside open-ended microfluidic capillaries. This approach enables a direct comparison of bubble formation by lasers with differing light emission timescales. The bubble growth dynamics play a crucial role in determining the available energy for subsequent liquid jet generation. The research demonstrates that the bubble growth rate is directly proportional to the energy delivered for both continuous-wave and pulsed laser sources, under conditions where their absorption coefficients are equivalent. This similarity suggests the interchangeability of these lasers for jet generation. However, the continuous-wave laser necessitates greater optical energy input, largely due to heat dissipation. Moreover, the continuous-wave laser-generated bubbles exhibit a slightly larger size variation and growth rate disparities under identical initial conditions, a phenomenon we attribute to the stochastic nature of thermocavitation.

Random partitions derived from stable subordinators of index $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ hold unique characteristics, enabling researchers to derive intricate properties with relative ease, including potential applications in combinatorial processes, random models, and Bayesian statistics. This class encompasses notable models based on the Poisson-Dirichlet distribution, and our research contributes to the broader interpretation of Gibbs partitions by embedding fundamental operations within this framework. We have resolved the challenge of extending Jim Pitman's 1999 Annals of Probability results, focusing on dual, infinite-block coagulation/fragmentation processes, and successfully integrated stable Poisson-Kingman models into this context. This yields nested families of Gibbs partitions, mass partitions, and detailed fragmentation operations. We have also derived corresponding coagulation operations, showcasing the versatility of our construction, and applied this to the Mittag-Leffler and generalized gamma models, effectively demonstrating the recovery of duality results through a novel approach.

To accurately track and manage the spread of disease, this research introduces a monitoring system capable of addressing data and modeling uncertainties. Based on historical epidemic data, it outlines procedures for identifying and quantifying key factors in disease transmission. Since such data may be contaminated, this approach also develops an observation strategy to accurately estimate disease status even in the presence of uncertain data and measurement errors. Building on these findings, this research then creates tailored control strategies to minimize potential damage from disease outbreaks by optimizing long-term health outcomes. The proposed methodology's efficiency is demonstrated through its application to a revised version of the SIR disease model.

One of the primary obstacles in treatment planning for microbeam radiation therapy (MRT) is obtaining rapid and precise dose predictions. A proposed solution in this paper employs a 3D U-Net machine learning model. This model predicts large doses of high intensity microbeams separately from the lower doses between them, adopting the concepts of macro peak doses and macro valley doses that represent larger scale dose quantities in volumetric spaces. The model mimics Monte Carlo data for detailed and realistic physical effects, including polarization. This macro dose distribution approach enables combining single microbeam predictions into a comprehensive beam field array, making it an appealing treatment planning option. Additionally, this proposed method demonstrates the capability to predict a full microbeam irradiation field efficiently, while achieving reasonable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in this context within a remarkably short timeframe of less than a minute.

We detected rapid and substantial radio enhancements of GRB 210702A 11 hours after the explosion using the ATCA telescope. Radio emission was tracked for 5 hours with a 15-minute interval over a 3 GHz frequency span at three specific frequencies. Analysis of 9.0 GHz light curves indicates that radio bursts reached a peak flux of 0.4 ± 0.1 mJy in approximately 13 hours after the explosion, displaying a rapid increase and subsequent decline in the emission. However, these findings conflict with internal and external shock theory, where radio waves from shockwaves are generally detected much later in timeframes. Swift observatory detected normal afterglow responses from this GRB in the optical and X-ray spectrum at times less than a day. Utilizing this information to apply the concept of wave propagation through a homogeneous interstellar environment, an electron power-law of 2.9 ± 0.1 and blast wave propagation speed through a homogenous environment were determined. It's possible the GRB radio burst can be attributed to weak light scintillation, an increase above detection limits for ATCA. Utilizing an equation for weak light scintillation, an upper size constraint for the GRB wave's dimension is set, indicating no greater than six billion billionth kilometers. It corresponds to forward shock predictions of wave propagation at this speed. It represents the smallest size of wave propagation for any known radio burst in history. It emphasizes the need to follow GRBs radio frequencies for 24-hour periods, tracking scintillation across numerous bands for capturing real-time data.

Human behavior understanding, through multimodal sentiment analysis and emotion recognition, is crucial for computational research. Psychologically, emotions are brief manifestations of feelings, whereas sentiments persist for a longer duration. Nonetheless, prior research predominantly treats sentiment and emotion as isolated entities, failing to fully exploit their interdependent knowledge. To address this gap, this paper presents UniMSE, a multimodal framework that integrates sentiment and emotion understanding tasks at feature, label, and model levels. UniMSE performs fusion at both syntactic and semantic modalities, as well as employs contrastive learning techniques to distinguish and recognize similarities between sentiments and emotions. Experimental results, using MOSI, MOSEI, MELD, and IEMOCAP benchmark datasets, verify the effectiveness of UniMSE, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

A key feature of a quantum neural network is its potential to precisely represent complex functions, theoretically making it an efficient tool for machine learning. Without this capacity, a quantum neural network might be unable to accomplish a task. Proposals aiming for universality include transforming quantum information into the identical format using a tensor product, but these attempts significantly increase the system's size and complexity. In response to this issue, a more straightforward design of a quantum neural network is proposed, its universality proven through rigorous examination. In comparison to other previously developed models, our new design requires fewer quantum bits and simpler circuitry, greatly minimizing the resource needs for its practical implementation and also making it less prone to noise. Additionally, it is easier to operate using current technological capabilities. Results from simulations reveal the model's ability to address a diverse range of tasks related to both classical and quantum learning, ultimately highlighting its practical value.

This review offers an extensive examination of mean-field coupled maps, covering a wide range of research in the field, from its origins in the physics literature to contemporary studies on ergodic theory in the thermodynamic limit of coupled maps, along with related self-consistent transfer operators. We also provide some connections to other relevant fields involving continuous-time mean-field coupled systems, along with potential applications.

Based on previous work by the authors, an associated "directive sequence" of diagrams is derived for every $S$-adic representation of a subshift $X$, including a cone representing the measure and another cone representing the letter frequency of each level's subshift $X_n$. This leads to a clear visualization allowing straightforward conclusions about $X$ to be drawn. Specifically, a broad category of minimal subshifts with zero entropy can be identified as having an infinite number of ergodic probability measures. Moreover, as a secondary result, an $S$-adic representation is constructed for any $d\geq2$, featuring a minimal, aperiodic, uniquely ergodic subshift $X$, with all level alphabets having cardinality $d$, while the bottom-level morphisms are not recognizable in their corresponding subshifts.

Developing molecules that effectively bind to specific proteins is a difficult goal in drug discovery, requiring accurate modeling of molecular interactions. Current approaches generate atoms in a sequential manner, focusing on element types and 3D coordinates separately, whereas in real systems, these factors are interlinked across the entire molecule. This leads to energy functions that couple the interactions of atoms, necessitating joint probability distributions rather than conditional ones. This results in potential violations of physical rules and poorly formed molecules from auto-regressive models. This work instead uses a generative diffusion model that incorporates contextual constraints from target proteins, generating molecules in a full-atom, non-autoregressive manner. By utilizing an equivariant network, our model simultaneously learns to remove noise in both element types and 3D coordinates of entire molecules given a specified binding site. The proposed approach has been experimentally demonstrated to outperform existing methods, yielding molecules with high affinity to proteins, optimal sizes, and favorable properties such as drug-likeness.

Ensuring fairness in healthcare decision-making is essential for promoting health equity,
but evaluating fairness of medical choices using observational data is complicated.
To address this issue, researchers have developed various fairness concepts,
with a growing focus on causality-based measures that can correct for biases
and account for confounding factors.
Yet, the application of causal fairness principles to large-scale health data remains
underdeveloped.
Our work introduces a Bayesian approach for inferring causality and quantifying a
fairness metric known as principal fairness within healthcare contexts.
We test the efficacy of this method on both synthetic data and actual patient records.

Deep learning methods have demonstrated their capability for effective Sentiment Analysis, with Recurrent neural networks like LSTM and Bidirectional LSTM establishing a benchmark for constructing precise predictive models. The high complexity and numerous hyperparameters involved raise concerns about the models' stability, leading to a critical evaluation in this research.

This study investigates how entanglement relates to global internal symmetries within de Sitter space. It focuses on two isolated regions, examining the correlations in this setting using entanglement as a gauge. Given that a theory with additive global internal symmetry can be dissected into individual subsystems with fixed global charge, this research breaks down the entanglement between two subsystems within de Sitter space. By analyzing two theories - free complex scalar fields and free Dirac fields - which each exhibit $U(1)$ symmetry, this paper examines the effects of global internal symmetry on entanglement within de Sitter space. It reveals that the distribution of symmetry-resolved entanglement entropy among subsystems is uniform when considering volumes that are significantly large. However, when considering small volumes, these entanglement patterns are disrupted. Therefore, in very large de Sitter spaces, symmetry-resolved entanglement entropy appears to distribute uniformly among subsystems.

Instance segmentation has numerous real-world applications, such as in autonomous driving and image analysis, but one significant challenge it faces is limited available data. The Visual Inductive Priors Challenge was established to address this issue by providing a data-deficient training environment, while still allowing competitors to use certain inductive priors to help overcome data shortages. In an attempt to resolve this data-deficient problem, our research introduces two innovative strategies: Task-Specific Data Augmentation to optimize model performance in low-data settings and Task-Specific Inference Processing to maximize the potential of inductive priors. We implemented and evaluated our proposed method, combining a Hybrid Task Cascade detector with the Swin-Base based CBNetV2 backbone on the Visual Inductive Priors Challenge. The results of our experiment show that our method successfully achieves high accuracy on the test set of the 2022 Visual Inductive Priors Challenge with a 0.531 AP@0.50:0.95.

This paper offers an upgraded catalog, RATAN-600 multi-frequency catalogue of blazars,
an extension of the BLcat catalog which now focuses on BL Lacertae objects and includes
flat-spectrum radio quasars. It consists of over 1700 blazars of varying types. A primary
attribute of this BLcat catalog is the compilation of radio data from quasi-simultaneous RATAN-600
measurements at 1.1, 2.3, 4.7, 7.7/8.2, 11.2, and 21.7/22.3 GHz, as well as radio data from other
sources to provide a complete study of radio properties and variability. Tools have been developed to
compute radio properties such as the spectral index, variability index, and luminosity for user convenience.
This updated catalog offers a description of key radio properties for its various subsamples.

Using data collected from electron-positron collisions with the BESIII detector at the BEPCII storage rings, the team has calculated and measured the differential cross sections of $\pi^0$ and $K^0_S$ production in relation to the hadron momentum, based on the overall $e^{+}e^{-} \to$ hadrons process. The results for center-of-mass energies spanning 2.2324 to 3.6710 GeV were obtained at various relative hadron energy coverage levels from 0.1 to 0.9, revealing significant discrepancies with theoretical predictions derived from fragmentation functions, particularly at lower energy levels.

Person re-identification, a fundamental task in computer vision, has experienced substantial advancements, but the emerging subfield of long-term person recognition in videos, specifically under clothing changes, warrants increasing focus. Most current methods focus on image-based scenarios, disregarding valuable temporal information. In this paper, we address the under-researched challenge of video-based person re-identification with clothes changes by examining the interplay between temporal cues and the problem's inherent issue of clothing inconsistencies. Our novel approach involves a dual-confidence based ranking framework for tackling the CCVReID issue, incorporating both visual and cloth-free gait features through a strategically weighted re-ranking strategy. Our work lays the groundwork for future investigations. Furthermore, to promote research in this area, we construct and release two new, large-scale CCVReID datasets – one comprising synthetically-generated videos, and the other with real-world recordings featuring people wearing varied clothing – along with the accompanying code for public access.

Research on low-energy and controlled molecular ions is fundamental to modern physics and chemistry studies. Cooling molecular anions specifically has significant implications for antihydrogen production, anionic Coulomb crystals creation, atmospheric research, and astrochemistry. However, a commonly applied technique for cooling anions by colliding them with a buffer gas has limitations due to the cryogenic cooling medium's temperature. Our research shows that an anionic OH$^{-}$ ensemble can be rapidly cooled using a laser beam, even with energies far beyond the photodetachment threshold of the anion. This resulted in lowering the initial temperature of 370 K to 2.2 K, an increase of three orders of magnitude in the ions' phase space density, nearly reaching the strong Coulomb coupling regime. Our experimentally based model quantitatively analyzed these results, accounting for intrinsic heating effects, and demonstrated that anions can be cooled to below the liquid helium temperature using this technique. This new approach enables anionic cooling to reach unprecedentedly low temperatures.

The significance of free/non-potential magnetic energy in identifying the trigger for solar eruptions is still not well understood. Using computational simulations that can produce coronal jets, we examine how the dynamics of magnetic energy and helicity evolve when the duration of driving force differs. Our simulations reveal that generating a helical jet involves a long phase of low-intensity magnetic reconnection before the jet emerges, in contrast to simulations where the system is driven briefly. As expected, we found that non-potential energy and helicity play crucial roles in producing the jet. Our analysis shows that magnetic energy levels remain steady between the end of driving and jet generation, while magnetic helicity evolves noticeably during this period. Furthermore, we found that the helicity eruptivity index, which increases before jet generation, declines as the jet emerges, accompanied by a decrease in free energy.

We used tempered Monte Carlo simulations to study the magnetic properties of a dipolar hard sphere system with varying levels of structural anisotropy and positional disorder. A crucial factor was considering a frozen, polarized state of the system obtained from the liquid state of the dipolar fluid at low temperatures. This anisotropic structure's degree is determined by the inverse freezing temperature and measured by a nematic order parameter. We found that both dipolar hard sphere systems and the corresponding dipolar Ising model with infinitely strong uniaxial anisotropy exhibit ferromagnetic behavior at low volume fractions below the isotropic threshold where isotropic dipolar hard sphere systems typically show a spin glass phase.

We establish a cellular decomposition of the totally nonnegative section of flag varieties from a Kac-Moody group's twisted product, which consists of closed ball homeomorphisms. It follows that the totally nonnegative braid variety forms a closed ball homeomorphism. Furthermore, our results confirm that the link of each totally nonnegative double Bruhat cell within a reductive group structure corresponds to a closed ball homeomorphism, addressing a longstanding question posed by Fomin and Zelevinsky.

The surge in generative models has been facilitated by vast datasets and pre-trained models. However, music notation datasets remain minuscule, which in turn hinders the performance of data-driven, multimodal models that process music. One potential remedy lies in exploiting pre-trained models from other mediums (like natural language processing), thus enhancing multimodal tasks specific to music notation. Our research is the first to investigate generating coherent music scores from descriptive texts and explores using publicly accessible natural language processing models to boost the efficacy of text-based music creation. Our study demonstrates that incorporating pre-trained models has a statistically significant impact on text-to-music tasks in terms of quality metrics such as the BLEU score and musical similarity measures like the edit distance. Furthermore, we delve into our model's strengths and limitations, aiming to understand the full potential of integrating music with natural language processing capabilities.

We have searched for a specific tree-diagram dominated process in $772 \times 10^6~B\overline B$ pairs collected by the Belle detector at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ energy using the KEKB collider. The searched process is the decay $B^+ \rightarrow p \overline{n} \pi^0$, marking the first Belle detector investigation of an anti-neutron containing decay. The experiment detected no significant evidence and established a $90\%$ credible upper limit on the branching fraction of $6.1\times10^{-6}$.

For autonomous vehicles, a robust camera relocalization system is required.
Conventional camera pose estimation models, which assume a stable environment, 
fail to account for changing driving conditions, including weather, lighting, 
season, and moving objects. RobustLoc, a proposed robust relocalization 
approach, incorporates neural differential equations to address such 
environmental perturbations. It leverages a convolutional neural network to 
process multiple images, a neural diffusion block to iteratively diffuse 
information, and a branched pose decoder to predict vehicle positions. Our 
experimental results confirm that RobustLoc outperforms current state-of-the-art 
relocalization models in diverse driving scenarios. Our code can be accessed at: 
https://github.com/sijieaaa/RobustLoc.

Stable hadronic composite particles within an additional, non-Abelian gauge sector offer promising avenues for exploring the role of Strongly-Interacting Dark Matter candidates. Theories featuring dark pions, which self-annihilate to determine the DM relic density, serve as an illustrative example. The Sp(4) gauge theory with two Dirac fermions provides a basic implementation of this concept, allowing us to investigate the meson multiplets in both degenerate and non-degenerate fermion configurations. We further derive a low-energy effective theory and report on the results obtained through lattice computations, focusing specifically on pseudoscalar and vector meson masses.

The unusual spin structure on SnTe's (001) surface holds great significance and has potential for advanced spintronics. We investigated the effects of weak optical modulation on magnetic impurities on a SnTe(001) surface with added dopants. Due to unique interactions between the spin and orbital elements, we observed an atypical non-collinear magnetic connection that includes Heisenberg, symmetric in-plane interactions, and asymmetric spin rotations. It is evident that the magnetic connection, including those with unusual spin rotations responsible for interesting patterns, necessitates the presence of doping in most cases. We suggested modifying the magnetic connection in situ through optical manipulation of the band structure and the subsequent addition of dopants. Notably, this manipulation disrupts the balance between electron and holes by incorporating spin rotations.

Pre-trained language models have made significant strides in code retrieval tasks by locating the most relevant code snippet when given a natural language query, but current models overlook one critical factor - using external knowledge to guide their searches. In this study, a novel query expansion framework is introduced, which integrates the capabilities of a code generation model into the code retrieval process, mimicking how humans search for information by first generating a rough idea of what they are looking for before searching for it specifically. By augmenting a code snippet search query with generated code, the model can more accurately locate the desired snippet and, as demonstrated on the CodeSearchNet benchmark, achieve significantly improved results that outdo existing benchmarks.

We investigate the possible breakdown routes of extremal charged black holes that have a vanishing temperature, within a framework of $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetric string theory. If not preserved by supersymmetry, these extremely compact black holes should deteriorate due to the weakness conjecture in gravity. This analysis focuses specifically on double extreme non-supersymmetric black holes that have consistent scalar field values across space and time, and we examine decomposition paths into BPS and anti-BPS components that have a more energetic preference. It has been found that tree-level breakdown pathways exist for an extensive range of these double extreme black holes. Furthermore, we also found stable non-supersymmetric black holes, implying the reassembly of supersymmetric and antisupersymmetric components into a non-supersymmetric structure.

To satisfy the growing performance needs of neural networks, specialized hardware is adopting multi-core and chiplet architectures. So far, these systems using multiple accelerators are taking advantage of increased parallelism by scheduling different neural network layers across batches of inputs. However, this does not fully exploit available hardware resources when applying it to latency-critical, layer-by-layer scheduling. This work enables the scheduling of deeply connected neural networks onto multi-core architectures at a more detailed level. It does this by using an open-source framework called Stream that allows for varying levels of detail in scheduling and optimization of execution schedules. This results in minimal energy consumption, reduced latency, and minimal memory usage for constrained edge devices. By comparing it with other state-of-the-art hardware implementations using the traditional scheduling approach, we see a close match with measured results. By utilizing the more detailed scheduling approach further, we find that high-level decisions greatly impact the efficiency of the hardware and can lead to significant reductions in energy consumption, especially in heterogeneous multi-core architectures. This results in up to 30 times less energy-delay product when using the new scheduling approach.

This paper delves into the necessary and sufficient characteristics of recognition networks to precisely replicate a generative model's posterior distribution, with a focus on probabilistic graphical modeling and Bayesian networks that incorporate conditional independence. Derived properties include both general and specific requirements for the network to be accurate, with a notable influence from 'perfectness' - where all parents of each node are connected.

Fine-tuning large Pre-trained Language Models for multiple downstream tasks is becoming increasingly costly due to their expanding size. To overcome this limitation, Parameter Efficient Tuning methods have emerged, such as low-rank adaptation techniques, which utilize learnable SVD modules in parallel or sequence to boost fine-tuning efficiency. Nonetheless, these approaches are constrained by limited representational power. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel solution that leverages Kronecker products instead of traditional low-rank representations, and present KronA, an efficient Kronecker product-based adapter for fine-tuning large Transformer-based language models. We demonstrate that integrating this novel module into the T5 model significantly surpasses the performance of existing Parameter Efficient Tuning methods, particularly when fine-tuned on the challenging GLUE benchmark.

Traditional variable control charts, such as the X-bar chart, are frequently used to track process variability. They have proven to be effective under certain conditions, namely when data is normally distributed without contamination and sample sizes are consistent. Nevertheless, these assumptions are not often met in real-world scenarios, limiting their broader application in industrial settings. To overcome this constraint, we introduce a new approach for creating robust X-bar control charts that can handle both data contamination and inconsistent sample sizes simultaneously. The proposed method optimizes process parameters using best linear unbiased estimation techniques. Simulation results and case studies demonstrate that standard control charts significantly underperform under contaminated data conditions and are overly sensitive to a single outlier, whereas our robust charts significantly outperform standard ones when data is compromised by anomalies, offering comparable results when data is uncontaminated.

The E36 experiment at J-PARC used advanced detectors to determine the branching ratio of the SD radiative $K^{+} \to e^{+} \nu_{e} \gamma$ decay in comparison to the $K^{+} \to e^{+} \nu_{e} (\gamma)$ decay with IB, where the IB effect was taken into account in the SD radiative decay. Combining the new data with a previously corrected CsI(Tl) result gave a new branching ratio value $Br(K_{e2\gamma(\gamma)}^{\rm SD})/Br(K_{e2(\gamma)})=1.20\pm0.07$. This result is consistent with a lattice QCD calculation but contradicts Chiral Perturbation Theory and a KLOE value. It also aligns with a gauged nonlocal chiral quark model, although not with a higher order Chiral Perturbation Theory prediction.

This thesis describes the theoretical and practical research into generating, identifying, and controlling quantum entanglement within a light-based system. It delves into two distinct aspects of quantum entanglement, starting with an experimental method for producing and analyzing a light source that generates entangled photons with correlated polarizations. The research then involves evaluating the strength of quantum connections in lower and higher-dimensional systems. The subsequent section focuses on how quantum connections can be disrupted and destroyed in a light-based system subjected to specific forms of interference and explores potential ways to mitigate this phenomenon through local operations. The investigation into entanglement degradation is extended to include higher-dimensional systems.

Galactic gas content is crucial for understanding various galaxy evolution processes including star formation, outflows, accretion, and feedback. Researchers can infer the importance of these processes by examining patterns within the mass-metallicity relationship in galaxy surveys like the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Utilizing a dataset of low-redshift galaxies, we investigated the sources of mass-metallicity relationship scatter and how galaxy mass influences it. Cold gas mass estimates derived from optical emission lines confirm a previously reported relationship where metal content inversely correlates with gas mass at lower stellar masses up to a threshold of 10^10.5 solar masses. Beyond this mass limit, we observed a change in scatter trend where it correlated more strongly with AGN activity rather than gas mass or halo size. This correlation shift is predicted by galaxy evolution simulations that attribute metal content fluctuations to interplay among gas flows, star formation, and feedback effects, ultimately shaping galaxy properties.

In the context of quantum mechanics, a bra-ket formalism is typically used to facilitate representation-free considerations, but it has its own set of limitations and complexities. A major issue with the bra-ket formalism is that it employs a dual-space approach when, in most instances, a one-space description would be preferable due to its more intuitive nature. To address this, a representation-free scheme based on the one-space description has been developed, offering the advantages of both approaches. The one-space scheme is also adaptable to fit the dual-space picture, as this description is still essential for various crucial purposes. Prior to this, the bra-ket formalism's benefits and drawbacks are briefly discussed, highlighting how the proposed scheme remedies the formalism's limitations while maintaining its functionality.

Our investigation into the potential of a strong first-order electroweak phase transition in the context of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, especially given recent findings in dark matter, the Higgs sector, and the LHC's searches for charginos and neutralinos, has indicated that while areas favorable to such an event are increasingly being ruled out by experimental searches, viable regions with complex implications continue to exist that are still resistant to new evidence. Moreover, we have calculated the expected production of stochastic gravitational waves from such an event using different models, as well as assessing the prospects for their detection in upcoming experiments designed to identify these signals.

A synthetic simulation of a tidal flow within an estuary system is achieved using a novel type of Physics-Informed Neural Network.  This model fuses both machine learning techniques and an understanding of real-world systems.  Our approach trains a neural network that optimally minimizes discrepancies in the Navier-Stokes equations for selected input parameters.  Notably, we utilize an innovative framework which assumes a time-varying, periodic flow.  We also analyze the effectiveness of adaptive sampling during training, a low-compute operation previously demonstrated to improve accuracy when batch sizes are limited.  Our paper concludes with an evaluation of its approximations and an assessment of their limitations, including the representation of turbulence in the Navier-Stokes equations and their compatibility with PINNs.

The source of hallucinations and inaccurate results in Natural Language Generation has been linked to mislabeled training data, thus necessitating its identification and elimination. A novel method is proposed to eliminate subpar training data contributing to unwanted output such as unfaithful summaries, where it is demonstrated that existing error tracking approaches, like those reliant on gradients, fail in detecting faithfulness inaccuracies in summaries. A contrast-based method is devised that compares incorrect outputs with corrections by humans and this method is found effective in detecting hallucinations, with it achieving an average precision of 0.91 across tasks with established truth values and an almost two-fold decrease in hallucinations in entity-based tests on the NYT dataset.

We've conducted a comprehensive investigation of the structural, electronic,
mechanical, and superconducting properties of the Zr$_2$Ir compound, possessing a
body-centered tetragonal crystal structure. Our computational analysis has shown
that Zr$_2$Ir exhibits mechanical and dynamical stability both with and without
the influence of spin-orbit coupling (SOC). Our calculation of various material
properties has led us to the conclusion that the compound demonstrates
ductile behavior. When comparing elastic constants $C_{11}$ and $C_{33}$, we
found that the application of SOC reverses their directionality, favoring greater
compressibility along the z-axis rather than the x-axis. Analysis of the
compound's electronic structure revealed metallic properties. Our study also
discovered that the compound exhibits superconducting properties with critical
temperature ($T_c$) and electron-phonon coupling constant ($\lambda$) values
of 7.50 K and 0.93 in the absence of SOC and 7.62 K and 0.96 in its presence,
respectively. These findings indicate that the inclusion of SOC slightly lowers
both the compound's critical temperature and electron-phonon coupling constant,
notwithstanding a relatively strong electron-phonon interaction in its native
state.

In string color models, the transverse momentum distribution (TMD) is obtained through the integration of the Schwinger mechanism with a variable distribution of string tensions, specifically a $q$-Gaussian distribution which accurately captures the key characteristics of the TMD at low and high transverse momentum values. The TMD's hard scale results from a heavy-tailed string tension fluctuation that expands with increased center of mass energy, multiplicity, or centrality. We extend the existing TMD representation in the color string percolation model by determining the color suppression factor, now influenced by the parameters of the $q$-Gaussian distribution. Our analysis incorporates data from various pp and AA collisions under distinct conditions. Notably, we discovered that, for minimum bias pp collisions, the $q$-Gaussian parameters and effective temperature consistently rise with center of mass energy. AA collisions show similar trends as centrality increases at fixed $\sqrt{s}$. We have synthesized this data into a phase diagram indicating the range of $q$-Gaussian parameters favorable for the creation of the quark-gluon plasma.

Quantum systems at the nanoscale can have their microscopic internal movements inferred by using thermodynamic probes. Techniques that measure the entropy of a device by observing electrical flow have been proposed and put into practice in individual-electron devices, with one requirement being that the nanoscale system and its environment remain in a state of equilibrium. However, this is limited, and the experimental conditions are much broader. We introduce an analysis approach using stochastic thermodynamics that works outside equilibrium states, and is applicable to a range of electronic devices where we can use it to determine how much entropy a device contains in its various charge states, and any governing principles in electron movements between the states. We use this non-equilibrium protocol on a device containing single molecules, described by the Hubbard model, where electron movements can be represented in terms of two points.

Multiple Eisenstein series, serving as a unique fusion of classical Eisenstein series and multiple zeta values, are holomorphic in the upper-complex half-plane, and were introduced by Gangl-Kaneko-Zagier in 2006. Since their origin, various versions and regularizations have been extensively studied, connecting the realm of modular forms with multiple zeta values seamlessly. Building on the harmonic algebra framework developed by Hoffman, we establish a new algebraic perspective on stuffle-regularized multiple Eisenstein series, rooted in the underlying Hopf algebra structure.

Reinforcement Learning is a versatile tool for modeling decision-making processes, yet faces the open challenge of finding a suitable balance between exploring new options and leveraging past experience. Our investigation aims to address this challenge through the development of model-free exploration techniques, centered on the idea that for early-stage agents, actions derived from a close proximity of states may result in improved outcomes. Two new algorithms have been proposed, each designed to guide exploration by surveying the neighboring states, and one of them, known as the ${\rho}$-explore approach, consistently yields a superior performance over the Double DQN baseline in a discrete environment by a margin of 49\%, measured in terms of evaluation reward return.

We explore the leftover symmetry within light-cone electromagnetism in four dimensions. By revising the established boundary conditions inherent in the 'lc2' method that encompasses just two physical aspects, we uncover a subset of these residual symmetry transformations. By relaxing these boundary conditions, we determine the total leftover symmetry transformations for the theory. This enables us to pinpoint both true and extreme symmetry variations within light-cone electromagnetism. Additionally, we utilize the Newman-Penrose framework to pinpoint both incoming and outgoing radiated fields. Finally, we discuss the quadratic form structures typically found in Hamiltonians from lc2 gauge theories.

A successful retrieval approach for semantically related sentences using contrastive learning often relies on large batches or careful optimization. In contrast, we suggest a generative model for creating multilingual text representations, applicable to retrieving or scoring sentence pairs. This model processes parallel data across $N$ languages by efficiently separating semantic information shared across translations from stylistic and language-specific variations, leveraging an approximation introduced to improve efficiency. Notably, we conduct comprehensive large-scale evaluations to compare generative and contrastive methods for developing multilingual text embeddings, filling a gap in prior knowledge. The proposed Variational Multilingual Source-Separation Transformer model outperforms both baseline approaches in a suite of evaluations including semantic similarity assessment, bitext extraction, and cross-lingual question answering, the latter introduced in this work.

Our investigation centers around the pattern of arithmetic characteristics connected to Alexander polynomials in specific, limitless sets of links, all derived from a constant number of braids. We investigate the connections with number theory and how class groups disperse in various sets of number fields, thereby opening new paths in the convergence of arithmetic topology and statistics.

In ecology, numerous systems are subject to physical boundaries. The non-negativity requirement is a fundamental constraint affecting variables such as time duration, population counts, and the overall quantity of resources within an ecosystem. We have developed a novel method that involves incorporating these dynamic systems into a state-space model using a moment matching approach, based on lognormal distributions. Our method respects the positivity constraint and accommodates diverse dynamics, offering the flexibility of being described with a precise, closed-form transition density. We have evaluated two prominent lognormal models and our proposed model using extensive synthetic datasets to assess forecasting under incomplete modeling assumptions and the accuracy of parameter estimates. The findings show that our method outperforms its counterparts, especially when accounting for variance inconsistencies and extending prediction intervals. Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the practicality of our method in a difficult application - a process-based ecosystem model - used for predicting leaf area indices. The comparison revealed that our method outshines an existing model, offering superior results and adaptability over a lengthy forecasting period. Overall, our research provides valuable insights for modelers about the importance of designing realistic dynamics when applying complex systems for out-of-sample forecasting purposes.

Individuals living with dementia are prone to exhibiting potentially hazardous behaviours that pose risks not only to themselves, but also to those around them. In the long-term care setting, pre-existing video surveillance systems can be leveraged to monitor these risk-inducing behaviours, alerting staff to take preventative measures in cases where injury or death may occur. Despite this, these risk-inducing behaviours are relatively infrequent compared to typical events. Moreover, processing raw video footage also raises privacy concerns. In our research, we have developed two novel video-based approaches that safeguard personal privacy while identifying potentially hazardous behaviours among individuals with dementia. One method involves extracting the skeletal structure and semantic boundary information to conceal identities, differing from most existing video anomaly detection methods that centre on visual features potentially infringing on individual rights and being vulnerable to pixel-based interference. We employed anonymized normal activity footage to train spatio-temporal convolutional autoencoders, thereby enabling the identification of risk-inducing behaviours as anomalies. In our research, we conducted a study at a real dementia care unit using 21 hours of training data comprising normal activities and approximately 9 hours of data incorporating both normal and risk-inducing behaviours for evaluation purposes. Our methods demonstrated equivalent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve performance when compared to original RGB videos, with scores of 0.807 and 0.823 respectively, representing a groundbreaking investigation in integrating personal privacy for identifying potentially hazardous behaviours among individuals with dementia.

Building upon the research in twisted bilayer graphene under the magic angle condition, a novel lattice mean-field model is introduced to investigate the quantum anomalous Hall effect in a moiré framework.
